### 105. [What are prisms?]

<margin>15</margin> **Prisms** are those solids which, starting from a rectilinear base, connect to a rectilinear surface [at the top] through the joining of rectilinear figures <note>Essentially, a prism has two identical flat ends and flat sides</note>.

### 106. [Which among the figures are neither pyramids nor prisms?]

<margin>20</margin> Those that are neither pyramids nor prisms are solids which, starting from a rectilinear base, meet at a single straight line through the joining of rectilinear figures <note>This describes a "wedge" shape, where the sides slope up to a ridge rather than a single point (pyramid) or a flat top (prism)</note>.

### 107. [Which are the parallel-sided prisms?]

<margin>25</margin> are those that are **hexahedrons** <note>six-sided solids</note> and have their opposite planes parallel to one another.

->HERON<-

### 108. [What are parallelepipeds?]

**Parallel planes** are those which, when extended, do not meet one another, or those in which, if equal triangles are drawn [on each plane], their corresponding sides remain parallel. <note>original: *parallelepipeda*. Heron is defining the boundary surfaces of a solid where opposite faces never intersect.</note>

<margin>5</margin>
### 109. [What is the perpendicular in a solid?]

A **perpendicular** <note>original: *kathetos*</note> in a solid is the name given to a line drawn from a point in space down to a plane, which is at right angles to all the lines touching it within that plane.

### 110. [Which are the right-angled parallel-sided prisms, 
<margin>10</margin>and which are not right-angled?]

Among **parallel-sided prisms**, some are right-angled and others are not. Right-angled prisms are those which have each of their corners <note>original: *gonion*</note> contained by three right-angled plane figures; those that are not constructed this way are not right-angled. <note>original: *parallelo-pleura*. These are prisms where the sides are parallelograms. A "right-angled" version is what we would call a rectangular cuboid.</note>

<margin>15</margin>
### 111. [What is a cube?]

A **cube** <note>original: *kybos*</note> is a specific type of the right-angled parallel-sided shapes mentioned previously. <note>In Heron’s system, a cube is a special case of the rectangular prism where all edges are equal.</note>

### 112. [What is a beam?]

<margin>20</margin>A **beam** <note>original: *dokos*</note> is a solid that has a length greater than its width and its thickness; sometimes the width and thickness are equal. Let **thickness**, **depth**, and **height** be considered the same term. <note>A "beam" is an elongated rectangular prism, similar to a timber joist. Heron clarifies that while we use different words for vertical or horizontal dimensions, they refer to the same mathematical property.</note>

->DEFINITIONS<-

### 108. [What are parallelepipeds?]

**Parallel planes** are those which, when extended, do not meet one another, or those in which, if any equal triangles are drawn, all of their sides are parallel to each other in pairs. <note>Heron is describing the boundary surfaces of a "parallelepiped," a solid where opposite faces are parallel, much like a slanted box.</note>

<margin>5</margin>
### 109. [What is a perpendicular in space?]

A line is called a **perpendicular** in space when it is drawn from a higher point down to a plane such that it forms right angles with all the straight lines in that plane that meet it.

<margin>10</margin>
### 110. [Which are the parallel-sided right-angled prisms, and which are not right-angled?]

Among the **parallel-sided prisms**, some are right-angled and others are not. **Right-angled** ones are those that have each of their angles <note>In this context, the "angle" refers to the solid vertex where three faces meet.</note> enclosed by three right-angled straight lines; those that do not meet this condition are **not right-angled**. <note>A right-angled parallel-sided prism is what we commonly call a rectangular cuboid or a box shape.</note>

<margin>15</margin>
### 111. [What is a cube?]

A **cube** is the specific figure among the right-angled, parallel-sided shapes that was defined previously (in section 100). <note>A cube is a special case of a prism where all sides are equal squares.</note>

<margin>20</margin>
### 112. [What is a beam?]

A **beam** <note>original: *dokos*</note> is a parallel-sided right-angled prism that has a length greater than its width and thickness; sometimes the width and thickness are equal. The terms **thickness**, **depth**, and **height** are intended to mean the same thing.

->HERON'S [DEFINITIONS]<-

### 113. [What is a tile?]

A **tile** <term>plintis: literally a "brick" or "plinth"</term> is a shape that has a length smaller than its width and depth; sometimes these latter two are equal to each other. <note>While a "beam" is elongated like a pillar, a "tile" is flattened like a paving stone.</note>

### 114. [What is a wedge?]

<margin>5</margin>A **wedge** <term>sphēniskos: a "small wedge"</term> is a shape that has length, width, and depth all unequal to one another. Some people also call such a figure a **small altar** <term>bōmiskos: a diminutive of "altar," describing a prism with unequal sides</term>.

### 115. [How many types of contact are there in geometric figures, and between what things?]

<margin>1</margin>A line touches another line, a surface, or a solid at a point or along a line. When a <margin>10</margin> point touches another point, they become one. When a line touches another line along its whole length, they similarly become one. A straight line is said to be **tangent** to a circle when it touches the circle but, even if extended in either direction, does not cut through the circle. Circles are said to be **tangent** to one another <margin>15</margin> when they touch but do not intersect.

<margin>2</margin>A straight line is **perpendicular** to a plane when it forms right angles with all the straight lines in that same plane that touch it.

<margin>3</margin>A plane is **perpendicular** to another plane when the <margin>20</margin> straight lines drawn in one of the planes at right angles to their common intersection are also at right angles to the remaining plane.

<margin>4</margin>**Parallel planes** are those that never meet <note>original: *asymptōta*, meaning "not falling together"</note>.

<margin>15</margin> whole to whole in planes or in solids according to the same convergence, or in part, or by arrangement. Equal circles are those whose diameters are equal to one another; for from the same diameters it is impossible to conceive of one circle and then another. Given the diameter, 
<margin>20</margin> the circle is also given in magnitude. Straight lines are said to be **equally distant** from the center when the perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal; the distance is greater for the line upon which the larger perpendicular falls. Equal solid figures 
<margin>25</margin> are those contained by equal planes that are situated similarly and are equal in both number and magnitude.

# DEFINITIONS

In lines, similarity and equality are distinct. Thus, at any rate, in the 6th book of Euclid’s *Elements* (Proposition 25), the problem is posed: given two rectilinear figures, construct one that is similar to one and equal to the other. <note>original: "VI. Buche des Eukleides (25)". Heron refers to Euclid's method of "application of areas," which allows a geometer to scale a shape's size while keeping its proportions.</note> And there, we solve the task by finding a **mean proportional** <term>mittlere Proportionale: a middle value in a geometric ratio, used here to scale areas</term>; 
<margin>5</margin> however, in the case of solids, this is achieved through **two mean proportionals**. <note>The "Delian problem" or doubling the cube requires two mean proportionals, a feat Heron achieved using a mechanical device known as a "mesolabe."</note>

### 117. [On equal lines.]

Now we speak generally about equal magnitudes, saying that lines, surfaces, and bodies are equal if 
<margin>10</margin> they coincide entirely, either part for part or according to their configuration. Something is also called "equal" both in terms of being **isoperimetric** <term>dem Umfang nach... gleiche: having an equal boundary or perimeter</term>—referring to the enclosure—and in terms of the lines being equal while the surface area is also 
<margin>15</margin> equal, as well as things equal in surface area alone. Equal angles, however, are those that coincide entirely within planes or solids under the same **convergence** <note>German: "Zusammenziehung". This refers to the inclination or meeting of the lines forming the angle.</note>, either part for part or according to their configuration. Equal circles are those whose diameters 
<margin>20</margin> are equal to one another; for upon the same diameters, it is not possible to conceive of different circles, and if the diameter is given, the circle is also given according to its magnitude. Straight lines are said to be **equally distant** from the center when the 
<margin>25</margin> perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal; those upon which a larger perpendicular falls are said to be further away. Equal solid figures, however, are those enclosed by equal and similarly situated planes, equal in number and size.

### 119. [On the infinite in magnitudes.]

**Magnitude** <term>Μέγεθος: any measurable extent</term> is that which can be increased and divided unto infinity; and there are three types: line, surface, and solid. The **infinite** is a magnitude of which nothing greater can be conceived in any <margin>20</margin> substantial size whatsoever, such that it has no limit.

<meta>This page continues Heron’s definitions of geometric terms, moving from the definition of infinite magnitudes to the specific nature of a "part" (meros) and the distinction between homogeneous and non-homogeneous measures. It addresses the classical geometric paradox of the horn-angle and introduces the concept of mathematical multiples and proportions.</meta>

<page-num>76</page-num>
<header>OF HERON</header>

...in the case of a line drawn from the end of the diameter of a circle, we say that the angle formed **outside** the semicircle is a **part** of the right angle. However, it is impossible for the right angle to be measured out by this angle, which is called **horn-like** <term>κερατοειδὴς: the "angle" formed between the curved circumference of a circle and a straight tangent line</term>, <margin>5</margin> since the horn-angle is smaller than every rectilinear angle. <note>original: "πάσης γωνίας εὐθυγράμμου ἐλάττονος οὔσης τῆς κερατοειδοῦς" — Heron is highlighting a famous paradox: because a horn-angle is smaller than any angle made with straight lines, it cannot be used as a unit of measure for them.</note> Therefore, we should rather understand the "part" in magnitudes as applying to things of the **same kind** <term>ὁμοιογενῶν: homogeneous; objects of the same dimension, such as a line measuring a line</term>, and we shall define a "part" in magnitudes in the same way we say an angle of one-third of a right angle is a part of the right angle. <margin>10</margin> For we must set aside that common little sophism which claims: "If a part is that which measures, and the measuring thing is a part, and a solid is measured by a one-foot line, then the one-foot line is a part of the solid," which is absurd. A one-foot line measures the **length** <margin>15</margin> of the solid, and its **depth** and its **width**—which are of the same kind as the line itself—but it does not measure the solid [volume] itself.

-> 121. [On the multiple.] <-

A **multiple** <term>Πολλαπλάσιον</term> is the greater of a lesser magnitude when it is measured by that lesser magnitude.

-> 122. [On proportion according to magnitudes.] <-

<margin>20</margin> Now, what a "part" is, and what a "ratio" is, and what things are "of the same kind" as well as what "proportion" is, has been stated more precisely in the works preceding the *Introduction to Arithmetic*. # DEFINITIONS

...in which the head is a part of a human being; but it is just as little a part in the way that we say—when a perpendicular line is drawn to the diameter of a circle at its endpoint—that the angle taken outside the semicircle is a "part" <margin>5</margin> of the angle formed by the perpendicular. For it is impossible for the right angle to be measured without a remainder by this angle, which is called **horn-shaped** <term>horn-angle (keratoeides): the infinitesimal angle formed between the curved circumference of a circle and a straight tangent line</term>, because the horn-angle is smaller than any rectilinear angle <note>original: "gradlinige Winkel"—angles formed by straight lines. Heron is explaining that because a curved angle is fundamentally different from a straight one, it cannot serve as a unit of measure for it.</note>. We shall therefore instead take the "part" in magnitudes to refer to things of the **same kind** <margin>10</margin> <term>homogeneous: magnitudes of the same dimension, such as a line measuring another line</term> and use the term "part" for magnitudes in the same way we call an angle that is one-third of a right angle a "part" of that right angle. 

For one must set aside that well-known sophistical conclusion <note>original: "sophistischen Schluß"; a "sophism" is a clever but false argument used to deceive</note> which goes: "If a part is that which measures, then that which measures is also a <margin>15</margin> part; now, a solid body is measured by a one-foot straight line; therefore, the one-foot straight line is a part of the body"—which is absurd. For the one-foot straight line measures the **length**, **depth**, and **width** of the body, which are of the same kind as the straight line itself, <margin>20</margin> but it by no means measures the body <note>meaning the 3D volume</note> itself.

### 121. [On the Multiple.]

A **multiple** is the larger of a smaller magnitude when it is measured exactly by that smaller one.

### 123. [What kind of ratio do magnitudes have toward one another?]

Magnitudes are said to have a **ratio** <term>logos: the relationship between two magnitudes of the same kind in terms of size</term> to one another, which <margin>5</margin> are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another <note>This is the famous "Archimedean Axiom" (though found in Euclid): for a ratio to exist, you must be able to add a magnitude to itself enough times until it becomes larger than the other.</note>. But against those who oppose this definition and say that only those things have a ratio which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another—and that nothing is as "same-kinded" <term>homogeneous: of the same nature or dimension</term> as a point is to another point, it would therefore be clear (according to them) that a <margin>10</margin> multiplied point will exceed another point—to these people it must be said that a point does not admit of multiplication *in terms of magnitude*. For that which lacks magnitude also lacks the ability to be multiplied in magnitude; it will only admit multiplication <margin>15</margin> **numerically**. Thus, since there are infinite points in a line, such-and-such a number of points are multiples of another number of points. In general, they speak as if the point has some extension, whereas the **Author of the Elements** <term>Stoicheiotes: Euclid, the author of the "Elements" of geometry</term> expressly defined the point as **indivisible** <note>original: "amerēs"—literally "without parts" or "dimensionless"</note>, and stated that ratio <margin>20</margin> applies to magnitudes.

### 124. [What magnitudes are in the same ratio?]

Magnitudes are said to be in the **same ratio**—the first to the second and the third to the fourth—when the equal multiples of the first and the third, [taken together], are compared to the equal multiples of the second and fourth... <margin>25</margin>

# DEFINITIONS

...generally among things of the same kind, so it is also applicable to those which are of the same kind among magnitudes.

### 123. [What relationship do magnitudes have to one another?]

It is said that magnitudes have a **ratio** <term>logos: the relationship between two magnitudes of the same kind in terms of their size</term> to one another, <margin>5</margin> which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another <note>This is the "Archimedean property." To have a ratio, a smaller length must be able to "catch up" to a larger length if you add it to itself enough times. A point can never "catch up" to a line, so they have no ratio.</note>. However, to those who oppose this definition and say: those things which have a ratio among themselves are simply things that can exceed each other when multiplied; but nothing is so "of the same kind" <term>homogeneous: of the same nature</term> as a point is to another point; therefore, <margin>10</margin> it is clear that a point, when multiplied, will exceed another point—to these people, one must reply that a point does not allow for an increase in size through multiplication. For that which does not participate in magnitude <term>megethos: physical size or extension</term> likewise does not participate in the multiplication of magnitude, but will only allow for <margin>15</margin> multiplication in **number**. Thus, since a straight line has infinitely many points, a certain number of points is a multiple of another certain number. In general, these critics speak of the point as if it were a magnitude having a certain extension, even though Euclid in the *Elements* (Book I, Definition 1) <margin>20</margin> explicitly defined the point as indivisible and stated (Book V, Definition 4) that it is **magnitudes** which have a ratio among themselves.

### 124. [Which magnitudes are those that stand in the same ratio?]

Magnitudes are said to be in the same **ratio** <margin>1</margin> <note>This is the definition of proportionality, the core of ancient Greek geometry.</note>—the <margin>25</margin> first to the second and the third to the fourth—whenever equal multiples of the first and the third are simultaneously either greater than, equal to, or less than any other multiples [of the second and fourth]...

For just as the boundary <term>horos: boundary, limit, or term</term> of a circle is its circumference and the boundaries of triangles are their sides, so the boundaries of the ratio of 9 to 6 are those very numbers. <note>original: "ὅροι" (horoi). ### 125. [*Various proportions of magnitudes.*]

<margin>10 1</margin> When three magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have a **duplicate ratio** <term>diplasios logos: in modern terms, the ratio of the first to the third is the square of the ratio of the first to the second</term> to the third compared to its ratio to the second. For example, Eratosthenes says that just as with equal distances laid out on a straight line the total distance is doubled, <margin>15</margin> so it is with ratios: when they are laid out, as it were, in a straight line, the first has a duplicate ratio to the third compared to its ratio to the second. For 9 is a **hemiolian** <term>hemiolios: a ratio of 1.5, or 3-to-2</term> of 6, and 6 is the same hemiolian of 4; therefore, 9 is "two hemiolians" away from 4. For indeed, the two <margin>20</margin> differences are equal to the single difference between the ends, as in the case of 9, 6, and 4. For 9 exceeds 6 by three, and 6 exceeds 4 by two; and the three and the two added together make five, which is the difference <note>original: "ὑπεροχή" (hyperochē) — the amount by which one thing exceeds another.</note> between 9 and 4. Just as when moving from larger magnitudes to <margin>25</margin> smaller ones these differences create duplicate and triplicate ratios, so too from smaller magnitudes do the "deficiencies" <note>original: "ἐλλείψεις" (elleipseis). Heron is noting that the logic of ratios works the same way whether you are looking at how much larger the first term is or how much smaller the last term is.</note>.

### 125. [Various Ratios of Magnitudes]

But just as the excesses form duplicate and triplicate ratios when moving from the larger numbers to the smaller, so do the deficits when moving from the smaller to the larger.

<meta>This page continues Heron’s commentary on Euclid’s Elements, Book V. Having previously discussed "greater ratios," Heron now moves into the formal definitions of ratio manipulations (composition, separation, alternation) and the fundamental concepts of commensurability that bridge geometry and number theory.</meta>

->OF HERON<-

**Composition of a ratio** is the taking of the antecedent <note>the 'leading' or first term in a ratio, such as the 4 in 4:2</note> together with the consequent <note>the 'following' or second term, such as the 2 in 4:2</note> in relation to the consequent itself. <note>In modern notation, if we have a ratio $a:b$, the "composed" ratio is $(a+b):b$.</note>

**Separation of a ratio** is the taking of the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent, in relation to the consequent. <note>Commonly known as *dividendo*; if the ratio is $a:b$, the separated ratio is $(a-b):b$.</note>

<margin>5</margin> **Conversion of a ratio** is the taking of the antecedent in relation to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent. <note>Modern: $a:(a-b)$.</note>

**Alternation of a ratio** is the ratio of the antecedent to the antecedent and of the consequent to the consequent. <note>If $a:b = c:d$, then $a:c = b:d$.</note>

<margin>10</margin> **Ratio by equality** <term>di' isou: literally 'through equality'</term> occurs in an ordered proportion when, as an antecedent is to a consequent, so another antecedent is to another consequent, and furthermore, as the consequent is to something else, so the other consequent is to something else; it is the taking, in both cases, of the antecedent in relation to the final term—that is, when the <margin>15</margin> intermediate terms have been removed in an alternating fashion. <note>This explains how to compare the first and last terms in a chain of ratios, e.g., if $a:b = d:e$ and $b:c = e:f$, then $a:c = d:f$.</note>

### 128. [On commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes.]

Which things are **irrational** <term>alogoi: literally 'without speech' or 'without ratio'</term> and **incommensurable**, and which are **rational** <term>rhētoi: expressible</term> and **commensurable**, has been discussed in the works preceding the *Arithmetical Introduction*; but now, following Euclid the author of the *Elements*, regarding <margin>20</margin> magnitudes, we say that **commensurable magnitudes** <term>symmetra megethē: magnitudes measured by a common measure</term> are those measured by the same measures, while **incommensurable magnitudes** are those for which no common measure is possible.

   **Separation of a ratio** <note>original: 'Subtrahiertes Verhältnis'; traditionally called *dividendo*</note> is the taking of the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent, 
<margin>5</margin> in relation to the consequent.
   **Conversion of a ratio** <note>original: 'Umgewendetes Verhältnis'; traditionally called *convertendo*</note> is the taking of the antecedent in relation to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent.
   **Alternation of a ratio** <note>original: 'Umgetauschtes Verhältnis'; traditionally called *alternando*</note> is that of the antecedent to the 
<margin>10</margin> antecedent and of the consequent to the consequent.
   **Ratio by equality** <term>di' isou: literally 'through equality'</term> occurs in an ordered proportion when, as an antecedent is to a consequent, so another antecedent is to another consequent, and at the same time, as the [first] consequent is to something else, so the [second] consequent is to something else; it is the taking on 
<margin>15</margin> both sides of the [initial] antecedent in relation to the [final] something else—that is, by removing the intermediate cross-terms.

128. [On commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes.]

   Which magnitudes are irrational and incommensurable, and which are rational and commensurable, has been stated in the introduction 
<margin>20</margin> to the Elements of Arithmetic; but here we say, following the Elements of Euclid (Book X, Definition 1), regarding magnitudes: that those are called **commensurable** which are measured by the same measures, while **incommensurable** are those for which a common 
<margin>25</margin> measure cannot exist.

->Straight Lines.<-]

   Straight lines are commensurable only in power <note>original: 'in Potenz'; meaning their squares are commensurable even if their lengths are not</note> when the...

# HERON'S WORKS

In brief, each unit is arranged as follows, as previously stated, according to the current standards of geometry—that is, for the purposes of tax registration <note>original: *kinsos*; referring to the Roman census or land survey for taxation</note>.

After the **finger** <term>original: *daktylos*; the smallest unit, approximately the width of a finger or an inch</term>, which is the smallest part of 
<margin>5</margin> all, there is the **palm** <term>original: *palaistēs*; also called a "hand-breadth"</term>, which some also call a "fourth" because it contains 4 fingers. After this is the **span** <term>original: *spithamē*</term> of 3 palms. Then, in summary, the **foot** <term>original: *pous*</term> contains 4 palms. Then the **cubit** <term>original: *pēchys*</term> contains 2 feet or 8 palms. A **step** <term>original: *bēma*</term> is equal to a cubit. A **fathom** <term>original: *orgyia*; the distance of a man's outstretched arms</term> has 4 1/2 feet <note>Greek L' signifies 1/2</note> or 18 palms. 
<margin>10</margin> The **akaina** <term>a ten-foot measuring rod</term> has 12 feet or 48 palms. The **vine-pole** <term>original: *ampelos*; a unit for vineyard measurement</term> has 5 feet or 20 palms. The **pace** <term>original: *passus*</term> has 6 feet or 24 palms. The **plethron** <term>a standard unit of Greek land measurement</term> has 1,200 feet or 4,800 palms. The **iugerum** <term>a Roman unit of land area, roughly 0.6 acres</term> has 2,400 feet or 9,600 palms. The **stadium** has 600 feet or 2,400 palms. The **mile** has 4,500 feet.

<margin>15</margin> ### 132. [Linear, Area, and Volume Measurements]

The **linear palm** <term>original: *euthymetrikos*; one-dimensional length</term> contains 4 fingers. The **square palm** <term>original: *epipedos*; two-dimensional area</term> contains 16 fingers. The **cubic palm** <term>original: *stereos*; three-dimensional volume</term> contains 64 fingers.

The **linear foot** contains 4 palms or 16 fingers. The **square foot** 
<margin>20</margin> contains 16 palms or 256 fingers. The **cubic foot** contains 64 palms or 4,096 fingers.

The **linear cubit** contains 2 feet, 8 palms, or 32 fingers. The **square cubit** contains 4 feet, 64 palms, or 1,024 fingers. The **cubic cubit** 
<margin>25</margin> contains 8 feet, 512 palms, or 32,768 fingers.

-># DEFINITIONS<-

In brief, however, each unit relates as follows, as previously stated, according to the current standards of land surveying—that is, the land registry <note>original: *kataster*; referring to the official list of land for tax purposes, often associated with the Roman *census*</note>:
Following the **finger** <term>original: *daktylos*; the smallest unit, roughly the width of a finger</term>, which is the smallest part of all, is the **palm** <term>original: *palaistēs*</term>, which some also call a "fourth,"
<margin>5</margin> because it contains 4 fingers (that is, 1/4 of a foot). Next is the **span** <term>original: *spithamē*</term> = 3 palms; then the primary unit, the **foot** <term>original: *pous*</term> = 4 palms; then the **cubit** <term>original: *pēchys*</term> = 2 feet = 8 palms; the **step** <term>original: *bēma*</term> = 1 cubit; the **fathom** <term>original: *orgyia*</term> = 4 1/2 feet = 18 palms; the **akaina** <term>a measuring rod</term> = 12 feet = 48 palms; the **am-**

<margin>15</margin> ### 132. [Linear, Surface, and Cubic Measures.]

A **palm**, as a linear measure, is 4 fingers; as a surface measure <note>i.e., a square palm</note>, it is 16 fingers; but as a cubic measure, it is 64 fingers.
A **foot**, as a linear measure, is 4 palms or 16 fingers; as a surface measure, however, it is 16 palms or 256 fingers; the
<margin>20</margin> **cubic foot**, however, is 64 palms or 4,096 fingers.
A **cubit**, as a linear measure, is 2 feet, 8 palms, or 32 fingers; as a surface measure, however, it is 4 feet <note>meaning 4 square feet</note>, 64 palms, or 1,024 fingers; but the **cubic cubit** is 8 feet <note>meaning 8 cubic feet</note>, 512 palms, or 32,768 fingers.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of units of measurement used in land surveying (the land registry). It transitions from the definition of linear units to the classification of geometric shapes and the foundational principles of plane and solid geometry as established by Heron of Alexandria.</meta>

<page-num>92</page-num>
->### HERO<-

<margin>133, 1</margin> These are the various types of measurement: **squares**, **triangles**, **rhombi**, **trapezoids**, and **circles**. They possess eighteen theorems, categorized as follows:

There are 2 theorems for **squares**:
1. The equilateral rectangle <term>original: *tetragōnon isopleuron orthogōnion*; what we simply call a square</term>.
2. The parallelogram rectangle <term>original: *tetragōnon parallēlogrammon orthogōnion*; what we call a rectangle</term>.

<margin>5</margin> There are 6 theorems for **triangles**:
1. The equilateral triangle.
2. The isosceles triangle.
3. The scalene triangle.
4. The right-angled triangle.
5. The acute-angled triangle.
6. The obtuse-angled triangle.

There are 2 theorems for the **rhombus**:
1. The rhombus.
2. The rhomboid <term>a shape where opposite sides and angles are equal, but it is neither equilateral nor right-angled</term>.

There are 4 theorems for **trapezoids**:
<margin>10</margin> 1. The right-angled trapezoid.
2. The isosceles trapezoid.
3. The acute-angled trapezoid.
4. The obtuse-angled trapezoid.

There are 4 theorems for **circles**:
1. The circle.
2. The arch, also known as the semicircle.
3. The segment larger than a semicircle.
4. The segment smaller than a semicircle.

# DEFINITIONS

The forms of measurement are the following: squares, <margin>1</margin> 133, 1 triangles, rhombi, trapezoids, and circles. They comprise 18 theorems as follows: 2 theorems for squares—the equilateral rectangle <note>a square</note> and the parallel-sided rectangle; 6 theorems for triangles—the equilateral triangle, the isosceles <margin>5</margin> triangle, the scalene triangle, the right-angled triangle, the acute-angled triangle, and the obtuse-angled triangle; 2 theorems for the rhombus—the rhombus and the rhomboid; 4 theorems for <margin>10</margin> trapezoids—the right-angled trapezoid, the isosceles trapezoid, the acute-angled trapezoid, and the obtuse-angled trapezoid; 4 theorems for circles—the circle, the arch or semicircle, the segment larger than a semicircle, and the segment smaller than a semicircle.

<margin>2</margin> These are the forms and theorems as far as they pertain to <margin>15</margin> surface measurements; however, for solid bodies, thickness is added to every measurement, and ten specific theorems for solids result as follows: sphere, cone, obelisk <note>original: *obeliskos*; a tapered pillar</note>, cylinder, cube, wedge, <margin>20</margin> meiuros <term>original: *meiuros*; literally "mousetail," referring to a truncated cone or pyramid</term>, column, plinthis <term>original: *plinthis*; a brick or tile-shaped solid</term>, and pyramid.

<margin>3</margin> There are also the following established norms for measurement: In every triangle, the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining side; and in every right-angled triangle, the squares of the two sides enclosing the right <margin>25</margin> angle are equal to the square of the hypotenuse; and in every circle, the circumference is 3 1/7 times as large as the diameter; and in surface measure, the diameter multiplied by the circumference is equal to the area of 4 circles <note>This ancient formula relates the total surface area of a sphere to four times the area of its great circle.</note>.

<page-num>96</page-num>
<header>OF HERO</header>

<margin>135</margin>
### Definition of geometry.

<margin>1</margin>
Geometry is the science of magnitudes and shapes, and of the surfaces and lines that bound and limit them, as well as the properties <note>original: *pathōn*; here referring to the characteristics or attributes that "happen" to shapes</note>, relationships, and operations occurring within these forms, and the qualities of their motion. <margin>5</margin> Properties, then, refer to things concerning divisions; relationships refer to the ratios and positions of magnitudes relative to one another, which they present to us both individually and when compared to each other.

<margin>2</margin>
### That magnitude in bodies is continuous. <margin>10</margin>

Things are continuous <note>original: *synechē*</note> when they are uniform throughout and where the process of cutting or dividing them can proceed to infinity; examples include a body, place, time, motion, surface, and line. For every part of a body is itself a body, and because of this, there is no such thing as a "smallest" body. Since every body has three dimensions—length, width, <margin>15</margin> and depth <note>original: *mēkos, platos, bathos*</note>—and since every part of a body occupies a place, there is also no "smallest" place; for every place has physical dimensions equal to the body within it. Similarly, every part of time is also time. And there are other continuous things: a line is continuous because one can find a common boundary <margin>20</margin> where its parts join, which is a point <note>original: *stigmēn*</note>; a surface is continuous because the parts of the plane join at a common boundary, which is a line. The same principle applies to the solid body.

<margin>3</margin>
### On certain principles of geometry.

<margin>25</margin>
Some say that the principles of geometry are the dimensions of the mathematical body; there are three: length,

<header>DEFINITIONS. 97</header>

### Definition of Geometry. <margin>135</margin>

<margin>1</margin> Geometry is the science of magnitudes <note>original: *megethōn*; referring to sizes or quantities that have extension</note> and figures, and of the surfaces and lines that enclose and bound them, as well as their treatment, their relationships, and <margin>5</margin> their operations <note>original: *energeiōn*; referring to the active application or functioning of these forms</note> in terms of the shapes and qualities of motion. "Treatment" refers to that which concerns divisions, while "relationships" refers to the ratios and positions of magnitudes to one another, whether we consider them in isolation or compare them with one another.

<margin>10</margin> ### What continuous magnitude in bodies is. <margin>2</margin>

That which is continuous is uniform throughout and can be divided into infinity, such as a body, space, time, motion, surface, or line. For every part of a body is itself a body, and there is therefore no such thing as a "smallest" <margin>15</margin> body. And since every body has three dimensions—length, breadth, and depth—and since the place where every part exists (or from which it was removed) is a space, there is also no "smallest" space; for every space has the same physical dimensions as a body. Similarly, every part of time is time. And there are <margin>20</margin> also other continuous magnitudes, such as a line, because one can establish a common boundary which its parts approach—namely, the point—and a surface, because the parts of a plane approach a common boundary—namely, the line. And the same applies to the body.

<margin>4</margin>
### What is the goal of geometry?

The goal of this science is very similar to that of arithmetic, except that it seeks to understand the properties that occur in **continuous substance** rather than in **discrete substance** <note>original: *diōrismenē*; discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted individually, like numbers, whereas continuous quantity refers to things like lines or surfaces</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
### Concerning logistics.

Logistics <note>original: *logistikē*; in the ancient world, this was the practical art of calculation used in commerce and engineering, distinct from theoretical arithmetic</note> is the theory that deals with **numbered things**, rather than **numbers** themselves. It does not take "number" in its true, abstract sense, but assumes that "one" is a unit and "the thing being numbered" is a number—for example, treating three things as a "triad" and ten things as a "decad." Upon these objects, it applies the theorems of theoretical arithmetic. Therefore, it investigates what Archimedes called the **Cattle Problem** <note>original: *boïkon problēma*; a famous and complex mathematical puzzle involving the calculation of the sizes of herds of the Sun God's cattle</note>, as well as "apple numbers" and "bowl numbers"—the former referring to a flock or herd, and the latter to contents of a bowl. It examines the quantities of other types of **perceivable bodies**, declaring any further abstraction to be unnecessary.

<margin>6</margin>
### What is the subject matter of logistics?

It has already been said that it is all things that are counted. Since "the one" <note>original: *to hen*</note> is the smallest part within physical matter—just as the **unit** <note>original: *monas*</note> is in theoretical arithmetic—logistics makes use of "the one" as the smallest of the things belonging to the same group. ### What is the goal of geometry?

Its goal corresponds to that of arithmetic, except that it seeks to understand properties not in **discrete matter** <note>things that can be counted individually, like pebbles</note>, but in **continuous matter** <note>things that are unbroken, like a line or a solid block</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
### On the art of calculation.

The art of calculation <note>original: *logistikē*; referring to practical, applied mathematics rather than theoretical number theory</note> is a study that treats **countable things**, not the numbers themselves. It does not seek the number in its abstract essence, but instead takes the "one" as a unit and the "countable thing" as a number—for example, treating 3 as a **triad** and 10 as a **decad**. Upon these objects, it then demonstrates the theorems that correspond to arithmetic. First, it treats what Archimedes called the **Cattle Problem** <note>a famous, extremely difficult mathematical puzzle involving the calculation of vast herds of cattle</note>; second, it treats **sheep-numbers** and **bowl-numbers**, investigating the former in a flock and the latter in a vessel, as well as the quantities of physical bodies in other forms, which requires no further explanation.

<header>OF HERON</header>

...treating a human being within a crowd of humans as indivisible <note>original: *adiaireton*</note>, though not just once; and treating a single drachma <note>a Greek silver coin</note> among many drachmae as an "atom" <note>original: *atomon*; meaning an indivisible unit in this context</note>, even if it can be divided as a currency.

<margin>7</margin> Geodesy <note>original: *Geōdaisia*; the practical science of surveying and measuring land</note> is the science of the magnitudes and shapes found in perceptible bodies, capable of both dividing and combining them.

<margin>8</margin> ### What is the subject matter of geodesy?

It takes shapes that are neither perfect nor exact because they are based on physical matter, just as the art of calculation does. For instance, it measures a heap of grain as a cone, circular wells as cylindrical shapes, and tapered shapes <note>original: *meioura*, literally "mousetails"; used to describe truncated cones or figures that narrow toward the top</note> as truncated cones. Just as geometry makes use of arithmetic, so geodesy makes use of the art of calculation.

It employs various instruments for surveying lands: dioptras <note>an ancient sighting instrument used for measuring angles and leveling</note>, rods, plumb-lines, gnomons <note>upright markers used to cast shadows for measurement</note>, and similar tools for the measurement of distances and heights. This is done sometimes by observing shadows, sometimes by sightings through the dioptra, and at other times the desired measurement is hunted down through reflection.

Just as the geometer handles conceptual straight lines in many instances, the geodesist <note>land-measurer</note> makes use of perceptible lines. Of these lines, the more accurate are those established through the rays of the sun, or through sights or alignments. The more physical lines, however, are established through the tension and pulling of cords or a plumb-line. By using these, the geodesist measures lands from a distance, observing the elevation of grounds, the height of walls, and the width and depth of rivers, and—

<margin>13</margin> ## What is Scenography?

The scenographic <term>Scenography|the branch of optics dealing with the representation of three-dimensional objects on a flat surface; the precursor to modern perspective</term> part of optics investigates how <margin>15</margin> one ought to draw the images of buildings. Since things do not appear as they truly are, scenographers consider how they might not showcase the actual underlying proportions, but rather produce them as they will *appear* to the eye. Indeed, the goal for the architect is <margin>20</margin> to make the work well-proportioned according to the imagination <note>meaning the visual perception of the viewer</note> and, as far as possible, to discover remedies against the deceptions of sight—not aiming for the truth of equality or proportion, but for what is perceived by the eye. For instance, since a cylindrical column <margin>25</margin> would appear to the sight to be "broken" or distorted in the middle by narrowing, the architect makes it wider at those points <note>this refers to 'entasis', the slight convex curve in the shaft of a column to prevent the optical illusion of concavity</note>; and sometimes he does not draw a circle as a circle, but...

### The Origins of Geometry
Geometry was first discovered among the Egyptians, <margin>10</margin> and Thales brought it to the Greeks. After Thales came Mamertios, the brother of the poet Stesichorus, and Hippias of Elis; and after these, Pythagoras, who examined its principles from a higher perspective <margin>15</margin> and investigated the theorems in an immaterial and intellectual way <note>A reference to how Pythagoras shifted geometry from practical land-surveying to an abstract, philosophical science.</note>. After him came Anaxagoras and Plato, and Oenopides of Chios, and Theodoros of Cyrene, and Hippocrates (who lived before Plato). Following these were Leodamas of Thasos, Archytas of Tarentum, Theaetetus of Athens, and Eudoxus of Cnidus, who added three more proportions to the existing three; <margin>20</margin> and many others. Not much younger than these is Euclid, who collected the *Elements*. He lived during the time of the first Ptolemy; he was younger than Plato but older than Eratosthenes and Archimedes, for they were contemporaries of one another. <margin>25</margin>

### The History of Geometry
Geometry was originally invented by the Egyptians, but Thales brought it to the Greeks. Following Thales was Mamertios, brother of the poet Stesichorus, and Hippias of Elis, and then Pythagoras, <margin>15</margin> who traced back its foundations and investigated the theorems abstractly <note>original: "stofflos," literally without material/substance</note> and with pure thought; and after him Anaxagoras and Plato and Oenopides of Chios and Theodoros of Cyrene and Hippocrates (who lived before Plato). # HERON'S WORKS

<margin>2 CFHN</margin> We say that the name of "mathematics" and "mathematical sciences" was given to these disciplines because all so-called "learning" <note>original: "mathesis"</note> is actually a recollection <note>original: "anamnesis," the Platonic theory that the soul remembers truths it knew before birth</note>. It is not something implanted into the soul from the outside, in the way that images <margin>5</margin> from the senses are imprinted upon the imagination. Nor is it an incidental occurrence, like the knowledge gained through mere opinion. Rather, it is awakened from the things we see, but it is brought forth from within by the mind <note>original: "dianoia," referring to discursive or mathematical reasoning</note> itself, as it turns back into itself according to its own form. The mind has already grasped the sciences within itself, and even if it <margin>10</margin> is not actively working with them, it possesses them all essentially and in secret. Each science reveals itself when the obstacles of the senses are removed. For while the senses bind the soul to divisible, material things, and the imagination traps it in shifting shapes, and our desires pull it toward <margin>15</margin> a life of passion, everything that is divisible and material acts as an obstacle to our turning back toward ourselves.

<margin>3</margin> Aristotle says somewhere: those who hold the knowledge of mathematics in contempt have never tasted the pleasures found within them. Plato, on the other hand, clearly states that mathematics is a means of purifying the soul and leading it upward to higher truths. <margin>20</margin>

<margin>4</margin> The various forms of mathematics fall short of the nature of the "indivisible" <note>the realm of pure, unchanging Intellect</note> but are situated far above "divisible" nature <note>the realm of physical matter</note>. They are secondary to the pure Mind <note>original: "nous"</note>, yet they are more perfect, more accurate, and purer than mere opinion.

---

# DEFINITIONS

We say that the name Mathematics and *Mathemata* <note>Greek: "things learned" or "lessons"</note> <margin>2</margin> was given to these sciences because all so-called learning is actually recollection <note>German: *Erinnerung*; Greek: *anamnesis*, the Platonic theory that learning is recovering knowledge the soul possessed before birth</note>. This is because knowledge is not placed into the soul from the outside—in the way that images <margin>5</margin> arising from sensible objects are formed in our imagination—nor is it external like knowledge based merely on opinion. Rather, while it is provoked by outward appearances, it is generated from within by the soul itself as the reasoning faculty <note>German: *Denkvermögen*; Greek: *to dianoetikon*</note> returns to its own essence. <margin>10</margin> This faculty contains the concepts of these sciences within itself in advance; even if it is not actively working with them, it possesses them all essentially and in a hidden state. Each concept comes to light <note>The translator has corrected the Greek text here from "appearing" to "comes to light" based on Proclus</note> as soon as the obstacles residing in our sensory impressions are removed. For the senses <margin>15</margin> link the soul <note>Greek: *he psyche*</note> to that which is divisible <note>Material objects that can be broken down</note>, while our imaginations link it to the movements of form, and our impulses pull it toward a life of passion. Everything divisible, however, is an obstacle to our return into ourselves.

Aristotle says somewhere: all those who despise the knowledge of <margin>3</margin> <margin>20</margin> mathematics have never tasted its joys; and Plato says that mathematics is clearly purifying and uplifting for the soul.

The mathematical concepts fall short of the indivisible <margin>4</margin> essence, but they stand above that which is divisible; they <margin>25</margin> are lesser than pure thought, but more perfect, more exact, and purer than mere opinion.

# OF HERO

<margin>5</margin> For the unification and differentiation of all things, the Creator <note>Greek: *demiourgos*; the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</note> has employed Identity <note>Greek: *tautotes*</note> along with Alterity <note>Greek: *heterotes*; also translated as "Difference"</note> for the completion of the soul, and in addition to these, Rest <note>Greek: *stasis*</note> and Motion; it is from these primary kinds that He constituted the soul's essence.
<margin>5</margin> It must be stated that, according to the soul's **Alterity** and the division of its rational principles <note>Greek: *logoi*</note> and its multiplicity, the intellect <note>Greek: *dianoia*</note>—having stood still and understood itself as being both one and many—projects numbers and the knowledge of these, which is **Arithmetic**.
But according to the **Unification** of this multiplicity and the fellowship and bond the soul has with itself, it projects **Music**; since the soul is first divided by the Creator's hand, and then in this way is bound together by these rational principles.
<margin>10</margin> And again, according to the **Rest** <note>Also "Stability"</note> within herself, having established her internal activity, she revealed **Geometry** from within herself; but according to **Motion**, she revealed **Spherics** <note>The study of the motion of the celestial spheres; Astronomy</note>.

<margin>6</margin> <margin>15</margin> According to Aristotle, an **Axiom** <note>Greek: *axioma*; a self-evident truth</note> occurs when the starting point taken is both familiar to the learner and credible in itself, such as: "things equal to the same thing are also equal to each other."
But when the listener does not possess a self-evident conception of what is being said, yet is nonetheless persuaded and grants it to the one making the argument, such a thing is a **Hypothesis** <note>Greek: *hypothesis*; a premise taken for the sake of argument</note>.
<margin>20</margin> For while a person does not inherently know that a circle is a specific type of figure without being taught, upon hearing the description, they grant it without requiring a proof.

<margin>7</margin> Every **reduction to the impossible** <note>Greek: *apagoge eis to adynaton*; a logical proof where one proves a statement by showing its opposite leads to a contradiction</note> takes that which is in conflict with the object of inquiry and, having hypothesized this pre-

# DEFINITIONS. 113

<margin>5</margin> For the unification and separation of the whole, the **Demiurge** <note>Greek: *demiourgos*; the divine "craftsman" or creator of the universe in Platonic thought</note> has employed **Identity** and **Heterogeneity** <note>Also known as "Difference" or "the Other"</note> to complete the soul, and additionally **Rest** and **Movement**; from these constituent parts, He created it.
<margin>5</margin> It must be said that the faculty of thought—by virtue of its heterogeneity, the separation of concepts, and multiplicity—pauses and reflects that it is both one and many; in this way, it generates numbers and the knowledge of them, which is **Arithmetic**. 
By virtue of the unification of multiplicity, however, and the internal coherence and connection, it generates **Music**<gloss>Therefore, Arithmetic precedes Music. See Proclus p. 36, 24.</gloss>, since the soul is first divided during the activity of the Demiurge, and then subsequently bound together through these concepts. Furthermore, 
<margin>10</margin> by virtue of the **Rest** inherent within it, the soul has caused **Geometry** to emerge by fixing its energy; 
<margin>15</margin> whereas by virtue of **Movement**, it has produced **Spherics** <note>The study of the motion of the celestial spheres; essentially Astronomy</note>.

<margin>6</margin> According to Aristotle, an **Axiom** is when that which is taken as a foundation is intelligible to the learner and is believable in itself; for example, that things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other. But if the listener does 
<margin>20</margin> not have a self-evident internal conception of what is said, yet nonetheless allows himself to be persuaded and yields to the person making the postulate, then this is a **Hypothesis**. For the listener has not understood from the 
<margin>25</margin> outset, without instruction and by virtue of a general concept, that a circle is a figure of such and such a nature; however, once he has heard it, he admits it without proof.

# HERO’S DEFINITIONS. 114

...they are, until the argument reaches a recognized absurdity <note>Greek: *atopon*; literally "out of place," used in logic to mean an impossible or contradictory conclusion</note>, and through that, by overturning the hypothesis, it confirms the original goal of the inquiry. For in general, one must know that all mathematical proofs are either from the first principles or toward the first principles, as **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on logic and Euclid's Elements</note> also says somewhere.

<margin>5</margin> Those proofs which proceed *from* first principles are themselves of two kinds: for they either set out from **common notions** <note>Also known as axioms—truths so obvious they require no proof, such as "the whole is greater than the part"</note> and from self-evident clarity alone, or from things previously demonstrated. 

Those proofs which proceed *toward* the first principles are either constructive of those principles or destructive of them.

<margin>10</margin> Those that are constructive of principles are called **analyses**, and **syntheses** are opposed to these; for it is possible to proceed in an orderly fashion from those principles to the object of inquiry, and this is synthesis. 

But those proofs that are destructive [of a hypothesis] are called **reductions to the impossible** <note>original: *eis adynaton apagogai*; commonly known by the Latin term *reductio ad absurdum*</note>. For the task of this approach is to overturn something that is already agreed upon and self-evident.

<margin>15</margin> And in this case too, there is a kind of syllogism, but not the same as in analysis; for in reductions to the impossible, the logical construction follows the **second type of hypothetical syllogisms** <note>Specifically *Modus Tollens*: If P, then Q; but not Q; therefore, not P</note>, for example:

<margin>20</margin> "If, in triangles having equal angles, the sides **subtending** <note>To "subtend" an angle means to be the side opposite that angle</note> the equal angles are not equal, then the whole is equal to the part. But this is impossible. Therefore, in triangles having two equal angles, the sides subtending the equal angles are themselves equal."

<margin>8</margin> <margin>25</margin> It must be known that the space around a single point is divided into four right angles <note>i.e., 360 degrees</note>, and only these three [regular] polygons are able to fill the entire space around a single point... <note>This refers to the geometric fact that only equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons can tile a flat surface without leaving gaps.</note>

...upward and continues in this way until it encounters a recognized absurdity <note>Greek: *atopon*; a contradiction that violates a known truth</note> and, by thereby overturning the assumption, confirms the original object of the search. # HERON
### [THE PHILOSOPHY OF ANGLES]

...infinitude <note>original: *apeiria*</note>; for what equality is in quantities, this similarity is in qualities.

<margin>11</margin> Since rectilinear angles are established according to both **limit** and **infinitude**, the principle proceeding from **limit** produced the **right angle** <note>original: *orthē gōnia*; literally "upright angle."</note>—a single form governed always by equality, admitting neither increase nor decrease. However, the principle proceeding from **infinitude**, being secondary and dyadic <note>A Pythagorean term meaning "two-fold" or "dual," representing the source of diversity and change.</note>, revealed two types of angles surrounding the right angle. These are divided by inequality into the "greater" and "lesser," and they possess a movement without limit toward the "more" or "less"—the one becoming more or less **obtuse**, the other becoming more or less **acute**.

For these reasons, in the divine orders and among the more particular powers, they attribute **right angles** to the **undefiled beings** <note>A reference to higher spiritual entities in Neoplatonic hierarchy that remain untainted by the material world.</note> as the causes of unswerving providence over secondary things. For being upright, unswerving toward the worse, and unchanging belongs to those divine beings. But they say the **obtuse** and **acute** angles are assigned to the providers of progression, movement, and the variety of powers. For the **obtuse** is an image of the expansion of forms spread over all things, while the **acute** has received a resemblance to the cause that divides and moves all things.

And indeed, even among existing things, "rightness" resembles **substance** <note>original: *ousia*; essence or core being.</note> because it preserves the same definition of being; whereas the **obtuse** and **acute** resemble **accidents** <note>original: *symbebēkosin*; in philosophy, these are non-essential qualities (like color or size) that can change without changing what a thing is.</note>. For these admit the "more" and "less," and they never cease changing indefinitely. Therefore, [the angle] is also a symbol...

# HERON’S WORKS

...a complete proposition consists of both parts; the **Exposition** <term>exposition: the act of stating the specific given data of a problem</term> 
separates the given data by itself and prepares it 
for the inquiry; the **Specification** <term>specification: a statement defining the exact objective</term> clarifies separately what the 
thing sought actually is; the **Construction** <term>construction: the addition of lines or figures needed to complete a proof</term> 
<margin>5</margin> adds what is missing from the given data for the 
hunt <note>original: θήραν. The author uses the metaphor of "hunting" for the solution to a geometric problem.</note> of the object sought; the **Proof** <term>proof: the logical chain of scientific reasoning</term> scientifically

**Conclusion** <term>conclusion: the final statement confirming the goal has been met</term> returns again to the enunciation, 
confirming what has been demonstrated. And while all the parts 
<margin>10</margin> of both **problems** and **theorems** are this many, 
the most necessary and ever-present ones are the 
**enunciation**, the **proof**, and the **conclusion**. For it is 
necessary both to know the object sought beforehand, and to 
demonstrate it through intermediate steps, and to collect 
<margin>15</margin> the result; it is impossible for any of these 
three to be missing. The others are employed in many 
places, but in many others they are omitted as providing 
no use. For **specification** and **exposition** are not found 
in every problem.

<margin>14</margin> Of **problems**, some are solved in one way, others <margin>20</margin> 
in two ways, others in many ways, and others in infinite ways. 
In one way: such as the **equilateral triangle**; of the 
remaining, one may be constructed in two ways, another 
in three; such problems might occur in infinite ways: 
"To cut a given straight line into three proportional parts." <margin>25</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from the practical parts of a geometric proof (as seen on page 123) into the metaphysical foundations of geometry. It explores how universal concepts like "the line" or "the unit" exist both as abstract ideas and as objects visualized in the mind's eye. It draws heavily on the Neo-Platonic commentary of Proclus.</meta>

### HERO

Regarding the things that exist—to speak summarily—let us consider the differences between the **universal forms** <term>Katholika eidē: the general archetypes or patterns that define a class of things</term> which exist within the many and fulfill the individual parts. We should define two types of participants in these forms: those that are perceived by the senses, and those that have their existence in the **imagination** <term>Phantasia: the mental faculty that allows a mathematician to "see" a perfect circle or line in the mind</term>. <margin>5</margin> For "matter" is twofold: one type is paired with the senses, and the other with mental images.

<margin>16</margin> For everything that is universal, one, and encompassing of the many, either is visualized in individual things and has its existence within them—being inseparable from them, <margin>10</margin> arranged within them, and either moving or standing still along with them—or it exists **prior** to the many. In this latter case, it is the generative cause of the multitude, providing reflections of itself to the many; it remains indivisible and ranked before the things that participate in it, while supplying varied ways for secondary things to share in its nature. <margin>15</margin>

<margin>17</margin> The **form of the line** contains a twofold power: the indivisible and the divisible. For it possesses the **point** <term>Sēmeion: a geometric position with no magnitude or parts</term> in an indivisible way, but it possesses **intervals** <term>Diastēmata: the extensions or lengths of the line</term> in a divisible way. <margin>20</margin>

<margin>18</margin> They say that the **unit** <term>Monad: the primary principle of number</term> is a "point without position," whereas the **point** is a "unit having position." The point is projected in the imagination and comes to be as if in a place; it is "enmattered" according to **intelligible matter** <term>Noētē hylē: the "mental substance" that allows abstract shapes to have extension and location in the mind</term>. The unit, therefore, is "without position" because it is immaterial.

# DEFINITIONS

<margin>5</margin>
Since, however, the **universal ideas** <term>Forms: the perfect, abstract archetypes of things</term> are primarily of three kinds,<note>original: "drei Arten"; Namely the three types designated on page 122, lines 26–27.</note> we can conceive of differences within that in which things participate—which exists in the many and fulfills individual things—according to the underlying **matter** <term>Hyle: the "stuff" or substrate that receives a form</term>. We should assume that those things which participate in these forms are also of two kinds: partly sensory and partly existing through **imagination** <term>Phantasia: the mental faculty that allows a mathematician to "see" a perfect circle or line in the mind's eye</term>. For matter is also of two kinds: partly belonging to things associated with the senses, and partly to things that are imagined.

<margin>10 15 16</margin>
For everything that is universal and one, encompassing the many, is either<note>Following the precedent of Plato; see Proclus, page 50, line 17.</note> visualized in individual things and has its existence within them—inseparable from them, arranged within them, and either moving or remaining stationary along with them—or it exists **prior** to the many things and generates the multitude by providing reflections of itself to the many from its own being, while itself standing indivisible at the head of the participating things and providing varied participation to the secondary things.

<margin>17 20</margin>
The **idea of the line** [the soul has within itself] by combining a twofold power: one that is indivisible and one that is divisible. For it possesses the **point** <term>Sēmeion: a geometric position with no magnitude or parts</term> without parts, and it possesses **extensions** <term>Diastēmata: the lengths or distances</term> in parts.

<margin>18 25</margin>
The **Unit** <term>Monad: the abstract principle of "one"</term> they<note>The Pythagoreans.</note> call a point without position, but the **Point** they call a unit with position. The Point, however, emerges and is, so to speak, in space within the imagination, and it is "material" within the **intelligible matter** <term>Noētē hylē: the mental "space" where geometric figures are constructed</term>. The Unit, therefore, is without position.

...and outside of all extension and place; the **point** has its position as if in the folds of **imagination** <term>Phantasia: the mental workspace where a mathematician "sees" perfect geometric shapes that do not exist in the physical world</term>.

<margin>19</margin> The **point** is twofold: it exists either by itself or within a line. Because it acts only as a boundary and is a single unit that has neither a "whole" nor "parts," it mimics the very summit of reality. For this reason, it is considered analogous to the **monad** <term>Monad: the number one, representing unity and the indivisible source of all things</term>. By extension, the **line** corresponds to the **dyad** <term>Dyad: the number two, representing the first step into extension and plurality</term>, and the **surface** to the **triad** <term>Triad: the number three, the first number to define a shape or plane</term>.

<margin>20</margin> The **Pythagoreans** <note>An ancient school of philosophers who believed that "all is number"</note> used to say that the surface belongs to the triad because all shapes upon it have the triad as their primary cause. For even the **circle**, which is the origin of all curved lines, possesses a hidden triadic nature in its center, its extension <note>original: "diastasei," referring here to the radius or the distance from the center</note>, and its circumference. Furthermore, it is obvious to everyone that the **triangle**, which leads all straight-lined shapes, is governed by the triad and is formed according to it.

<margin>21</margin> The "One" is called the **Limit**, the **Infinite**, and the **Mixed**; for all existing things are unified from these three. <note>These are the three "ontological principles" discussed in Plato’s Philebus.</note>

<margin>22</margin> They divide **knowledge** into that which is "non-hypothetical" and "hypothetical." Non-hypothetical knowledge is capable of knowing the "wholes" <note>The universal principles of the entire universe</note>, ascending even to **the Good** and the highest cause of all things, making the "upward path" its ultimate goal. Hypothetical knowledge, however, sets forth fixed principles <note>Axioms or starting assumptions</note> and demonstrates the consequences following from them; it does not move toward a first principle, but rather toward a conclusion. ...of the shape that underlies it. For this reason, the **Oracles** <note>original: "τὰ λόγια" (ta logia). This refers to the Chaldean Oracles, a collection of mystical verses that Neoplatonists viewed as divine revelation.</note> call the angular junctions of shapes **connective bonds** <note>original: "συνοχηΐδας" (synocheidas). <margin>10</margin> Among the angles in surfaces, some represent the primary and unmixed unions, while others represent those that hold together the infinite progressions of the things moving within them. Some unify the **intellectual forms** <term>Noetic forms: the pure, abstract archetypes existing in the divine Mind</term>, while others unify the **sensible principles** <term>Logoi: the formative, rational patterns that give shape to the physical world</term>, and still others unify the connections between these two realms.

<margin>15</margin> Therefore, **angles formed by circular lines** <note>original: "περιφερόγραμμοι" (peripherogrammoi). <margin>20</margin> However, **rectilinear angles** <note>original: "εὐθύγραμμοι" (euthygrammoi). Angles formed by straight lines.</note> preside over the physical world we perceive with our senses and provide the connection for the principles within it. Finally, **mixed angles** <note>original: "μικταί" (miktai). Angles formed by the intersection of a straight line and a curved line.</note> preserve the communion of both the sensible and the intellectual realms according to a single, unshakeable union. Looking toward these divine archetypes, we must also assign the specific causes for each individual case.

Finally, the **mixed** angles <note>Angles formed by one straight and one curved line.</note> are those that maintain the community of the sensible and the intellectual in a union without wavering. One must, therefore, with these examples in mind, also state the causes of the particulars.

# DEFINITIONS #

->### OF HERON ###<-

<margin>25</margin> The **soul** <term>Psyche: in this context, the cosmic or individual soul that mediates between the divine realm and the physical world.</term> is said to move **circularly** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, circular motion represents a return to one's source, unlike linear motion which leads away into the material world.</note> through its **intellectual powers** in this way: the **intelligible** <note>original: "noēton" — the object of pure thought.</note> is like a center to the **intellect** <term>Nous: the divine Mind or intuitive understanding.</term>, and the intellect holds itself around this center, loves it, and is unified with it through all its intellectual activities from every side. Upon these souls shines that which is **self-living** and **self-moving**, <margin>5</margin> which allows the soul to be turned toward the intellect and to "dance" around it, and to be restored through its own proper cycles as it unfolds the **indivisibility** <note>original: "amereia" — the quality of being without parts, typical of divine principles.</note> of the intellect. Furthermore, the intellectual orders possess a superiority toward the souls, acting like centers, while the souls <margin>10</margin> act in a circle around them. Indeed, every soul is centered according to its own intellectual part and its very highest **"One,"** <note>The "One" in the soul is the highest spark of divinity that connects it directly to the Absolute.</note> yet according to its plurality, it travels in a circle, longing to embrace its own intellect.

<margin>26</margin> There are **seven types of triangles**: the **equilateral** <margin>15</margin> is of one single form; the **isosceles** <term>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</term> is either **right-angled**, **obtuse-angled**, or **acute-angled**; and the **scalene** <term>A triangle where all three sides are unequal.</term> is likewise divided into those three types.

<margin>27</margin> It is impossible to find a **square number** that is double another square number <note>This refers to the "irrationality of the square root of 2." The Greeks proved that you cannot have a square with an area exactly double another square if the sides are whole numbers.</note>, nor can one find an **equilateral triangle** that is right-angled or has a **hypotenuse** <margin>20</margin> equal to the two sides containing the right angle.

<margin>28</margin> There is a difference between the **Monad** and the **Henad** <term>Monad (monas) usually refers to the mathematical "one," while the Henad (henas) refers to a divine, singular "Unity."</term> as follows: since there is a principle of "form-making" and identity among existing things, it is called the **Monad**. But there is also "otherness," which is called the **Dyad**. There is yet another <margin>25</margin> higher power, a common source of these two, which understands all things; this is called **the One**. Thus, the One is higher...

It is said that the **soul** moves **circularly** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, circular motion represents a return to one's divine source, whereas linear motion represents a descent into the material world.</note> through its **intellectual faculties** in the following sense: the **intelligible** <note>original: "das Gedachte" / Greek: "noēton" — the object of pure thought.</note> acts as a center for **pure thought** <term>Intellect: the "Nous" or divine mind.</term>, and pure thought revolves around it, striving toward it and 5 uniting with it from all sides through all its intellectual powers. The souls receive their light through their own life, their own movement, their orientation toward pure thought, and their choral dance around that thought—a circuit according to their own proper periods—unfolding the **indivisibility** 10 of pure thought. For again, the intellectual orders will take precedence over the souls, acting as their centers, while the souls act in a circle around them. For every soul also has its center in its own intellectual part and in its very highest **unity** itself; 15 however, by virtue of its **plurality**, it moves in a circle, longing to embrace its own pure thought.

<margin>26</margin>
There are seven types of **triangles**: the **equilateral** <note>A triangle with three equal sides.</note> is simple; the **isosceles** <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> is either right-angled, obtuse-angled, or acute-angled; 20 and the **scalene** <note>original: "ungleichseitig" — a triangle where all sides have different lengths.</note> is likewise.

<margin>27</margin>
It is impossible to find a **square number** that is twice as large as another square number <note>This refers to the proof of the irrationality of the square root of 2; no two squares of integers can have a 2:1 ratio.</note>, or an **equilateral right-angled triangle** <note>Geometrically, an equilateral triangle cannot have a 90-degree angle; the author may be highlighting a logical impossibility or using "equilateral" to mean "isosceles" in this specific context.</note> whose **hypotenuse** would be equal to the 25 two sides enclosing the right angle.

# DEFINITIONS #

->### OF HERON ###<-

<header>OF HERON</header>

...is derived from the unit. It must be understood that, since there exists the **dyad**, the **unit** <note>original: "monas" — often translated as "monad," representing the principle of oneness and form.</note>, and **the One**, the bodies themselves are the **dyad**, the **form** within them is the **unit**, and **nature** is the One.

<margin>29</margin> **First philosophy** <note>What we today call "metaphysics"—the study of the fundamental nature of reality.</note> differs from **dialectic** in that first philosophy proceeds through the most certain truths, while dialectic proceeds from **probabilities**.

<margin>30</margin> It is possible to show that figures bounded by **curved lines** are equal to those bounded by **straight lines**. **Archimedes** demonstrated that every **circle** is equal to a **right-angled triangle**, in which the **radius** <note>original: "ek tou kentrou" — literally "the line from the center."</note> is equal to one of the sides containing the right angle, and the **perimeter** <note>The circumference of the circle.</note> is equal to the base of the triangle.

<margin>31</margin> **Analogy** <term>Proportion: the equality or similarity of two or more ratios.</term> is the similarity of **ratios**. An analogy exists in at least three terms. <note>For example, in the continuous proportion 2:4 :: 4:8, there are three distinct terms (2, 4, and 8).</note>

<margin>32</margin> A **proposition** is divided into the **given** <note>The data or conditions provided at the start of a problem.</note> and the **sought** <note>The goal or result to be found.</note>. However, this is not always the case; sometimes it states only the sought. But when the proposition contains both the given and the sought, then one finds both a **specification** <term>Diorismos: the part of a geometrical proof that defines the conditions of the problem's possibility.</term> and an **exposition** <term>Ekthesis: the step where the given elements are "set out" and labeled (e.g., "Let AB be the given line").</term>. When the given is missing, these are also absent; for the exposition and the specification belong to the given. For what could the one specifying say about a proposed problem, except that it is necessary to find an **isosceles triangle** of such-and-such a kind? This [the goal] was the proposition itself. Therefore, if the proposition does not contain the given but only the sought, the exposition is silenced because there is no given, and the specification is omitted.
