# DEFINITIONS #

...of these two, which encompasses all; this is called the **One**. The One is therefore superior to the **unit** <note>German: "Einheit," Greek: "monas." In this context, the "One" (Hen) is the transcendent source, while the "unit" (monad) is the principle of number.</note>. One must know, however, that since there exists the **dyad**, the **unit**, and the **One**, the **dyad** is the bodies themselves, the **unit** is the **idea** <note>or "form"</note> inherent in them, and the **One** is **nature**.

<margin>29</margin>
**First philosophy** <note>Metaphysics, or the study of fundamental reality.</note> differs from **dialectic** in that first philosophy operates with absolute truth, while dialectic starts from the **probable** <note>Following the Aristotelian distinction where dialectic deals with "endoxa" or generally accepted opinions.</note>.

<margin>30</margin>
It is possible to prove that **curvilinear figures** <note>shapes with curved boundaries, like circles.</note> are equal to **rectilinear** ones <note>shapes with straight boundaries, like triangles.</note>. Thus **Archimedes** demonstrated that every **circle** is equal to a **triangle**, if its **radius** is equal to one of the sides forming the right angle, and the **circumference** is equal to the base.

<margin>31</margin>
**Proportion** is the equality of **ratios**. A proportion consists of at least three terms. <note>For example, in the proportion 4 is to 2 as 2 is to 1, there are three distinct terms: 4, 2, and 1.</note>

<margin>32</margin>
The **proposition** <term>Protasis: the initial statement of what is to be proved or constructed.</term> is divided into the **given** and the **sought**, though this does not always happen; sometimes it expresses only the **sought**. When the proposition contains both—the **given** and the **sought**—then there is also a **definition of goal** <term>Diorismus: a specification of the conditions of the problem.</term> and an **exposition** <term>Ekthesis: the step where the general proposition is applied to a specific figure (e.g., "Let AB be the given line").</term>. If, however, the **given** is missing, these are also missing; for the **exposition** and **definition of goal** are connected with the **given**. For what **definition of goal** should one give for the proposed problem <note>referring to Euclid Book IV, Proposition 10.</note> other than that an **isosceles triangle** of such and such a kind should be found? But that was precisely the **proposition**. If, therefore, the **proposition** does not contain the **given**, but only the **sought**, the **exposition** is suppressed because a **given** is not present, and the **definition of goal** is omitted.

<margin>10</margin> Neither the **rational** nor the **irrational** magnitude is something understood on its own, but rather each is defined by comparison to something else. For whatever things are commensurable with one another, these are called **rational** in relation to each other; and whatever are incommensurable with one another, these are called **irrational** in relation to each other. **Numbers** happen to be <margin>15</margin> commensurable, since each of them is measured by a certain **smallest measure** <note>the "unit" or "one".</note>. Similarly, a **cubit** and a **palm** <note>Ancient units of measurement: a cubit is roughly 18 inches, a palm is about 3 inches.</note> have a commensurability with each other; for each is measured out by a **smallest measure**, the **digit** <note>a "finger-breadth," roughly 0.75 inches.</note>, which, by the convention of our measurements, holds the position of the **unit**.
<margin>20</margin> However, because the division of physical magnitudes is **infinite** and no "smallest measure" exists by nature, it is clear that for a **rational magnitude**, there is no single, fixed smallest measure (like the "digit"). Instead, it is up to us to designate whatever size we wish as our **smallest known measure**, <margin>25</margin> in which the **unit** resides. A straight line in itself is neither **rational** nor **irrational**, but when compared to an assumed **unit** <term>unit: a standard reference length, like a meter or an inch, used to measure other lines.</term> placed in position, it is found to be either rational or irrational. Thus, if the side of a square is assumed to be rational, the **diagonal** is found to be rational **in power** <note>original: "dynamei" (δυνάμει). This means the area of the square formed by the diagonal is a rational number, even if the length of the diagonal itself cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note>; <margin>5</margin> for in **length** it is found to be irrational. And conversely, if the diagonal is existing as rational, the side is rational in power; meanwhile, each of them by itself is neither rational nor **unutterable**—that is, irrational—in its own nature <note>The author argues that "rationality" is not an inherent property of a line, but only exists in relationship to a chosen ruler or unit.</note>. Thus, having assumed a certain smallest measure of straight lines as a **linear unit**, <margin>10</margin> the mathematicians called it "rational," and those lines commensurable with it, "rational." Likewise, they called the square produced from it "rational," and the areas commensurable with this square, "rational areas." They similarly called the cube produced from it "rational," and the solids commensurable with this cube, "rational solids." One must understand as **unutterable**, <margin>15</margin> that is, **irrational**, a solid that is incommensurable with the cube of a rational line; a plane area that is incommensurable with the square of a rational line; and a length—that is, a straight line—that is incommensurable with a rational line. Regarding straight lines, since incommensurability is understood in two ways—one, when the lines themselves <margin>20</margin> are incommensurable, but the areas <note>In ancient geometry, "areas" often refers to the squares built upon the lines.</note> produced by them are commensurable with one another; the other, when even those areas are incommensurable with one another—there was a twofold distinction relative to the "rational" line according to the ancients. For some lines are called **rational** and **irrational** "in power," while the rest are so "in length." <margin>25</margin> Those that are rational "in power," as we said before, are those which...

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of geometric magnitudes (rational vs. irrational) attributed to Heron of Alexandria. It builds upon the previous page’s discussion of commensurability by explaining that "rationality" is not an inherent property of a line, but a relationship to a chosen unit. It concludes by beginning a distinction between lines that are incommensurable in length versus those incommensurable in power (area).</meta>

->### DEFINITIONS ###<-

A straight line in and of itself is neither **rational** nor **irrational**, but only through comparison with a **unit** <term>unit: a standard reference length, like a meter or an inch, used as a baseline to measure other lines</term> assumed by convention does it emerge as rational or irrational. If, for instance, the side of a square is <margin>5</margin> assumed as **rational**, the **diagonal** <note>original: "Durchmesser" (diameter). In Greek geometry, the term for the diagonal of a square was often the same as the diameter of a circle.</note> turns out to be rational only **in the square** <note>This is the concept of "rational in power" (dynamei). It means that while the diagonal's length might be a messy square root, the area of the square built upon it is a clean, whole number.</note>; for in **length** it turns out to be irrational. And conversely, if the diagonal is presented as rational, the side is rational only in the square, since both, in and of themselves, are neither rational nor <margin>10</margin> **non-rational**—that is, **irrational**.

Thus, the mathematicians assumed a certain straight line as a **unit**, serving as the smallest measure for straight lines, and they called this "rational" and those lines commensurable <note>Commensurable: lines that can both be measured by the same "ruler" without any leftover remainder.</note> with it "rational." Likewise, they also called its square "rational" and those <margin>15</margin> **areas** <note>original: "Flächenräume"</note> commensurable with it "rational," and likewise its cube and the **solids** <note>original: "Körper"</note> commensurable with it "rational." 

By **non-rational**, however—that is, **irrational**—one must understand the solid that is incommensurable with the cube of the rational straight line; the plane that <margin>20</margin> is incommensurable with the square of the rational straight line; and the length—that is, the straight line—which is incommensurable with the rational unit. 

Since one conceives of a twofold incommensurability regarding straight lines—one where the straight lines themselves are incommensurable, but the <margin>25</margin> areas described upon them are conversely commensurable; and another where these same areas are likewise incommensurable among themselves—so also, according to the ancients, the distinction from the rational was twofold; for some are [rational] in **power**...

# HERON'S WORKS

...[are] incommensurable with the rational line, but the squares produced from them are commensurable with the square on the rational line. They are commensurable in length, however, whenever the squares produced from them are either in square numbers or have sides commensurable with the rational line in length. And in general, that which is commensurable with the rational line is called **rational** <note>original: ῥητή (rhētē). This term refers to lines that can be expressed in relation to a chosen unit.</note>, whether it is commensurable in length <margin>5</margin> or in **power** <term>power: in Greek geometry, "power" (dynamis) refers to the area of the square built upon a line. A line might be irrational in length but "rational in power" if its square is a whole number.</term> only.

<margin>35</margin> They also define the **rational** line in this way: a rational line is one that is known through numbers. However, this is not an essential definition of "rational," but rather an **accidental property** <note>original: συμβεβηκός (symbebēkos). An "accidental" property is a feature that happens to be true but does not define what the thing actually is.</note> of it. For when, for the sake of example, rational lines are set out from a rational line of one cubit, we know <margin>10</margin> for each one how many palms or fingers it consists of; hence, from these accidental properties, we say a rational line is "known through numbers." A rational line differs from a **given** line <note>original: δοθείσης (dotheisēs). In geometry, a "given" line is one whose length or position is fixed for the sake of a problem, regardless of whether it is a whole number.</note> in that the rational line is always "given," but a given line is not necessarily rational. The rational line is known both by its **quantity** and its **quality** <margin>15</margin>, whereas the given line is known by its quantity and **magnitude** <note>original: μεγέθει (megethei)</note> only; for there are also some **irrational** <note>original: ἄλογοι (alogoi) — literally "without ratio" or "speechless."</note> lines that are "given."

<margin>36</margin> An infinite line can never be multiplied, nor can one ever be compared to another. For things that are not of the **same kind** <note>original: ὁμογενῆ (homogenē). For example, you cannot compare a line (1D) to a surface (2D).</note> cannot have a ratio to one another. A **ratio** <margin>20</margin> <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> is a certain relationship between two magnitudes of the same kind in respect to their size—such as line to line, and surface to surface, and the rest likewise.

<margin>37</margin> Of **proportions** <note>original: ἀναλογιῶν (analogiōn)</note>, some are continuous, and others are discrete.

# DEFINITIONS

...are called rational and irrational, while the others are so called in length.
Those that are **rational in power** <term>power: In Greek geometry, "power" (dynamis) refers to the area of the square built upon a line. They are rational **in length**, however, if their squares relate to each other as square numbers do, or if their sides are commensurable in length with the rational line. And in general, that which is commensurable with the rational line is called **rational**, whether in length or only in power.

<margin>35</margin>
Some also define the **rational** line as follows: a rational line is one determined by numbers. However, this is not a true definition of the "rational," but rather an **accidental property** <note>original: "Akzidens" / συμβεβηκός. For if one sets out a series of rational lines starting from a rational line one cubit long, we know for each one how many handbreadths or fingers <note>original: "Zoll" / δάκτυλοι. <margin>36</margin>
An **unlimited line** <note>original: "unbegrenzte Linie" / ἄπειρος γραμμή.</note> cannot ever be multiplied, nor can it be compared with another. For things that are not **homogeneous** <term>homogeneous: magnitudes of the same kind (e.g., two lines or two areas). You cannot have a ratio between a line's length and an area's size.</term> cannot have a ratio between them, because a "**ratio**" <note>original: "Verhältnis" / λόγος.</note> is a certain relation of two homogeneous magnitudes to one another, such as line to line, surface to surface, and so on.

# OF HERON

...Continuous ratios are those that follow one another and maintain their relationships without interruption, while discrete ratios are those that do not behave this way. Instead, in discrete ratios, the proportions are separated from one another and are not joined by a **middle term** <term>middle term: In a continuous proportion like A:B = B:C, the "B" is the middle term that links the two ratios. In a discrete proportion like A:B and C:D, there is no shared link.</term>. In a continuous proportion, the middle term leads one ratio and follows the other. 
<margin>5</margin>
An example of a **continuous** ratio is 8, 4, 2 <note>Because 8 is to 4 as 4 is to 2.</note>; a **discrete** ratio is 8 to 4 and 6 to 3 <note>Both simplify to 2:1, but they use different numbers and are not linked by a shared middle number.</note>.

A **Ratio** <term>ratio: original Greek "logos" (λόγος), which means both "mathematical proportion" and "reason/word."</term> is the interval between the magnitudes that have been set out.

<margin>38</margin>
The **right angle** is a symbol of activity that is held without deviation, characterized by equality, limitation, and boundary. 
<margin>10</margin>

<margin>15</margin>

Additionally, the **straight line** is a symbol of the knowledge of all things, moving infinitely and indefinitely. 

Regarding "the two right angles" or "the sum of two right angles": 
<margin>20</margin>
"Two right angles" is a specific property <note>Referring to two literal 90-degree angles.</note>, whereas "equal to two right angles" is a general property. This is because unequal things <note>Such as an acute angle and an obtuse angle.</note> can be brought into equality by together equaling the sum of two right angles <note>i.e., 180 degrees.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical commentary on Euclidean geometry. ### ->THE WRITINGS OF HERO<-

<margin>41</margin> Problems properly so-called <term>problem: in geometry, a "problem" is a task to be performed, such as "to construct a triangle," as opposed to a "theorem," which is a statement to be proved.</term> seek to avoid ambiguity.

<margin>42</margin> Among problems, some are "without cases" and others are "with many cases," just as is the case with theorems. <margin>5</margin> Those that possess the same logical force through many different diagrams—even when the positions of the elements change—yet preserve the same method of proof, these are said to have **cases**. <term>cases: (Greek: *ptōseis*) variations in the arrangement of a geometric figure that might require the proof to be adjusted slightly, though the core logic remains the same.</term> However, those that proceed according to only one specific position and one single construction, <margin>10</margin> these are "without cases." Simply put, a "case" is observed in the construction of both problems and theorems.

<margin>43</margin> Regarding geometric propositions, most are **affirmations** <note>original: *kataphaseis*</note> and do not have much need for **negations** <note>original: *apophaseis*</note>. However, a general negative statement requires affirmations if it is to be demonstrated; for without an affirmation, there is neither a proof nor a <margin>15</margin> syllogism <term>syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two or more assumed premises.</term>. Because of this, the demonstrative sciences for the most part prove things through affirmations.

<margin>44</margin> A thing can be "given" in four ways: first, by **position**, as when we say that an angle is situated at a certain line and a certain point; second, by **form** <margin>20</margin> <note>original: *eidos*</note>, as when we say an angle is right, acute, or obtuse, or generally rectilinear or mixed; third, by **ratio**, as when we say it is double or generally greater or smaller; fourth, by **magnitude**, as when we say it is one-third of a right angle.

<margin>45</margin> There are only three polygons capable of filling the space <margin>25</margin> [around a point...] <note>The text likely refers to the "tiling" theorem: only the equilateral triangle, square, and regular hexagon can perfectly tile a flat surface around a single point without leaving gaps.</note>

->## HERON'S [DEFINITIONS]<-
### 148

...a single point of place; an equilateral triangle, a square, and a hexagon which is both equilateral and equiangular.

<margin>46</margin> The term **given** <term>given: in Greek geometry, "given" (dedomenon) refers to information or objects provided at the start of a problem which the mathematician is permitted to use.</term> is used in four ways: first, regarding the **angle**; second, when **two straight lines** are provided; third, if **four magnitudes** are in proportion; and fourth, when it is required to **place a straight line equal to a given straight line at a given point.** <note>This fourth case refers to the construction found in Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Proposition 2.</note> From these, it is clear that the **exposition** <term>exposition: the "ekthesis," or the step in a geometric proof where the specific given elements of the diagram are laid out for the reader.</term> of a problem is likewise fourfold, concerning both what is given and what is sought.

<margin>47</margin> **Postulates** <note>original: *aitēmata*</note> contribute to the **constructions**, while **axioms** <note>original: *axiōmata*</note> contribute to the **proofs**. <term>Postulates vs. Axioms: Postulates are basic geometric actions you are allowed to perform (like drawing a line), while axioms are self-evident logical truths (like "the whole is greater than the part").</term>

<margin>48</margin> **Hypothesis** and **converse** <note>original: *antistrophē*</note> are terms used by geometers. For example, a triangle is **hypothesized** to be **isosceles**; [the theorem then states that] in every isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal to one another. Conversely, that which has its base angles equal is an isosceles triangle. There is another type of **converse**: in every triangle where two angles are equal, the sides **subtending** <note>the sides located opposite the angles</note> them are also equal; and conversely again in a similar fashion.

<margin>49</margin> They say that **virtue** stands according to **rectitude** <note>original: *orthotēta*, a word play meaning both "moral uprightness" and "right-angledness"</note>, while **vice** is based upon the indeterminacy of **obtuse** and **acute** angles. Vice is divided into **deficiency** and **excess**, and it reveals its own lack of measure by being "more" or "less" [than the right angle]. Thus, of perfection and...

<margin>48</margin> Geometers use the words **assumption** <note>or "hypothesis"</note> and **converse**. ->## OF HERON<-
### 150

...of unswerving activity, intellectual boundary, and limit, and similar things, we shall establish the rightness of **rectilinear angles** <term>rectilinear angle: An angle formed by straight lines, as opposed to curved lines.</term> as an image; but the **obtuse** and **acute** [angles] as an image of indeterminate motion, unrestrained progression, division, partitioning, and generally, infinity. And the rectilinear angle is the genus <term>genus: A general category that contains more specific "species" or types.</term> of both types of angles—the acute and the obtuse.

<margin>50</margin> A **Principle** <note>original: *Archē*</note> is the first limit of those things that follow. In this way, it is also their habit to often call that which exists eternally a "principle," and some of them have called God the principle of all existing things.

<margin>51</margin> The **definitions** <note>original: *horoi*</note> and the **limit** <note>original: *peras*</note> of each thing are introduced by whatever is immediately simpler than each of the beings. For indeed, the **soul** defines and perfects the activity of **nature**, and nature defines the motion of **bodies**; and prior to these, the **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*</note> measures the cycles of the soul, and the **One** <note>original: *to hen*</note> measures the life of the Intellect itself. For that [the One] is the measure of all things. Just as in geometric objects, the **solid** is bounded by the **surface**, the surface by the **line**, and the line by the **point**; for that [the point] is the limit of all.

<margin>52</margin> In the case of a **circle**, the straight line drawn through the center is called a **diameter**; in the case of a **sphere**, it is called an **axis**; and in the case of a **square**, a **diagonal**.

<margin>53</margin> There are said to be **seven types** of triangles and seven types of parallelograms.

<margin>54</margin> If the shape of the **rhombus** is moved <note>likely meaning "transformed" or "deformed" in a geometric sense</note>, it can become a **square**, and the **rhomboid** <term>rhomboid: A parallelogram where adjacent sides are unequal and angles are not right angles.</term> can become an **oblong** <note>original: *heteromēkes* — literally "other-length," referring to a non-square rectangle.</note>.

### 151

...we shall establish the **rectilinear angle** <term>rectilinear angle: An angle formed by straight lines.</term> as an image of perfection, of unswerving energy, of intellectual enclosure and limit, and things related to these; the **obtuse** and **acute** angles, by contrast, [we shall establish] as an image of indeterminate motion, of continuous progression, division, fragmentation, and generally, of infinity. And the genus <term>genus: The general category to which a specific thing belongs.</term> of these two angles, the acute and the obtuse, is the rectilinear angle.

<margin>50</margin> A **Principle** <note>original: *Archē*</note> is the first limit of those things that follow. In this way, they are often accustomed to calling that which is "always existing" a principle, and some of them have called God the principle of all existing things.

<margin>51</margin> In every thing, the enclosure and the limit of each always draw upon that which is immediately simpler; for the **soul** <note>original: *psychē*</note> limits and completes the energy of **nature**, and nature limits the motion of **bodies**; and prior to these, the **pure Intellect** <note>original: *nous*—often translated as 'Mind' or 'Divine Thought'</note> measures the circular motion of the soul, and **Unity** <note>original: *to hen*—The One, the highest principle in Neoplatonism</note> measures the life of the pure Intellect itself; for this Unity is the measure of all things. <margin>52</margin> In the case of a **circle**, the straight line drawn through the center is called the **diameter**; in a **sphere**, it is called the **axis**; and in a **square**, the **diagonal**.

<margin>53</margin> It is reckoned that there are seven types of **triangles** and **parallelograms**.

<margin>54</margin> Through displacement, the figure of the **rhombus** can become a **square**, while the **rhomboid** can become a **rectangle**.

<margin>55</margin> Of all figures, the **square** is the only one that has equal sides and right angles; therefore, it is also called more honorable. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who viewed numbers and shapes as the fundamental building blocks of reality.</note> compare it to the divine; since it possesses an unblemished <margin>5</margin> regularity through equality and rightness, it imitates a power at rest. Indeed, motion arises from inequality, whereas stillness arises from equality.

<margin>56</margin> But since the **soul** stands between the **intellectual** <note>The realm of pure thought and forms.</note> and the **sensible** <note>The realm of the physical senses.</note>, it acts according to the **circle** insofar as it <margin>10</margin> borders the intellectual world; but insofar as it presides over the sensible world, it provides for it according to the **straight line**. So much for the similarity of these forms to existing things. Regarding the straight line, **Euclid** has provided the following definition:

<margin>57</margin> <margin>15</margin> After the **Unity**, there are three forms of existence: the **Limit**, the **Unlimited**, and the **Mixed**. It extends through all of them, taking on the appropriate form in each instance. The **Mixed** is that which is mixed in every class. Thus, the Limit, the Unlimited, and the Mixed appear in all of these. <margin>25</margin> For this reason, the soul has also pre-enclosed both the straight and the curved in its own essence, so that it may govern the whole series of the Unlimited in the cosmos and—

...so that it might direct the entire cosmic **series** <term>series (sustoichia)</term> <note>A Pythagorean term for a column or alignment of related principles, such as light/dark or limited/unlimited.</note> of the infinite and every nature of an **odd-like form** <note>In Pythagorean thought, "odd" numbers and forms were associated with the Limit and the Divine.</note>, establishing their **progression** <term>progression (proodos)</term> <note>The outward movement of existence from its divine source into the world.</note> by the **straight**, and their **return** <term>return (epistrophē)</term> <note>The movement of existing things back toward their divine source.</note> by the **circular**, and leading them forward into multiplicity by the former <margin>5</margin> <insert>and bringing them all back into unity by the latter.</insert> <note>This insertion completes a gap in the text identified by the editor Hultsch, based on the writings of Proclus.</note> And it is not only the **soul** but also the one who established the soul and handed down these powers to it who contains the primary causes of both within himself. The **straight line** is a symbol of providence that is unwavering, undistorted, pure, unfailing, all-powerful, and present to all; whereas the <margin>15</margin> **circumference** and the act of circling are symbols of activity that inclines toward itself, winds back toward itself, and holds dominion according to a single intellectual goal of the whole. -># DEFINITIONS<-

...all things. The **straight line** is a symbol of **providence** <term>providence (pronoia)</term> <note>The divine care or guidance of the universe.</note> that is unwavering, undistorted, pure, unfailing, all-powerful, and present to all things; the **arc**, however, and the **circular motion** represent the **energy** <term>energy (energeia)</term> that converges upon itself, rolls back into itself, and governs the whole through a conceptual boundary. One must know that for every geometric theorem, six parts <note>original: "κεφάλαια" (kephalaia), literally 'headings' or 'chapters'</note> are employed: **proposition**, **exposition**, **specification**, **construction**, **proof**, and **conclusion**. The **proposition** <term>proposition (protasis)</term> is divided into the subject and the predicate; from the subject comes the **exposition** <term>exposition (ekthesis)</term> <note>The step where the specific diagram or given elements are "set out."</note>, and from the predicate comes the **specification** <term>specification (prodiorismos)</term> <note>The statement of what exactly is to be proven regarding the specific elements.</note>.

2. One must know that the **postulates** <term>postulates (aitēmata)</term> <note>Foundational assumptions required to perform a task.</note> assist us in the **construction** <term>construction (kataskeuē)</term>, while the **common notions** <term>common notions (koinai ennoiai)</term> <note>Self-evident axioms, such as "things equal to the same thing are equal to each other."</note> assist in the **proof** <term>proof (apodeixis)</term>.

3. It is necessary to recognize that regarding a proposition such as "Man is an animal," the "man" is the subject according to the philosophers, and "animal" is the predicate. However, in geometry, the proposition is taken either as a **problem** <note>A challenge to construct something.</note> or as a **theorem** <note>A statement to be proven.</note>; the **given** <term>given (dedomenon)</term> replaces the subject of the proposition, and the **sought** <term>sought (zētumenon)</term> replaces the predicate.

4. There is a commentary by **Taurus of Sidon** <note>A 2nd-century CE Platonic philosopher.</note> on Plato's *Republic*, in which the following appears: Plato defined **geometry** <term>geometry (geōmetria)</term> in the *Meno* thus: "Right opinion bound by the calculation of the cause" <note>original: "δόξαν ὀρθὴν δεθεῖσαν αἰτίας λογισμῷ"</note>. **Aristotle** defined it as "Understanding <note>original: "ὑπόληψιν" (hupolēpsin), often 'supposition' or 'conception'</note> joined with proof," and **Zeno** <note>Likely Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> defined it as "A disposition in the reception of appearances" <note>original: "ἕξιν ἐν προσδέξει φαντασιῶν"</note>.

### 5
How is it that the geometer contemplates the **point** <term>point (sēmeion)</term> <note>Defined in geometry as that which has position but no magnitude or parts.</note> as indivisible, even though the **imagination** <term>imagination (phantasia)</term> receives all things in a shaped and divisible manner? For indeed, the imagination, according to its own nature, receives the appearances of intellectual and divine forms—providing forms to those things that are formless, and shapes to those that are shapeless. <margin>5</margin> <image-desc>A small square box containing the Greek letter alpha (α).</image-desc> This is because the form of the imaginative movement neither [proceeds...] <note>The text is damaged here.</note> from the formless into that which is shaped. For if the imagination were divisible, it would not be able to preserve the many types of forms within itself, as new incoming impressions would obscure those that came before; <margin>10</margin> yet if it were strictly indivisible, belonging to the pure intellect, it would not perform its activities in a shaped or "picturing" way. <margin>15</margin>

### 6
The **principles** of geometry are divided into **axiom**, **hypothesis**, and **postulate**; those things that follow from the principles are divided into **problem** and **theorem**.

### 7
What is an **axiom**? When the concept being introduced as a principle is well-known to the learner and is credible in itself, such a thing is an axiom; <margin>20</margin> for example, "things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another."

### 8
What is a **hypothesis**? When the listener does not have a self-evident concept of what is being said, but it is nonetheless posited and granted to the person making the argument, such a thing is a hypothesis.

OF HERON

...each of these used to be named separately, and there was no common name for both. They gave them this name <note>The name "mathematics," derived from the Greek word "manthanō," meaning "to learn."</note> because they found in them a nature that was scientific and suitable for instruction. For they saw that these studies were concerned with things that are eternal, unchanging, and pure—the only realm in which they believed true science <note>original: "epistēmē"</note> could exist. 

However, the moderns <note>Likely referring to scholars of the Hellenistic period who expanded the curriculum beyond pure geometry and arithmetic.</note> extended the name further. They claimed that the mathematician should not only deal with incorporeal <note>Non-physical or abstract</note> and intellectual matter, but also with that which touches upon physical and sensory substance. For the mathematician must be a theorist of the motion of stars, their speed, sizes, shapes, and distances. Furthermore, he should be an investigator of the experiences of sight, researching the causes through which objects do not appear as they truly are or in their actual size when viewed from various distances. While these objects maintain their true proportions to one another, they create false impressions of both their position and order; this happens in the heavens and the air, as well as in mirrors and all smooth surfaces, and even in transparent bodies and similar objects. 

In addition to these subjects, they thought the mathematician ought to be a master of mechanics <term>mēchanikos</term> <note>One who understands the principles of machines and motion</note>, a land-surveyor <term>geōdaistēs</term>, and an expert in calculation <term>logistikos</term> <note>The practical art of calculation, distinguished from "arithmetic," which was the theoretical study of number properties.</note>. Moreover, he should occupy himself with the causes of the harmonious blending of sounds and the composition of melody—things which are either physical bodies themselves or, at the very least, relate back to sensory matter.

> fixes its head in heaven and walks upon the earth." <note>original: "ἥτ’ ὀλίγη μὲν πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει." These lines are from Homer's *Iliad* (4.442-443), originally describing Strife (Eris). Heron uses them here as a metaphor for how mathematics begins with a tiny point and grows to explain the entire universe.</note>
For it begins from a single point and a line, but then occupies itself with the study of the heavens, the earth, and the entirety of all things.

->How many parts of mathematics are there?<-

<margin>5</margin> Of the more honorable and primary part, there are two general divisions: <margin>10</margin> **arithmetic** <note>The theoretical study of the properties of numbers.</note> and **geometry**. Of the part which occupies itself with sensory objects <note>Applied mathematics that deals with things we can see and touch.</note>, there are six divisions: **calculation** <term>logistikē</term> <note>Practical computation, as opposed to the theory of arithmetic.</note>, **geodesy** <note>The measurement of land and distances on earth.</note>, **optics**, **canonics** <note>The mathematical theory of musical intervals and harmony.</note>, **mechanics**, and **astronomy**. Note that neither the so-called "tactics" <note>Military formations and maneuvers.</note>, nor "architecture," nor "popular music," <margin>15</margin> nor the study of "phases" <note>The appearances and disappearances of stars or the moon.</note>, nor even that which is commonly called "mechanics" <note>Likely referring to simple manual labor or non-mathematical craft.</note> (as some suppose), are true parts of mathematics. As our discourse proceeds, we shall demonstrate this clearly and methodically.

<margin>6</margin> Note that the circle <note>This likely refers to the "elements" or properties associated with the sphere or the construction of specific geometric solids within a circle.</note> possesses eight solids, six planes, and four <margin>20</margin> angles.

## 166

...proceeds according to ratios, numbers, and proportions. Under **Geometry**, however, fall **Optics** and **Geodesy** <note>The practical science of measuring and dividing land.</note>; and belonging to both fields, though even more specialized, are **Mechanics** and **Astronomy** <note>original: <foreign>ἀστρολογική</foreign> (astrologikē). In the ancient world, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of the stars' movements.</note>.

<margin>8</margin> **That mathematics derives its principles from hypothesis and deals with hypothesis.** 
The term "hypothesis" <term>hypothesis</term> <note>Literally "a placing under," meaning a foundation or an assumption used as a starting point.</note> is used in three ways, or perhaps even more. 
In one sense, it refers to a **dramatic plot**, such as when we speak of the "hypotheses" of the plays of **Euripides**. 
In a second sense, it refers to the **investigation of specific cases** in rhetoric, which is how the Sophists <note>Professional teachers and orators in 5th-century BCE Greece.</note> use the term when they say one must "posit a hypothesis." 
In the third sense, a hypothesis is the **starting point of a mathematical demonstration**, being a request for certain things to be granted for the sake of constructing a proof. 
For example, it is said that **Democritus** <note>The "laughing philosopher" who proposed that the world is made of indivisible units.</note> used "atoms and the void" as his hypothesis, while **Asclepiades** <note>A prominent Greek physician who believed the body was composed of "fragmented particles" and "pores."</note> used "corpuscles and pores." Mathematics, then, is concerned with this third type of hypothesis.

<margin>9</margin> **That Pythagoras was not alone in honoring arithmetic.**
Not only did **Pythagoras** hold it in the highest regard, but his students and associates did as well, frequently declaring:
->**"All things are like unto number."**<- <note>original: <foreign>ἀριθμῷ δέ τε πάντ' ἐπέοικεν</foreign>. This Pythagorean maxim reflects the belief that the universe is fundamentally mathematical.</note>

<margin>10</margin> **The proper goal of arithmetic.**
Primarily, its goal is **scientific contemplation** <note>original: <foreign>theōria</foreign>. This refers to the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake, rather than for practical utility.</note>, than which there is no goal greater or more beautiful. Secondarily, its goal is to grasp, in a unified way, all the properties that belong to the definite essence of things.

# GEOMETRY

<margin>8</margin> If <term>geometry</term> <note>original: "geōmetria"; literally "earth-measurement."</note> were to be judged strictly on its own merit, it might be thought to contribute nothing to human life. In the same way that a carpenter's tools <insert>and</insert>, perhaps, if viewed only by themselves, might seem to be useless—yet if you look at the use performed through them, you will find it to be neither small nor insignificant—in the same way, geometry is found to be a vain pursuit when stripped of the practical results achieved through it.

<margin>5</margin> However, when we look toward its benefit for <term>astronomy</term> <note>original: "astronomia"; the study of the laws governing the stars.</note>, we marvel at the subject; for it serves as the very **eye of astronomy**. For since astronomy deals with magnitudes, numbers, and

<margin>10</margin> proportions—as it busies itself with the size of the sun and moon, the quantity of the stars, and their proportions to one another—geometry teaches us about two dimensions in planes: width and length. Without these being known,

<margin>15</margin> <term>solids</term> <note>original: "sterea"; three-dimensional objects.</note> could never be constructed, which happen to consist of three dimensions: width, length, and depth. By providing us with knowledge of magnitude, geometry contributes the greatest help toward astronomy. Furthermore, there is the knowledge derived from number, which is discussed in the

<margin>20</margin> seventh, eighth, and ninth <note>These refer to the "Arithmetical Books" of Euclid’s *Elements*, which provide the number theory necessary for calculating planetary ratios.</note> books.

### OF HERON ###

**Geometry** <term>geometry</term> <note>original: "geometria"; literally, "earth-measurement."</note> is the science of shapes and magnitudes and the properties pertaining to these. Its purpose is to treat these matters, and its method of teaching is **synthetic** <note>A method of building complex ideas from simple ones, rather than breaking them down.</note>; for starting from a **point** which is dimensionless,

<margin>5</margin> passing through the intermediate **line** and **surface**, it arrives at the **solid**. Its utility contributes directly to philosophy; for this also seemed true to the divine **Plato**, where he says: "whether these mathematical studies are difficult or easy, one must go this way." <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic* or *Laws*, emphasizing mathematics as a necessary path to higher truth.</note> They are inscribed as **Elements** <note>original: "stoicheia," meaning fundamental principles or "building blocks."</note> because he who has not

<margin>10</margin> been led through these first is unable to understand any of the geometrical theorems. Geometry creates its teaching through **abstraction**; for taking a **physical body**, which is three-dimensionally extended with **resistance** <note>original: "antitypia"; the quality of matter that prevents other matter from occupying the same space.</note>, and separating the resistance from it, geometry produces the

<margin>15</margin> **mathematical body**, which is the **solid**, and by abstracting further, it arrives at the **point**.

# GEOMETRICAL MATTERS. 175 #

To state [the definition of] geometry: **Geometry** is therefore the science of **figures** and **magnitudes** and their variations, and its purpose is to treat these matters. The method of its presentation, however, is **synthetic** <note>A method of teaching that builds complex ideas starting from the simplest components.</note>; for it begins with the <margin>5</margin> **point**, which is without extension, and via the **line** and **surface**, it reaches the **body** <note>In this context, "body" refers to a three-dimensional solid.</note>. Its utility serves philosophy directly; for this is indeed the opinion of the divine **Plato**, where he says: "whether these studies are difficult or easy, the path goes through them." <note>A reference to the *Epinomis* 992a, a work associated with the Platonic school.</note> It is titled*) **Elements**, <margin>10</margin> because whoever has not first been educated through them is unable to grasp any of the geometrical theorems. Geometry has built its presentation through **abstraction**; for it takes the **physical body**, which has three dimensions and **materiality**, and by the removal of its <margin>15</margin> materiality, geometry has formed the **mathematical body**, which is solid, and through further abstraction, it has then reached the **point**.

# Heron's Beginning of Geometrical Matters.

<margin>2</margin>
According to what ancient history teaches us, the majority of people were occupied with the measurements and distributions of land, which is why it was called **geometry** <note>From the Greek *ge* (earth) and *metron* (measure). The text emphasizes the practical roots of the science.</note>. This concept of measurement was discovered by the **Egyptians**; for because of the rising of the **Nile**, many areas that were visible became invisible upon the flood, and many others remained so even after the water receded, so that it was no longer possible for each person to distinguish their own property. Because of this, the Egyptians devised this method of measurement, sometimes using the so-called <term>surveying rope</term> <note>original: *schoinion*</note>, sometimes a <term>measuring reed</term> <note>original: *kalamos*</note>, and sometimes other measures. Since measurement was necessary, the need for it spread to every person who loves learning.

<margin>2</margin>
### Heron’s Beginning of Geometrical Investigations.

As ancient accounts teach us, most people were occupied with the measurement and distribution of land, from which the name **Geometry** <note>literally "earth-measurement," from the Greek *ge* (earth) and *metron* (measure)</note> originated. The invention of measurement, however, was made by the **Egyptians**; for because of the rising of the **Nile**, many plots of land that were clearly recognizable became unrecognizable due to the flood, and many remained so even after the waters receded. It was no longer possible for the individual to distinguish his own property; therefore, the Egyptians invented this method of measurement, sometimes with the so-called <term>measuring cord</term> <note>original: *schoinion*, a rope used by "rope-stretchers" to survey land</note>, sometimes with the <term>rod</term> <note>original: *rhabdos*</note>, and sometimes with other measures. Since measurement was a necessity, its use spread to all people who were eager to learn.

<margin>3</margin>
### Heron’s Introduction to Geometrical Investigations.

<margin>1</margin>
Plane geometry consists of <term>cardinal directions</term> <note>original: *klimata*</note>, <term>markers</term> <note>original: *skopelloi*, literally "lookouts" or "points of observation"</note>, **lines**, and **angles**, and it contains types, forms, and theorems.

<margin>2</margin>
There are 4 **cardinal directions**: East, West, North, and South.

<margin>3</margin>
A **marker** is any point that is taken.

<margin>4</margin>
There are ten types of **lines**: Straight, Parallel, Base-line, Vertex-line, Side-line <note>or "leg"</note>, Diagonal, Cathetus (which is also called the **Perpendicular**), Hypotenuse, Circumference, and Diameter.

<margin>5</margin>
A **straight line** is a line that is stretched straight.

<margin>6</margin>
A **parallel line** is another straight line that runs alongside a straight line and has the perpendicular distances at the endpoints equal to one another.

-># HERON<-

7. A **Base** <note>original: *basis*</note> is a straight line placed to receive another straight line, whether it is placed at the vertex, at right angles, or along the perimeter.

8. A **Vertex** <note>original: *koryphe*; in this context, Heron often refers to the side opposite the base, such as the top of a triangle or trapezoid, as the "summit" or "vertex line"</note> is the straight line placed upon the base.

9. **Legs** <note>original: *skele*; referring to the sides of a figure</note> are the straight lines <margin>5</margin> dropped from the ends of the vertex to the ends of the base.

10. A **Diagonal** is the straight line drawn from angle to angle in squares and similar figures.

11. A **Perpendicular** <note>original: *kathetos*</note>—also called "at right angles" [or even "center"]—is the straight line <margin>10</margin> dropped from the vertex to the base, making the two angles around it equal to one another.

12. A **Hypotenuse** <note>literally "stretching under"</note> is the straight line extending under the right angle.

13. A **Perimeter** <note>original: *perimetros*; here Heron uses the term to define what we call the circumference of a circle</note> is the line drawn from a given center and distance <margin>15</margin> <note>the radius</note>, having all the straight lines drawn from the center to itself equal.

14. A **Diameter** is a straight line cutting through the center and dividing the perimeter into two segments.

15. There are three **Angles**: right, acute, and obtuse.

16. A **Right angle** <margin>20</margin> occurs when a straight line standing upon another straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to each other; for then both are right angles.

17. But when one angle is larger and the other smaller, the larger—that is, the wider—is **Obtuse**, while the smaller—that is, the narrower—is **Acute**. <margin>25</margin>

**18** There are three kinds of measurement: linear, area, and solid.

-># GEOMETRICA #<-

<margin>18</margin> There are three kinds of measurement: linear measurement, surface measurement, and solid measurement.

<margin>19</margin> Linear measurement is anything measured in a straight line, as it has only length; it is also called "origin" and "number."

<margin>20</margin> <margin>5</margin> Surface measurement, however, is that which has length and width, and by which the area is recognized; it is also called <term>power</term> <note>original: *Potenz*, translating the Greek *dynamis*; in ancient mathematics, this refers to the square of a line or a two-dimensional area</note>.

<margin>21</margin> Solid measurement is that which has length, width, and thickness <margin>10</margin> and by which all physical bodies are recognized; it is also called a "cube."

<margin>22</margin> There are five forms of measurement: squares, triangles, rhombi, trapezoids, and circles.

-># OF HERON #<-

<margin>24</margin> These, then, are the forms and theorems regarding plane surfaces. Regarding solid bodies, when thickness is added to each measurement, there are ten special theorems of solids which are demonstrated in their own right, as follows: <margin>5</margin> the sphere, the cylinder, the cone, the truncated cone <note>a cone with the top cut off</note>, the cube, the wedge, the <term>meiouros</term> <note>original: *meiouros*; literally "mouse-tailed," referring to a four-sided figure that tapers toward the top but does not come to a single point like a pyramid</note>, the triangular pyramid, the truncated pyramid, and the <term>theater</term> <note>original: *theatron*; in Heron's geometry, this refers to a specific solid shape resembling the seating area of a semicircular theater</note>.

<margin>25</margin> There are also fixed rules of measurement established as follows: in every triangle, any two sides are greater <margin>10</margin> than the remaining side, no matter how they are compared. Also, in every right-angled triangle, the squares formed from the two sides containing the right angle are equal to the square formed from the hypotenuse <note>this is the famous Pythagorean theorem</note>. In every circle, the circumference is three times the diameter and one-seventh more <note>the approximation of Pi as 22/7</note>. Finally, <margin>15</margin> eleven squares of the diameter of the circle are equal in area to fourteen circles <note>original: *embadois dekatetrassi kyklōn*; this expresses the area of a circle as 11/14 of the square of its diameter, which follows from the Archimedean approximation of Pi</note>.

<margin>4</margin> The units of measure were discovered based on the parts of the human body: the finger-breadth <note>original: *daktylos*</note>, the palm <note>original: *palaistē*</note>, the span <note>original: *spithamē*</note>, the forefinger-span <note>original: *lichas*; the distance between the thumb and forefinger</note>, the foot <note>original: *pous*</note>, the cubit <note>original: *pēchys*</note>, the pace <note>original: *bēma*</note>, and the fathom <note>original: *orgyia*; the distance between the tips of the fingers when arms are outstretched</note>.

<summary>Hero introduces the ten primary solid figures of stereometry and defines fundamental geometric constants, including the Pythagorean theorem and the 22/7 approximation for a circle's circumference. He also provides the anthropometric origins of standard Greek units of measure.</summary>
<keywords>stereometry, solid geometry, Pythagorean theorem, Pi, Archimedean approximation, units of measure, Greek mathematics, Heron of Alexandria</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from two-dimensional plane geometry to the study of three-dimensional solid bodies. It categorizes ten specific types of solids and defines the standard geometric constants and anatomical units of measurement used in the Heronic tradition.</meta>

-># GEOMETRY #<-

<margin>24</margin> These are the forms and theorems of plane geometry; but in the case of solid bodies, thickness is added to every measurement. There are ten special theorems for solids that are demonstrated only in their particular context, namely: the sphere, the cylinder, the cone, the truncated cone <note>a cone with the top cut off</note>, the cube, the wedge, the tapered prism <note>literally "point-ending" prism</note>, the pyramid on a triangular base, the truncated pyramid, and the "theater" <term>theatron</term> <note>original: *theatron*; a solid shape resembling the tiered seating of a semicircular theater</note>.

<margin>25</margin> There are also the following fixed norms for measurement: in every triangle, any two sides, however they are swapped, are greater than the remaining side. In every right-angled triangle, the squares on the two sides enclosing the right angle are equal to the square on the hypotenuse <note>the famous Pythagorean theorem</note>. Also, the circumference of every circle is three times the diameter and one-seventh more <note>the approximation of Pi as 22/7</note>, and eleven squares on the diameter of a circle are equal in area to fourteen circles <note>this reflects the formula: Area = 11/14 of the diameter squared</note>.

---

<margin>4/1</margin> The units of measurement are derived from the parts of the human body: the finger <note>digit</note>, the palm, the span, the opening of the index finger <term>lichas</term>, the foot, the forearm <term>cubit</term>, the step, and the fathom <term>orguia</term>.

<margin>ss<sup>b</sup> 2</margin>
And a fathom <term>orgyia</term> <note>the distance between the fingertips of a man’s outstretched arms</note> is 96 fingers <term>dactyls</term>; a step <term>bema</term> is 40 fingers; and a cubit <term>pechys</term> <note>the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> is 24 fingers. The cubit contains 1 and 4/5 <note>original: 1 and 1/2 + 1/5 + 1/10</note> Roman feet, so that 9 feet are equal to 5 cubits.

<margin>3</margin>
The Philetaireian foot <note>a larger standard of measurement used in Pergamon and Egypt</note> contains 16 fingers; the Italian foot contains 13 and 1/3 fingers. The span <term>spithame</term> <note>the distance from the thumb to the pinky finger</note> is 12 fingers, and the index-span <term>lichas</term> is 8 fingers.

<margin>4</margin>
The palm <term>palaiste</term> is 4 fingers.

<column-break/>

<margin>AC 2</margin>
The smallest of all units is the finger, which is also called a "unit" <term>monad</term>. Sometimes it is divided further, for it permits a half, a third, and other fractions.

<margin>3</margin>
After the finger, which is the smallest part of all, is the palm. Some also call this a "fourth" because it contains four fingers, or because it is a fourth part of a foot. Others call it a "third" because it is a third of a span; for the span contains three palms, while the foot contains four.

<margin>4</margin>
The index-span <term>lichas</term> consists of two palms, or rather eight fingers, and it is called "two-thirds" of a span. The *lichas* is defined as the opening between two fingers—I mean the thumb and the index finger. Some people also call this the "dog’s mouth" <term>kynostomon</term>.

->### HERO'S GEOMETRICS ###<-

<page-num>190</page-num>

->HERO<-

<margin>10</margin> The palm <term>palaistes</term> <note>roughly the width of the four fingers of the hand</note> has 4 fingers <term>daktyloi</term>. The "lick" <term>lichas</term> <note>the span between the thumb and index finger</note> has 2 palms, or 8 fingers. The span <term>spithame</term> <note>the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger</note> has 3 palms, or 12 fingers; <margin>5</margin> it is also called the wood-cutter's cubit. The foot <term>pous</term> has 4 Royal or Philetaerian <note>original: "Philetaireious"; a measurement standard likely established by the Attalid dynasty of Pergamon</note> palms, or 16 fingers. <margin>10</margin> The Italian foot, however, has 13 1/3 fingers. The short-cubit <term>pygon</term> <note>the distance from the elbow to the first knuckles</note> has 5 palms, or 20 fingers. The cubit <term>pechus</term> <note>the standard cubit from elbow to fingertip</note> has 6 palms, or 24 fingers. <margin>15</margin> The Nilotic cubit <note>a standard used in Egypt for measuring the Nile's rise</note> has 7 palms, or 28 fingers. The Stoic cubit has 8 palms, or 32 fingers. The pace <term>bema</term> has 1 1/6 cubits, <margin>20</margin> or 10 palms, or 40 fingers, or 2 1/2 feet. The rod <term>xylon</term> <note>literally "wood"; a measuring stick</note> has 4 1/2 feet, or 3 cubits, or 18 palms, or 72 fingers.

# GEOMETRICA. #

<page-num>191</page-num>

<margin>10</margin> The palm <term>palaistes</term> <note>originally "Handbreit"; a unit based on the width of the four fingers</note> now consists of 4 digits <term>daktyloi</term> <note>originally "Zoll"; the smallest standard unit of length</note>; the "lick" or index-finger opening <term>lichas</term> has 2 palms, or 8 digits; the span <term>spithame</term> has 3 palms, or 12 digits, and it is also called the wood-cutter’s cubit. <margin>5</margin> The Royal and Philetaerian foot has 4 palms, or 16 digits, but the Italian foot has 13 1/3 digits. <margin>10</margin> The short-cubit <term>pygon</term> <note>the distance from the elbow to the first knuckles</note> has 5 palms, or 20 digits; the standard cubit <term>pechus</term> has 6 palms, or 24 digits. <margin>15</margin> The Nilotic cubit <note>used in Egyptian water-level measurement</note> has 7 palms, or 28 digits, while the Stoic cubit has 8 palms, or 32 digits. And the pace <term>bema</term> has 1 2/3 cubits, <margin>20</margin> which equals 10 palms, or 40 digits, or 2 1/2 feet. The rod <term>xylon</term> <note>a measuring pole or "wood"</note> has 4 1/2 feet, or 3 cubits, or 18 palms, or 72 digits.

<column-break/>

The stone-cutter's cubit has 2 spans, or 1 1/2 feet, or 6 palms, or 24 digits; the wood-sawyer's cubit is exactly the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>11</margin> The fathom <term>orguia</term>, with which arable land <note>land suitable for sowing crops</note> is measured, consists of 9 1/4 royal spans <term>spithamai</term>, or 6 feet and 1 1/4
<margin>5</margin> spans, or 27 palms—otherwise known as "fists" <term>gronthoi</term>—plus a thumb-width <term>anticheiron</term>. This is to say, twenty-six
<margin>10</margin> measures of a clenched hand, and the last one (or the first) with the large finger of the hand extended; this extended finger itself is called a "quarter-span" and consists of
<margin>15</margin> 3 digits. From this, you shall construct a fathom-measure on a reed or a piece of wood. After this, you ought to make a cord <term>schoinion</term> or rope <term>sokarion</term>
<margin>20</margin> ten fathoms long, and in this way measure the area you intend to survey. For the rope used for arable land ought to be ten fathoms, but for
<margin>25</margin> meadowland and boundaries, it should be twelve fathoms.

<margin>12</margin> And when using the ten-fathom cord, the area of a <term>modios</term> <note>A unit of land area based on the amount of grain needed to sow it; here specifically 200 square fathoms</note> consists of 
<margin>30</margin> exactly two hundred fathoms, but with the twelve-fathom [cord] it has <note>The text breaks off here</note>

<margin>13</margin> feet. The plethron <term>plethron</term> <note>a Greek unit of land measurement</note> consists of 10 rods <term>akainai</term> = 66 2/3 cubits <term>pecheis</term> = 100 Philetaerian feet <note>A standard foot unit used in Egypt and Asia Minor, slightly larger than the common Greek foot</note> = 120 Italian feet. 

The jugerum <term>iougeron</term> <note>the Roman acre</note> consists of 2 plethra = 20 rods = 133 1/3 cubits = 200 Philetaerian feet = 240 Italian feet. 

The stadium <term>stadion</term> consists of 6 plethra = 60 rods = 80 reeds <term>kalamoi</term> = 100 fathoms <term>orguiai</term> = 240 paces <term>bemata</term> = 400 cubits = 600 Philetaerian feet = 720 Italian feet. 

The double-course <term>diaulos</term> <note>a sprint of two stadia</note> consists of 2 stadia = 12 plethra = 120 rods = 160 reeds = 200 fathoms = 480 paces = 800 cubits = 1,200 Philetaerian feet = 1,440 Italian feet.

The long-course <term>dolichos</term> <note>a long-distance race</note> consists of 12 stadia...

<column-break/>

However, the smallest <margin>13</margin> and flat stretches must be measured with the ten-fathom cord <term>schoinion</term>, while the boundaries <margin>5</margin> of suburbs and areas measured all around must be measured with the twelve-fathom cord. 

This is because within the boundaries themselves, there are often <margin>10</margin> dry streambeds, lava <note>original: "Lava" — likely referring to volcanic rock or slag heaps common in certain regions</note>, brushwood, and other unusable spots. 

Alternatively, if they are measured with the ten-fathom <margin>15</margin> cord, a deduction must be made: either from the product of the measuring ropes, **one** measuring rope for every ten measuring ropes; or from the calculation of modii <margin>20</margin>, one modius <term>modius</term> <note>A unit of area based on the amount of grain needed to sow a field</note> for every ten modii, for the reasons mentioned above.

Of these, a 1/200th part becomes 79 1/4 1/8 1/200 <note>Heron uses unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/200 equals 76/200.</note>; and this is 79 modii <term>modius</term> <note>original: "modion"; a land unit equal to 200 square fathoms.</note> of land and 15 1/5 litrae <term>litra</term> <note>original: "litra"; a subdivision of a modius. Since 1 modius = 40 litrae, 1 litra = 5 square fathoms.</note>; <margin>5</margin> for the 15,876 fathoms, when divided by the 200, make 79 modii of land, and the remaining 76, when divided by the five, make 15 litrae of land and 1 fathom.

<margin>C 9</margin> **To find the diagonal of an equilateral right-angled square.** Do it thus: the 12 of one of the sides multiplied by itself; they become 144; these twice make 288; the square root of these is 17 <note>The square root of 288 is approximately 16.97; Heron rounds to the nearest whole number.</note>; and the diagonal is 17.

<margin>10</margin> **To find the diagonal of a rectangular parallelogram.** Do it thus: the 12 of the side multiplied by itself; they become 144; the 5 of the height multiplied by itself is 25; together they make 169; the square root of which becomes 13; and the diagonal is that many units.

# GEOMETRICA

Area. 1/200 × 15,876 = 79 1/4 1/8 1/200; and it is 79 fathoms <term>fathom</term> <note>original German: "Klafter"; representing the Greek "orguia", a unit of roughly 6 feet.</note> and 15 1/5 litrae <term>litra</term> <note>original German: "Liter"; a unit of land measurement.</note>; for 15,800 fathoms divided by 200 make 79 modii <term>modius</term> <note>original German: "Modien"; a land unit containing 200 square fathoms.</note> of land, and the remaining 76 divided by 5 make 15 litrae and 1 fathom of land.

<margin>5</margin> **To find the diagonal of an equilateral right-angled square.** Do it thus: 12 of the one side × 12 = 144; 2 × 144 = 288; the square root of 288 is approximately 17; and the diagonal is = 17 <note>The square root of 288 is ~16.97. Heron often uses the nearest whole number for simplicity in practical examples.</note>.

<margin>10</margin> **To find the diagonal of a rectangular parallelogram.** Do it thus: 12 of the side × 12 = 144; 5 of the <margin>15</margin> vertical side × 5 = 25; 144 + 25 = 169; the square root of 169 = 13; and that is the length of the diagonal.

<header>HERON'S GEOMETRY</header>

<margin>A 3</margin>
A rectangular parallelogram <note>A four-sided shape where opposite sides are equal and all angles are right angles.</note> has lengths of 80 <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: ὀργυιῶν; an "orguia" or fathom was the distance between the tips of the fingers of the two arms outspread, roughly 6 feet.</note> each and widths of 60 fathoms each. To find its area: multiply the 80 of the length by the 60 of the width; the area of the parallelogram thus becomes 4,800 fathoms. A two-hundredth part of these <note>Heron is using a specific conversion factor for land surveying: 200 square fathoms equals one modius.</note> becomes 24; and this is a land measure of twenty-four <term>modii</term> <note>original: μοδίων; the modius was a Roman dry measure used here to define an area of land that could be sown with one modius of grain.</note>.

<margin>C 4</margin>
A right-angled and equilateral quadrilateral <note>A square.</note> has an area of 100 fathoms. To find how many fathoms each side is: proceed as follows: take the square root of the 100; it becomes 10. Each side is this many fathoms.

<margin>AC 5</margin>
A rectangular parallelogram, which is also called "oblong" <note>original: ἑτερόμηκες; literally "of another length," meaning the sides are not equal.</note>, has lengths of 8 <term>chords</term> <note>original: σχοινίων; a "schoinion" or chord was a surveyor’s rope, often 100 feet or 60 cubits long.</note> each, and an area of 40 chords. To find the width: proceed as follows: take one-eighth of the 40; it becomes 5. The width is this many chords. To find the measurement in modii: multiply the 5 of the width by the 8 of the length; it becomes 40. Of these, take the half; it becomes <unclear>—</unclear> and it is a land measure of 20 modii.

# GEOMETRIC CALCULATIONS

<margin>3</margin> A rectangular parallelogram <note>A four-sided shape where opposite sides are parallel and the angles are 90 degrees.</note> with lengths of 80 <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: Klafter (German), representing the Greek "orguia." A fathom is approximately the span of a man's outstretched arms, or about 6 feet.</note> each and widths of 60 fathoms each; to find its area. Multiply the 80 of the length by the 60 of the width; the area of the parallelogram thus becomes 4,800 fathoms.
<margin>5</margin> <margin>1/200</margin> 1/200th of 4,800 = 24; and it equals 24 <term>modii</term> <note>original: Modien; a unit of land area based on the amount of seed required to sow it.</note> of land.

<margin>4</margin> A right-angled and equilateral quadrilateral <note>A square.</note> whose area is 100 fathoms; to find how many fathoms each of its sides measures. Proceed as follows: $\sqrt{100} = 10$; each side is that many fathoms.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>10</margin> A rectangular parallelogram, also called a rectangle <note>original: Rectangel</note>, whose lengths are 8 <term>chords</term> <note>original: Schoinien; a "schoinion" was a measuring rope used by surveyors, typically equal to 10 fathoms.</note> each and whose area is 40 chords; to find the width. Proceed as follows: $1/8 \times 40 = 5$; the width is that many chords. To find the number of modii: 5 for the width times 8 for the length equals 40; $1/2 \times 40$
<margin>15</margin> $= 20$; and it is 20 modii of land.

<meta>This page continues the geometric demonstrations of Heron, moving from a 30-40-50 triangle to one with sides 9, 40, and 41. It then introduces a new problem involving the conversion of linear measurements (chords and fathoms) into area and agricultural land units (modii).</meta>

### HERON

... [with] a base of 40 feet, a **hypotenuse** of 41 feet, and a **vertical height** of 9 feet; find its area and the vertical line.

->**RIGHT-ANGLED TRIANGLE**<-
Vertical side: 9
Base: 40
Hypotenuse: 41
**Area: 180**
Fig. 6.

I calculate it thus: 41 by itself <note>original: "ἐφ' ἑαυτά" (eph’ heauta); an ancient Greek mathematical expression for squaring a number.</note> becomes 1,681; and 40 by itself becomes 1,600. I subtract these from the 1,681 feet; the remainder is 81 feet; the square root <margin>6</margin> of these is 9 feet. Now I multiply the vertical by the base; it becomes 360; half <note>original: "$\angle'$"; a standard Greek symbol for 1/2.</note> of these becomes 180 feet. Let the area be 180 feet.

<column-break/>

... [a ba]se of 8 <term>chords</term> <note>original: "schoinia"; a Greek unit of length based on a surveyor's rope, roughly 100 feet or 60 cubits.</note> or 80 <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: "orguiai"; the distance between a man's outstretched arms, roughly 6 feet.</note>, and the vertical—that is, the side at right angles—is 6 chords or 60 fathoms, <margin>5</margin> and the hypotenuse is 10 chords or 100 fathoms; find the area. In the case of the chords, <margin>6</margin> proceed thus: taking half of the base, <margin>10</margin> namely the 4 chords, multiply them by the 6 of the vertical; the result is 24; and the area of the right-angled triangle is 24 chords. Half of these <margin>15</margin> becomes 12; and it is 12 <term>modii</term> <note>original: "modioi"; a unit of land area based on the amount of grain needed to sow a field, here used as a standard land measure.</note> of land. In the case of the <margin>7</margin> fathoms, proceed thus: taking the half of the base, <margin>20</margin> namely the 40 fathoms, multiply them by the 60 of the vertical thus: 40 [times] 60 = 2,400; and the area of the right-angled triangle is 2,400 fathoms. A two-hundredth part <margin>25</margin> of these becomes 12; and so it is also 12 modii of land.

---

<margin>AC 8</margin>
It should be known that for every right-angled triangle, the multiplications of the two sides of the right angle <note>i.e., the squares of the legs.</note> are equal to the multiplication of the remaining side, the hypotenuse <note>i.e., the square of the hypotenuse. This is a clear statement of the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>.

### HERON'S WORKS

9 For example, as a demonstration, let the two sides of a right-angled triangle forming the right angle be: the larger side—the one on the base, clearly—is 8 <term>chords</term> <note>original: "schoinia"; a Greek unit of length based on a surveyor's rope, roughly 100 feet.</note>, and the other is 6, that is, <margin>5</margin> the vertical side. To find the number of the hypotenuse from these, do as follows: multiply the 8 of the base by itself; it becomes 64. And multiply the 6 of the vertical by itself; it becomes 36. Then add the products of both sides together, namely 64 and 36; it becomes 100. Of these, take the square root; it becomes 10. And the hypotenuse is 10 chords [and <margin>10</margin> do the same for others likewise].

10 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A right-angled triangle, whose base is 16 chords, the vertical side is 12 chords, and the hypotenuse is 20 chords; to find the area. Do as follows: the 16 of the base times the 12 of the vertical; it becomes <margin>15</margin> 192. Half <note>original: "$\angle'$"; a symbol for one-half.</note> of these becomes 96; the area is that many chords. To find the <term>land-measure</term> <note>original: "modismos"; the calculation of area in land-units called modioi.</note>: take half of the 96;

11 it becomes 48; and it is 48 <term>modioi</term> <note>original: "modioi"; a unit of land area based on the amount of grain needed to sow a field.</note> of land. But if you wish [from the two sides about the right angle] to find the <margin>20</margin> hypotenuse, do as follows: the 16 of the base by itself; it becomes 256. And the 12 of the vertical by itself; it becomes 144. Together, 400; of which the square root

12 is 20; the hypotenuse is that many chords. If you <margin>25</margin> wish to find the vertical side, do as follows: the 20 of the hypotenuse by itself; it becomes 400. From these, take the 16 [of the base] by itself, [which becomes] 256; the remainder is 144. Of which the square root becomes 12; that is how many

13 chords the vertical side is. If you wish to find the base, likewise take from the 400 the product of the 12 of the vertical side by itself, 144; the remainder is 256. Of which the square <margin>30</margin> root becomes 16; the base is that many chords.

# GEOMETRIC WORKS

9 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Suppose, for example, in a right-angled triangle, of the two sides forming the right angle, the larger is 8 <term>chords</term> <note>original: "schoinia"; a Greek unit of length based on a surveyor's rope, approximately 100 feet.</note>—the one at the base, specifically—and the other, that is the vertical side, is 6. To find the length of the hypotenuse from these, proceed <margin>5</margin> as follows: multiply the 8 of the base by 8, which is 64; and multiply the 6 of the vertical side <note>original: "kathete"; the perpendicular side of a right triangle.</note> by 6, which is 36. Add the products of the two sides together, that is 64 + 36 = 100. The square root of 100 is 10; and so the hypotenuse is 10 chords.

10 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A right-angled triangle, whose base is 16 chords, <margin>10</margin> the vertical side is 12 chords, and the hypotenuse is 20 chords; to find the area <note>original: "Rauminhalt"; while this usually means 'volume' in modern German, in this historical context it refers to the surface area of the land.</note>. Proceed as follows: the 16 of the base multiplied by the 12 of the vertical side is 192. Half of 192 is 96; the area is that many chords. To find the <term>land-measure</term> <note>original: "modienzahl"; the calculation of area in units called modioi.</note>: half of 96 is 48; and it is 48 <term>modioi</term> <note>original: "modioi"; a unit of land area based on the amount of grain required to sow it.</note> of land. <margin>11</margin> If you wish to find the hypotenuse, proceed as follows: the 16 of the base times 16 is 256, and the 12 of the vertical side times 12 is 144; 256 + 144 = 400. The square root of 400 is 20; the hypotenuse is that many chords. <margin>12</margin> If you wish to find the vertical side, proceed as follows: the 20 of the hypotenuse times 20 is 400. From 400, subtract the square of the base (16 times 16, which is 256); 400 minus 256 is 144. The square root of 144 is 12; the vertical side is that many chords. <margin>13</margin> If you wish to find the base, likewise take 400 and subtract the square of the vertical side (12 times 12, which is 144); 400 minus 144 is 256. The square root of 256 is 16; the base is that many chords.

# HERON'S [GEOMETRY]

...perpendicular height of 26 <term>schoenia</term>.] <note>A schoenion was a standard unit of length used by ancient Greek surveyors, approximately 100 to 150 feet depending on the region.</note> Multiply these by the base, that is by 30; the result is 780; half of which is 390; and the area remains 390 schoenia. Of these again, take half; the result is 195; and it is 195 <term>modii</term> of land. <note>In agricultural geometry, land area was often expressed in modii, representing the amount of seed required to sow the field.</note>

->**On Isosceles Triangles**<-

<margin>11 SV 1</margin>
An <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>A triangle with two sides of equal length.</note>, whose <term>perpendicular height</term> <note>original: "kathetos." The vertical line from the peak to the base forming a right angle.</note> is 20 feet, and the base is 12 feet; to find its area. I proceed thus: the base times the height; the result is 240 feet; half of which; the result is 120 feet. Let the area be 120 feet.

<margin>2</margin>
In an isosceles triangle where each of the equal sides is 25 feet, and the base is 14 feet; to find its area and its height. I proceed thus: square each side; the result is 625 feet; I take half of the base; the result is 7 feet; multiply these by themselves; the result is 49 feet; the remainder is 576 feet; of which the <term>square root</term> <note>original: "pleura tetragonike," literally "the side of the square."</note> is 24 feet.

<margin>AC 1</margin>
An isosceles triangle is measured thus: let an isosceles triangle have each of its equal sides as 5 schoenia, and the base as 6 schoenia; to find the height. Do as follows: multiply one of the equal sides by itself; the result is 25; and half of the base, namely 3, multiplied by itself; the result is 9. Then subtract the 9 from the 25; the remainder is 16; of which the square root is 4; the height is so many schoenia.
