GEOMETRY.

## On scalene triangles. <margin>12</margin>

<margin>1</margin> Let there be an acute-angled <term>scalene triangle</term> <note>A triangle where all three sides have different lengths.</note>, whose shorter side is 13 <term>schoenia</term> <note>A Greek unit of land measurement.</note>, the base is 14 schoenia, and the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "hypoteinousa." In this context, Heron uses the term for the longest side of any triangle, not just a right-angled one.</note> is 15 schoenia; to find its <margin>5</margin> <term>perpendicular height</term> <note>original: "kathete." The vertical line from the top vertex to the base.</note>. Proceed as follows: 13 (the shorter side) $\times$ 13 = 169; 14 (the base) $\times$ 14 = 196; 15 (the hypotenuse) $\times$ 15 = 225. Then add the product of the base and that of the hypotenuse, that is, 196 + 225 = 421; from this, subtract the product of the shorter side, 421 - 169 = 252; $\frac{1}{2} \times$ 252 <margin>10</margin> = 126; 126 divided by 14 (the base) = 9; this many schoenia is the <term>segment</term> <note>original: "apotome." The part of the base from a corner to where the height line meets it.</note>.$^{*)}$ 9 $\times$ 9 = 81; subtract 81 from the product of the hypotenuse, that is, 225 - 81 = 144; the square root of 144 is 12; this many schoenia is the perpendicular height.

<margin>2</margin> By another method. Add the product of the base <margin>15</margin> and that of the shorter side, that is, 196 + 169 = 365; subtract from this the product of the hypotenuse, that is, 365 - 225 = 140; $\frac{1}{2} \times 140 = 70$; $\frac{1}{14} \times 70 = 5$; this many schoenia is the [other] segment.$^{**)}$ 5 $\times$ 5 = 25; 169 - 25 = 144; the square root of 144 is 12; this many schoenia is the perpendicular height.

<margin>3</margin> <margin>20</margin> And to find the <term>area</term> <note>original: "Rauminhalt," literally "volume" or "content," but used here for the surface area.</note>. Proceed as follows: $\frac{1}{2} \times$ the base = 7; 7 $\times$ the perpendicular height = 7 $\times$ 12 = 84; this much is the area of the scalene triangle. $\frac{1}{2} \times 84 = 42$; and it is 42 <term>modien</term> <note>A unit of land area, originally a dry measure for grain, used here to denote the amount of seed required to sow the field.</note> of land.

---

$^{*)}$ $y = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2b}$ ($b$ is the base, $a$ the shorter side, $c$ the hypotenuse, and $y$ is the projection/segment of the base under side $c$). &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $^{**)} b - y = \frac{b^2 + a^2 - c^2}{2b}$

OF HERON

<margin>4</margin> The measurement is performed in another way for such a triangle, whose base is 13 <term>schoenia</term> <note>A Greek unit of land measurement, roughly 100-200 feet depending on the region.</note>, the greater side 15 schoenia, and the smaller side 14 schoenia; to find its perpendicular height. Do it as follows: combine the <margin>5</margin> square of the base and the square of one of the sides, namely 169 <note>original: "$\overline{\rho\xi\theta}$." $13 \times 13$.</note> and 196 <note>original: "$\overline{\rhoϟς}$." $14 \times 14$.</note>; they make 365. From these, subtract the square of the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "hypoteinousa." Here used for the remaining side, 15.</note>, namely 225; the remainder is 140. Of these, take the half, which is 70. Divide these by the 13 units of the base; the result is 5 units and 5 <term>thirteenths</term> <note>original: "$\iota\gamma'$." Heron works here with fractions of 13.</note>.
<margin>5</margin> This is the length of the <term>segment</term> <note>original: "apotome." The segment of the base created by the drop of the perpendicular height line.</note>. Square this value: it results in <margin>10</margin> 29 units minus a <term>thirteenth of a thirteenth</term> <note>original: "$\iota\gamma'$ τὸ $\iota\gamma'$." This is $1/169$. $(5 + 5/13)^2 = 70/13 \times 70/13 = 4900/169$, which equals $28 + 168/169$, or $29 - 1/169$.</note>. The multiplication is done as follows: 5 times 5 is 25; and five times the 5 thirteenths is 25 thirteenths; and again, 5 thirteenths times the 5 units is 25 thirteenths; and 5 thirteenths times the 5 thirteenths results in 25 <margin>15</margin> thirteenths of a thirteenth. Together, these make 25 units and 50 thirteenths and 25 thirteenths of a thirteenth. These 50 thirteenths make 3 units and 11 thirteenths. Thus, the total is 28 units, 11 thirteenths, and 25 thirteenths of a thirteenth. <note>In Heron's precise system, $11/13$ is $143/169$. $143/169 + 25/169 = 168/169$. As noted before, this is 29 units minus 1/169.</note> Subtract this from the square of the adjacent side, that is, from 196. The remainder is 167 <note>The OCR reads "$\overline{\rho\xi\xi}$" (166), but the calculation $196 - (29 - 1/169)$ requires $167 + 1/169$.</note> units and a thirteenth of a thirteenth. The square root of this is 12 units and 12 thirteenths.
<margin>6</margin> This many schoenia will be the perpendicular height. The 12 units and 12 thirteenths are multiplied thus: 12 times 12 is 144; and 12 times the 12 thirteenths is 144 thirteenths; and again 12 thirteenths times the 12 units is 144 thirteenths; and 12 thirteenths times the 12 thirteenths <margin>25</margin> is 144 thirteenths of a thirteenth. Together, this makes 144 units, 288 thirteenths, and 144 thirteenths of a thirteenth. The 288 thirteenths make 22 units and 2 thirteenths. Therefore, the total is 167 units and a thirteenth of a thirteenth. Consequently, the perpendicular height of the present triangle is 12 <margin>30</margin> schoenia and 12 thirteenths.

OF HERON

...84 <term>cords</term> <note>original: "schoinia." A Greek unit of length used in land surveying, often roughly 100 or 200 feet depending on the region.</note>. Of which the half is 42; and it is 42 <term>modii</term> <note>original: "modioi." <margin>C 29</margin> Another right-angled scalene triangle, of which the greater side is 20 cords, the smaller side is 15 cords, and the base is 25 cords; of the greater <margin>5</margin> segment, the base is 16 cords, of the smaller, it is 9 cords, and the **perpendicular** <note>original: "orthē." Referring to the altitude or height of the triangle.</note> of both is 12 cords. To find its **area** <note>original: "embadon." The surface area.</note>: do it thus: multiply the 12 of the height by the half of the base—that is, by 12 1/2; the result is 150. And the area <margin>10</margin> of the whole triangle is 150 cords. Of which the half becomes 75; and it is that many modii of land.

### Another general measurement for every triangle.

<margin>AC 30</margin> You shall measure any triangle whatsoever in this way: for example, let one of the sides of a triangle be 13 cords, another 14 <margin>15</margin> cords, and the third 15 cords. To find its area: do it thus: add the 13 and the 14 and the 15; the sum is 42. Of these, the half is 21. From this 21, subtract the three sides one by one; that is, subtract 13, remainder 8; and 14, remainder 7; and 15, remainder 6. <margin>20</margin> Multiply these by one another: 21 times 8 is 168; this times 7 is 1,176; this times 6 is 7,056. Of these, the **square root** <note>original: "pleura tetragoniki," literally the "side of the square."</note> is 84. The area of the triangle is that many cords.

<margin>31</margin> Alternatively: let the sides be 13, 14, and 15. Together they are 42. The half is 21. Subtract from the 21 <margin>25</margin> the 13, remainder 8; and the 14, remainder 7; and the 15, remainder 6. Multiply the 6 by the 7, which is 42; this times the 8 is 336; this times the 21 is 7,056. Of these, take the square root; it is 84. The area of the triangle is that much. ### HERON

...sides, and for isosceles, and for scalene, and for right-angled triangles, we always do this.

<margin>32</margin> A **scalene right-angled** triangle <note>A triangle with a 90-degree angle where all three sides are of different lengths.</note>, of which the base is 12 <term>cords</term> <note>original: "schoinion." A standard Greek unit of length used in surveying, approximately 100 feet.</note> and the side at right angles is 5 cords, and the **hypotenuse** <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the 90-degree angle.</note> is 13 cords; to find its area. Proceed according to the previously described method <note>This refers to Heron’s Formula, which calculates area using only the lengths of the sides.</note>. Add the three sides together; they become 30; of which the half is 15. From these 15, subtract each side: from 12, the remainder is 3; from 5, the remainder is 10; from 13, the remainder is 2. And combine all the remainders—that is 3, 10, and 2; they become 15 <note>The author notes that the sum of the differences from the semi-perimeter (15) equals the semi-perimeter itself as a check of the math.</note>. Multiply these <note>the semi-perimeter, 15</note> by the 2; they become 30. And the 30 by the 3; they become 90. And the 90 by the 10; they become 900. Of which the **square root** <note>original: "pleura tetragonike," literally "the side of the square."</note> is 30. The area of the scalene triangle will be that many cords. And this method is valid for every triangle.

First, then, one must find how many cords the extended line is, and how many the perpendicular is. <margin>34</margin> It is found thus: multiply the 17 of the side opposite the obtuse angle by itself; it becomes 289. From these, subtract the 9 of the base multiplied by itself, which is 81, and the 10 of the obtuse side multiplied by itself, which is 100; together they make 181. The remainder is 108. Of which the half is 54. Divide these by the 9 of the base; it becomes 6. The extended line is that many cords. <margin>35</margin> And so the additional triangle was formed, whose base is 6 cords, the side <note>The hypotenuse of the new small right triangle</note> is 10 cords, and the perpendicular is 8 cords; to find the area of the...

...base line = 6 <term>schoinia</term> <note>A schoinion is an ancient Greek unit of distance, literally a "measuring rope," often used in land surveying.</note>, the obtuse side = 10 schoinia, the perpendicular = 8 schoinia\*; to find the area of the added triangle <note>This "added triangle" is the right-angled triangle created by extending the base of the main triangle to meet the perpendicular line.</note>. ### BY HERON

...angle is 36 <term>schoinia</term> <note>A unit of area here, though derived from the linear "measuring rope" of the same name.</note>, and the smaller part of the added calculation—the right-angled triangle—is 24 schoinia.

<margin>C 41</margin> In obtuse-angled triangles, the square on the side stretching under the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle. It is larger by twice the rectangle formed by one of the sides around the obtuse angle (the one upon which the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>Original Greek: "kathete."</note> falls) and the line segment cut off outside by the perpendicular at the obtuse angle.

<margin>42</margin> One must know that the <term>fathom</term> <note>Original Greek: "orguia." Usually the distance between the tips of the fingers of the outstretched arms.</note> consists of 9 1/4 <term>spans</term> <note>Original Greek: "spithamai."</note> or 28 <term>palms</term> <note>Original Greek: "palaistai."</note>, where the first palm has an additional "knuckle-breadth" <note>Original Greek: "kondylos."</note> added to it. And another way: let a man of average height, neither short nor tall, stand upright and extend his right hand upward; wherever the tips of his fingers reach, that is the measure of a standard fathom. And in another way: let a middle-aged man take a rope or a rod and step on the end of it with his toes; then let him pull the rope up to his shoulder, and from there bend it back down to his buttock; this will produce a most accurate fathom.

# HERON

Now, a rhombus is measured as follows: let there be a rhombus shape, of which each of the sides is 10 <term>schoinia</term> <note>A "rope measure" used in Greek surveying, roughly 100 feet</note>, one of the diagonals is 12 <term>schoinia</term>, and the other diagonal is 16 <term>schoinia</term>. To find the area of the rhombus: take 1/2 <note>original: "∠'"—the Greek symbol for one-half</note> of one of the diagonals and 
<margin>5</margin> multiply it by the other whole diagonal—that is, 6 times 16, or 8 times 12; the result is 96. And the area of the rhombus is 96 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of these <note>Hero often divides the square area by two to convert to land-tax units</note> results in 48; thus it is 48 <term>modii</term> <note>A unit of land area, roughly equivalent to a quarter-acre in this context</note> of land.

<margin>2</margin> Another way for the same figure: A rhombus, of which each side is 10 <term>schoinia</term>, and the diagonal is 12 <term>schoinia</term>. Find 
<margin>10</margin> both its perpendicular altitude and its area. Do it like this: take 1/2 of the 12 of the diagonal; it becomes 6. Square these; they become 36. And square the 10 of the side; they become 100. From these take the 36; the remainder is 64. The square root of these 
<margin>15</margin> becomes 8; the perpendicular altitude will be that many <term>schoinia</term>. And if you wish to find the area as well, do it like this: multiply the 8 of the perpendicular altitude by the 12 of the base; the result is 96. Take 1/2 of these; they become 48. This is the area in <term>schoinia</term> of half of the 
<margin>20</margin> rhombus, which means the whole rhombus is 96 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of these becomes 48; and the area of the whole rhombus is 48 <term>modii</term> of land.

<margin>25</margin> become 600. And the area of the rhombus is 600 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of these becomes 300; and it is 300 <term>modii</term> of land.

### GEOMETRY

...of the acute-angled triangles is 30 <term>schoinia</term> <note>A "rope measure" used in ancient surveying, roughly 100 feet or 30 meters</note> and each of the equal sides is 25 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of the base—or 15—multiplied by 15 equals 225; the side of 25 multiplied by 25 equals 625; 625 minus 225 equals 400; the square root of 400 is 20; this many <term>schoinia</term> will be the <term>cathetus</term> <note>The perpendicular height or altitude of the triangle</note>
<margin>5</margin> of each individual acute-angled triangle. This multiplied by half the base—or 20 times 15—equals 300; and the <term>area</term> of each individual acute-angled triangle is 300 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of 300 is 150; and these are both 150 <term>modii</term> <note>A unit of area; in this context, one modius is equivalent to half a square schoinion</note> of land each.

<margin>10</margin> <margin>5</margin> Let again the base of each individual obtuse-angled triangle be 40 <term>schoinia</term>, while each of the equal sides be 25 <term>schoinia</term>. 25 times 25 equals 625; half the base—or 20—times 20 equals 400; 625 minus 400 equals 225; the square root of 225 is 15; that many <term>schoinia</term> is the <term>cathetus</term> of each individual obtuse-angled
<margin>15</margin> triangle. 15 times half the base—or 15 times 20—equals 300; and the area of each individual obtuse-angled triangle is 300 <term>schoinia</term>. Again, half of 300 is 150; and each individual triangle is 150 <term>modii</term> of land. Together, the area of both triangles is 600 <term>schoinia</term>. Half of 600
<margin>20</margin> equals 300; and the area of the whole <term>rhombus</term> <note>An equilateral parallelogram</note> is 300 <term>modii</term> of land.

I divide these by the 8 of the base; the result is 2 <gloss>and</gloss> ½ <gloss>and</gloss> ¼ <note>equivalent to 2.75</note>. Therefore, the base of the smaller segment will be 2 ½ ¼ schoinia. Square these; they make 7 ½ <gloss>and</gloss> ¹/₁₆ <note>equivalent to 7.5625</note>.
<margin>10</margin>I subtract these from the 16; the remainder is 8 ¼ ⅛ ¹/₁₆ <note>equivalent to 8.4375</note>. The square root of this is approximately 2 ⅔ ¼. This is the length of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>original: κάθετος; the vertical height of the triangle.</note>. Again, I add the 8 of the base squared, 64, and the 6 of the larger side squared,
<margin>15</margin>36; they make 100 together. From these I subtract the 4 of the smaller side squared, 16; remainder 84, of which the half is 42. I divide these by the eight of the base; the result is 5 ¼. Therefore, the base of the larger segment will also be 5 ¼ schoinia. Square these; they make 27 ½ ¹/₁₆.
<margin>20</margin>I subtract these from the 36; the remainder is 8 ¼ ⅛ ¹/₁₆. The square root is approximately 2 ⅔ ¼. This is the length of the perpendicular. The 2 ⅔ ¼ of the perpendicular multiplied by half of the base—that is, by 4—makes 11 ⅔. And the area of each triangle is this many schoinia; and for both triangles, which is to say the whole
<margin>25</margin><term>rhomboid parallelogram</term> <note>A four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel, but with unequal adjacent sides and non-right angles.</note>, the area is 23 ⅓ schoinia. Half of this is 11 ⅔; and this is equal to 11 <term>modioi</term> <note>A unit of land area based on the amount of grain needed to sow it.</note> and 26 ⅔ <term>litrai</term> <note>A smaller unit of land measurement; in this system, 1 modios equals 40 litrai.</note> of land.

<margin>8</margin> A rhomboid parallelogram is divided into three sections: namely, into one rectangular parallelogram and into two scalene <note>A triangle with no equal sides</note> right-angled triangles. <margin>9</margin> The base of each individual right-angled triangle is 6 1/2 schoinia, and the perpendicular <note>The line meeting the base at a right angle (altitude)</note> is 6 schoinia and fractions of 1/13, 1/13, and 8. Together, the area of the three sections—that is, the one rectangular parallelogram and the two right-angled triangles—is again 79 1/3 1/26 1/78 schoinia, which is 39 1/2 1/8 1/39 modii of land.

**12**      If such a rhomboid is divided into one rectangular parallelogram and two <term>scalene</term> <note>a triangle where all sides are of different lengths</note> right-angled triangles, the measurement of each segment is found as follows: the top and the base of the rectangular parallelogram are each 4 1/2 schoinia, while the two <margin>15</margin> vertical sides correspond to the previously stated number for the altitude of the triangles. # THE GEOMETRICS OF HERON

...and the other of the diagonals likewise. Such a figure is bisected along the aforementioned diagonal and produces two <term>isosceles</term> <note>triangles with two equal sides</note> <term>obtuse-angled</term> <note>having one angle greater than 90 degrees</note> triangles. How one must measure such triangles has been written previously in many places, but for the sake of <margin>5</margin> a fuller understanding, it must be stated once again.

**18** The base of each individual isosceles obtuse-angled triangle is 24 <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: "orgyiai," a unit of length roughly equal to 6 feet, the span of a man's outstretched arms</note>, and each of the equal sides is 15 fathoms. The 15 of one of the sides, multiplied by itself, becomes 225; and <margin>10</margin> half <note>original: "$L'$"</note> of the base—namely the 12—multiplied by itself becomes 144. Subtract these from the 225; the remainder is 81. The square root of this is 9; the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>the vertical height or altitude</note> will be that many fathoms. These [9], multiplied by half of the base—namely by the 12 fathoms—becomes 108; and the area of each <margin>15</margin> individual triangle is 108 fathoms. Together, the area of both triangles—that is, of the whole rhomboid—is 216 fathoms, which is 1 <term>modius</term> <note>a unit of land area based on the amount of seed required to sow it</note> of land, 3 <term>litrai</term> <note>literally "pounds," here used as a fractional division of a modius of land</note>, and 1 fathom.

**19** The same rhomboid may also be divided into three parts: <margin>20</margin> namely, into one rectangular <term>parallelogram</term> and into two <term>scalene</term> <note>triangles with three unequal sides</note> right-angled triangles, as follows. The top and the base of the rectangular parallelogram are 12 fathoms each, and the two vertical sides are 9 fathoms each; to find its area: Multiply the 12 of the base <margin>25</margin> by the 9 of the one side; it becomes 108; and its area will be 108 fathoms. The base of each of the right-angled triangles is 12 fathoms, the vertical side is 9 fathoms, and the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>the longest side opposite the right angle</note> is 15 fathoms; to find the area of each of these: Take half the <margin>30</margin> base; it becomes 6. Multiply these by the 9 of the vertical side; it becomes 54; and the area of each tri- [angle is 54].

## Regarding the remaining four-sided figures, also called <term>trapeziums</term> <note>a four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides</note>. ##

<margin>5</margin> <margin>1</margin>
A right-angled trapezium, in which one of the <term>perpendiculars</term> <note>the "legs" or vertical sides of the shape</note> or lateral sides is 8 <term>schoenia</term> <note>a unit of land measurement, literally "surveying ropes"</note>, the other is 6 schoenia, and the base is 10 schoenia; to find its area: 8 + 6 = 14; 1/2 × 14 = 7; 7 × 10 (the base) = 70; and the area of the right-<margin>10</margin>angled trapezium is 70 schoenia. 1/2 × 70 = 35; and it is 35 modii of land.

<margin>2</margin>
Such a trapezium is also divided into a right-angled <term>parallelogram</term> <note>here meaning a rectangle</note> and a right-angled triangle. And the measurement of each of these is done as follows: the two <margin>15</margin> perpendiculars*) of the parallelogram are each 6 schoenia, and the two bases*) are each 10 schoenia; 10 (one base) × 6 (one perpendicular) = 60; and the area of the parallelogram is 60 schoenia. The base of the <margin>3</margin> right-angled triangle is 10 schoenia, while its <margin>20</margin> <term>altitude</term> <note>the vertical height of the triangular section, found by subtracting the shorter side (6) from the longer side (8)</note> is 2 schoenia. 1/2 of the base = 5 schoenia; 5 × 2 (the altitude) = 10; and its area is 10 schoenia. Everything together; and once again, the area of the two segments—that is, the parallelogram and the triangle—is 70 schoenia. 1/2 × 70 = 35; and <margin>25</margin> the space of the whole right-angled trapezium is 35 modii of land.

### GEOMETRICA ###

The vertical side—or <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "Kathete," the perpendicular leg of a right-angled shape</note>—is 12 <term>schoenia</term> <note>original: "Schoinien," a unit of measurement based on a surveyor's rope</note>, the top edge is 8 schoenia, and the base line is 16 schoenia; to find its area. Top edge plus base line, or 8 + 16 = 24; 1/2 × 24 = 12; 12 × 12 of the perpendicular <margin>5</margin> is 144; and its area is 144 schoenia. 1/2 × 144 = 72; and the land-measure of this same trapezium is 72 <term>modii</term> <note>original: "Modien," a unit of area where 1 modius typically equals 2 square schoenia in this context</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
The same right-angled trapezium divided into a right-angled <term>parallelogram</term> <note>here meaning a rectangle</note> and a scalene right-angled triangle. The base of the right-angled triangle is 8 schoenia, while its perpendicular—that is, the cathetus—is 12 <margin>15</margin> schoenia; 1/2 of the base, or 4 × 12 of the cathetus, makes 48, and these likewise indicate the area of the triangle. Everything together; and once again the area of both parts is 144 schoenia. Half of this is the number of modii. <margin>20</margin> The parallelogram is double the right-angled triangle.

<margin>7</margin>The base is 20 <term>schoenia</term> <note>original: "schoinia," a standard unit of length for land measurement</note>; square these; they make 400. The square of the other side is 208. To find its <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "kathetos," the perpendicular height</note>: add the square of the base and the square of the one side—that is, 400 and 208; <margin>5</margin> they make 608. From these, subtract the square of the other side—that is, 64; the remainder is 544. Half of these make 272. Dividing these by the 20 of the base makes 13 1/2 1/10. Therefore, the greater segment of the base will be this many schoenia. Likewise, add the 400 of the base and the 64 <margin>10</margin> of the lesser side; they make 464. From these, take away the 208 of the other side; the remainder is 256. Half of these is 128. Dividing these likewise by the 20 of the base makes 6 1/3 1/15. Thus, the lesser segment of the base will be 6 and two-fifths <note>original: "6 1/5 1/5", Heron often expresses 2/5 as 1/5 + 1/5</note> schoenia. Square these; they make <margin>15</margin> 40 units and four-twenty-fifths, and 4/25 of the 1/25. Subtract these from the 64; the remainder is 23 units and 1/25. The square root of these is 4 1/2 1/5 1/10. This many schoenia <margin>8</margin> is the perpendicular. Again, square the 13 1/2 1/10; they make 184 units and four-twenty-fifths and 4/25 of the 1/25. Subtract these <margin>20</margin> from the 208; the remainder is 23 units and 1/25. The square root of these is likewise 4 1/2 1/5 1/10. Therefore, the perpendicular will be this many schoenia. To find its area: take half of the base; it makes 10. Multiply these by the 4 1/2 1/5 1/10 of the perpendicular; the result is <margin>25</margin> 48. And the area of the obtuse-angled triangle is 48 schoenia. The area of both triangles together is 144 schoenia. Half of this is 72; and the measure of the whole right-angled trapezium is 72 <term>modii</term> <note>a unit of dry measure used here to denote area</note>.

An **isosceles trapezoid**, whose top line = 4 <margin>17</margin> <term>schoenia</term> <note>original: "schoinia"; a Greek unit of distance based on a surveyor's rope</note>, the base however = 16 schoenia and each of the equal sides = 10 schoenia; to find its perpendicular. <margin>15</margin> Base $-$ top line <note>The text uses a division symbol "$\div$" in the OCR, but the mathematical logic of the operation $16-4=12$ indicates a subtraction or finding the difference</note> or $16 - 4 = 12$; $1/2 \times 12 = 6$; $6 \times 6 = 36$; 10 of the one side $\times 10 = 100; 100 - 36 = 64; \sqrt{64} = 8$; and the perpendicular is so many schoenia. And to find the area. Do thus: top line + base or $4 + 16 = 20; 1/2 \times 20 = 10; 10 \times 8$ of the <margin>20</margin> perpendicular = 80; and the area of the same isosceles trapezoid = 80 schoenia. $1/2 \times 80 = 40$; and it is 40 modii of land.

The same isosceles trapezoid is divided into three pieces, <margin>18</margin> namely into a right-angled parallelogram and two <margin>25</margin> scalene <note>original: "ungleichschenklige"; literally "unequal-legged"</note>, likewise right-angled triangles. The top line and the base of the parallelogram = 4 schoenia, but the 2 legs*) each = 8 schoenia. To find its area. 4 of the width $\times$ 8 of the length = 32; and the area of the parallelogram = 32 schoenia.

20 Another isosceles trapezoid, of which the top is 2 schoenia, the base is 18 schoenia, and the two sides are 10 schoenia each; to find its perpendicular. <vocab>
**Schoenia**: (Greek: schoinia) Plural of schoenion, a measurement based on a surveyor's rope.
**Modii**: (Greek: modioi) Units of land measurement used here to calculate agricultural value or tax.
**Trapezoid**: A four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides.
**Altitude**: (German: Kathete/Senkrechte) The vertical height of a shape measured at a right angle to the base.
**Pythagorean Theorem**: The method used here (squaring the side and subtracting the squared base-segment) to find the height of the trapezoid.
</vocab>

Likewise, subtract from the same [8 1/2] the 6 of the second side, and 2 1/2 are left. In the same way, subtract the 8 of the remaining side, and 1/2 is left. Then multiply the half [1/2] by the 2 1/2; it becomes 1 1/4. Likewise, multiply the 1 1/4 by the 5 1/2; they become 6 1/2 1/4 1/8 <note>Equivalent to 6.875.</note>. The area of such a triangle is this many schoenia.

### HERON'S WORKS

<margin>43</margin> ...an obtuse-angled triangle <note>original: "βλυγώνιον" (amblygonion). The text likely refers to the relationship between the shapes being measured.</note> is four times the right-angled one. The measurement of each individual section is as follows: the base of the isosceles triangle is 12 <term>schoenia</term> <note>A Greek unit of length, used here in its square form for area.</note>, and its perpendicular height is 6 schoenia. Half of the base, namely 6, multiplied by the 6 of the height, equals 36; and the area of the isosceles triangle is 36 schoenia. Half of these equals 18; and it is 18 <term>modii</term> <note>A unit of land area; in this system, 1 modios is calculated as half the value of the area in square schoenia.</note> of land.

<margin>44</margin> The top of the right-angled trapezoid is 9 schoenia, the base is 3 schoenia, and its side at right angles is 6 schoenia. The 9 of the top and the 3 of the base added together equal 12; half of which is 6. These multiplied by the 6 of the side at right angles equal 36, and indicate the area of the same right-angled trapezoid. Then, being halved, they become 18, and indicate the <term>modios-measurement</term> <note>original: "modismos," the process of determining land value in modii.</note>; therefore, such a right-angled trapezoid is equal to the isosceles triangle.

<margin>45</margin> The two sides of the right angle of the right-angled triangle are 3 schoenia each. The 3 of the one side multiplied by the 3 of the other equals 9; half of which is 4 1/2; and the area of it is 4 1/2 schoenia. When these are subtracted from the area of the larger right-angled triangle—that is, from the 22 1/2 <note>This 22 1/2 refers back to the calculation concluding on the previous page.</note>—there remain 18, and they indicate

<margin>46</margin> the area of the scalene obtuse-angled triangle. Altogether: and again, the area of the four sections—the isosceles triangle, the smaller right-angled trapezoid, the smaller right-angled triangle, and the scalene obtuse-angled triangle—is 94 1/2 schoenia. Half of these equals 47 1/4; and the modios-measurement of these, or rather of the whole figure, is 47 modii and 10 <term>litrae</term> <note>A subunit of the modios; 1 modios = 40 litrae, so 1/4 modios = 10 litrae.</note>.

1 **Suppose there is a circle**, whose circumference = 22 <term>schoenia</term> <note>A schoenion was an ancient unit of measurement, often used in land surveying; here it refers to a linear unit, though the final area is in square schoenia.</note>, the <margin>1</margin> diameter = 7 schoenia; find its area. Do it this way: 7 of the diameter $\times$ 22 of the circumference = 154; $\frac{1}{4} \times 154 = 38\frac{1}{2}$;*) so many schoenia will the area <margin>5</margin> of the circle be.

2 **If you also want to find the area in another way**, <margin>2</margin> do it this way: $\frac{1}{2} \times$ diameter = $3\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{2} \times$ circumference = 11; $3\frac{1}{2} \times 11 = 38\frac{1}{2}$; so many schoenia will the area of the circle be.
<margin>10</margin> 3 **If you want to find the area from the circumference alone**, <margin>3</margin> do it this way: 22 of the circumference $\times$ 22 = 484; 7 $\times$ 484 = 3388; 3388 : 88 = $38\frac{1}{2}$; so many schoenia will the area of the circle be.*)

<margin>4</margin> 4 **Suppose there is a circle** whose diameter = 14 feet; the circumference will then be found, according to the description, to be 44 feet;*) for the area, however, do it this way: always the diameter multiplied by itself; gives 196; 11 $\times$ 196 = 2156; 2156 : 14 = 154; so much will the area be.

5 **According to Euclid**, however, <margin>5</margin> the circle is measured thus: the <margin>10</margin> diameter is multiplied by itself, and from the product you subtract $\frac{1}{7}$ and $\frac{1}{14}$, so that the area of the circle is $38\frac{1}{2}$ schoenia.*)

<meta>This page continues the mathematical handbook attributed to Heron of Alexandria. # GEOMETRY

...always multiply this by 7; it gives 308. Of these, take the 22nd part, which is 14. Determine that the diameter of the circle is that many <term>schoenia</term>. <note>A schoenion was a unit of measurement used in ancient land surveying; its exact length varied but was often around 150–180 feet.</note>

### 13. To find the area of a circle from the perimeter alone.
Proceed as follows: always multiply the perimeter by itself—that is, 44 × 44 = 1,936.
<margin>5</margin> 7 × 1,936 = 13,552.
1/88 of 13,552 = 154. Count the area of the circle as that many schoenia. <note>This formula is $Area = \frac{7 \times \text{Perimeter}^2}{88}$, which is derived from $A = \frac{P^2}{4\pi}$ using $\pi \approx \frac{22}{7}$.</note>

### 14. To find the area of a circle from the diameter alone.
Proceed as follows: 14 × 14 = 196.
Take 1/7 and 1/14 of 196, which is 42. <note>original: "1/7 1/14 × 196". This is a shortcut for 3/14 of the diameter squared. 196 / 7 = 28; 196 / 14 = 14; 28 + 14 = 42.</note>
<margin>10</margin> 196 minus 42 = 154. <note>The German OCR shows a division sign (÷), but the mathematical logic and the Greek manuscripts A and C indicate subtraction (196 - 42 = 154).</note> Count the area of the circle as that many schoenia in surface measure.

### 15. Another way to find the area of a circle from the diameter alone.
14 × 14 = 196.
<margin>15</margin> 11 × 196 = 2,156.
1/14 of 2,156 = 154. The area of the circle is that many schoenia. <note>This is the standard formula $Area = \frac{11}{14} \times d^2$.</note>

### 16. Another way to find the area of a circle from the diameter alone.
Let the diameter of the circle be 14 schoenia.
1/2 of the diameter = 7.
7 × 7 = 49.
<margin>20</margin> 3 × 49 = 147.
1/7 of 49 = 7.
147 + 7 = 154. The area of the circle is that many schoenia. <note>This method calculates the area as $3\frac{1}{7} \times r^2$.</note>

### 17. Again, in another way, we can calculate the circle from the diameter alone.
Let the diameter of the circle be 14 schoenia.
14 × 14 = 196.
1/4 of 196 = 49.
<margin>25</margin> 196 minus 49 = 147. <note>OCR says "÷", but logic requires subtraction: 196 - 49 = 147.</note>
1/21 of 147 = 7.
147 + 7 = 154. The area of the circle is that many schoenia.

### 21. Given the sum of the diameter and the perimeter of a circle.
Given that the diameter of a circle combined with its perimeter is 58 schoenia, separate them and find the length of the diameter and the perimeter.
<margin>20</margin> Proceed as follows: if you wish to find the diameter first, multiply the 58 by 7; it makes 406. Of these, take the 29th part; it makes 14. That is the diameter. Subtract these from the 58; the remainder is 44. That is the perimeter.
<margin>25</margin> If you wish to find the circumference <note>original: περιφέρειαν (*periphereian*). Heron uses this term interchangeably with "perimeter."</note> first, proceed as follows: multiply the 58 by 22; it makes 1,276. Of these, take the 29th part; it makes 44. That is the circumference of the circle. Subtract these from the 58; the remainder is 14. That is the diameter. <note>These calculations rely on the Archimedean ratio of 7 to 22 for the diameter and circumference. Since $7 + 22 = 29$, the diameter is $7/29$ of the total sum and the perimeter is $22/29$.</note>

<margin>35</margin> **35.** Given a circle of 38 1/2 units; to find its diameter.

...to find the area of the circle. Proceed as follows: since diameter

that much is the diameter.

...and to find its *perimeter*. Take the area, namely 38 1/2, [multiplied] eighty-eight times; it makes 3,388. A seventh part of these makes 484; the square root of which becomes twenty-two. The *perimeter* will be that much. <note>The formula used here is $P = \sqrt{Area \times \frac{88}{7}}$. With an area of 38.5, $38.5 \times 88 = 3388$; $3388 / 7 = 484$; $\sqrt{484} = 22$. This is the inverse of the area formula $A = \frac{P^2}{4\pi}$.</note>

<margin>23</margin> **23.** Another circle, whose diameter is 6 <term>schoenia</term>. <margin>5</margin> Therefore its perimeter—because it is three and one-seventh times the diameter—will be 18 and 6/7 schoenia. <note>original: "τριπλάσιος καὶ ἐφέβδομός" (triple and a seventh), the standard Greek expression for the ratio 22/7.</note> And since the [rectangle formed] by the diameter and the perimeter is four times the area of the circle, then the [rectangle formed] by the diameter and the fourth part of the *perimeter* will be equal to the circle. <margin>10</margin> The diameter of the circle is 6 schoenia, and 1/4 of the perimeter is 4 1/2 1/7 1/14 schoenia, or 4 schoenia and five-sevenths. These multiplied by each other make 28 1/4 1/28; and the area of the circle is that many schoenia. Half of which is the <term>modismos</term>. <note>The "modismos" refers to a calculation of grain capacity (measured in modii) based on the area of a field, a common practical application of geometry in the Roman and Byzantine periods.</note> <margin>15</margin>

<margin>24</margin> **24.** Another circle, whose diameter is 12 1/2 1/4 schoenia. To find its *perimeter*: do as follows: since the diameter is 12 schoenia and 3/4, break down the schoenia into quarters; together they make 51 quarters. Multiply these by 3; they make 153. <margin>20</margin> To these add also the 1/7 of 51, namely 7 and 2/7; the total becomes 160 and 2/7 quarters, which is 40 units and 1/14 of a unit. The perimeter is that many schoenia. <note>Heron converts the mixed fraction $12 \frac{3}{4}$ into $51/4$ to make the multiplication by $22/7$ easier. $51/4 \times 22/7 = 1122/28 = 40 \frac{1}{14}$.</note>

<margin>25</margin> **25.** To find the area of the circle from the diameter. <margin>25</margin> Proceed as follows: the 12 1/2 1/4 of the diameter squared; it makes 162 1/2 1/16. These [multiplied] eleven times; they make 1,788 1/8 1/16. A 1/14 part of these makes 127 1/2 1/7 1/14 1/112 1/224; the area of the circle is that many schoenia. <note>This uses the formula $Area = d^2 \times \frac{11}{14}$. Heron squares $12.75$ to get $162.5625$, multiplies by 11, and divides by 14 to reach approximately $127.727$. The complex series of fractions $1/2 + 1/7 + 1/14 + 1/112 + 1/224$ is the Egyptian-style unit fraction representation of $163/224$.</note>

<margin>34</margin> **Another way to find the area of a circle from the perimeter alone.** Since the perimeter of the circle is 51 <term>schoenia<note>A schoenion (plural schoenia) was a Greek unit of distance, originally a "surveyor's rope." In this context, it refers to square units when calculating area.</note></term> and 19/35 thirty-fifths, reduce the schoenia to thirty-fifths; they become altogether 1,804 thirty-fifths. Multiply these by themselves: they become 325 <term>myriads<note>A myriad (myrias) is the Greek unit for 10,000.</note></term> and 4,416. Multiply these by seven: they become 2,278 myriads and 912. The 88th part of these becomes 25 myriads and 8,874. When these are divided by 1,225 <note>original: "$\lambda\epsilon' \lambda\epsilon'$ τῶν $\lambda\epsilon' \lambda\epsilon'$" — this refers to 35 times 35, which is 1,225, the denominator used when squaring fractions of 35.</note> they become 211 1/4 1/25 1/28. Such is the area of the circle in schoenia. <margin>10</margin>

<margin>35</margin> **To find the area of the circle from the diameter and the perimeter.** Proceed as follows: take 1/4 of the perimeter, which is 12 schoenia and 31/35 thirty-fifths, and multiply them by the diameter, that is, by 16 schoenia and 14/35 thirty-fifths, as follows: 12 times 16 is 192; <margin>15</margin> 12 times 14/35 is 168 thirty-fifths; and 31/35 thirty-fifths times 16 schoenia is 496 thirty-fifths; and 31/35 thirty-fifths times 14/35 thirty-fifths results in 434 thirty-fifths of thirty-fifths, and these are 12 thirty-fifths and 14/35 thirty-fifths of thirty-fifths. Together this makes 192 schoenia, 35 thirty-fifths, <margin>20</margin> <margin>36</margin> 676 thirty-fifths and 14/35 thirty-fifths of thirty-fifths. The 676 thirty-fifths, when divided by 35, become 19 schoenia, with 11 thirty-fifths remaining. These 19 schoenia are added to the other 192, and together they become 211 schoenia, 11 thirty-fifths, and 14/35 thirty-fifths of thirty-fifths. These 14 thirty-fifths of thirty-fifths are 2/5 of 1/35. The 11 <note>This refers to 11/35 plus the additional fraction.</note> <margin>25</margin> divided by 35 become 1/4 1/25 1/28; for you say: 1/4 of 35 is 8 1/2 1/4; 1/25 of 35 is 1 1/3 1/15; and 1/28 of 35 is 1 1/4. And the area of the circle is 211 1/4 1/25 1/28 schoenia. Half of this is the <term>modismos<note>A modismos refers to a measurement in modii, a unit of capacity often used in land surveying to estimate how much seed a field would require, or as a unit of taxable land area.</note></term>. <margin>30</margin>

<summary>This page details two geometric proofs for calculating the area of a circle: first, by squaring the perimeter and applying a ratio (7/88), and second, by multiplying one-quarter of the perimeter by the diameter. Both methods yield the result of approximately 211 1/3 schoenia, demonstrating the consistency of Heron's mathematical rules.</summary>

### On Semicircles.

Let there be a semicircle or **arch**, whose perimeter <note>In this context, the perimeter refers specifically to the curved arc length, not the total boundary including the base.</note> is 11 <term>schoenia<note>A schoenion was a Greek unit of distance used in land surveying, roughly 100 to 150 feet.</note></term>, and the diameter is 7 schoenia; to find its area. Do it thus: 7 (the diameter) $\times$ 11
<margin>5</margin> (the perimeter) = 77; 1/4 $\times$ 77 = 19 1/4; of so many schoenia will the area be. And half of this is the <term>modius count<note>A "modius" (or modios) was a unit of area measurement used in Greek surveying, derived from the capacity of a grain measure; here it refers to the number of area-units.</note></term>.

<margin>2</margin>
Another semicircle or **arch**, whose base is 14 schoenia and the height is 7 schoenia; to find its
<margin>10</margin> perimeter. Do it thus: 3 $\times$ height, and add 1/7 of the height; thus you will find the perimeter. For example, let the height of the given semicircle be 7 schoenia; 3 $\times$ 7 = 21; 21 + 1/7 $\times$ 7 = 21 + 1 = 22; of so many schoenia will the perimeter of the semicircle be.

<margin>15</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
In another way. Base + height = 21; 1/21 $\times$ 21 = 1; 21 + 1 = 22; of so many schoenia will the perimeter of the semicircle be.

### On segments larger than a semicircle.

<margin>20 AO 1</margin> Let there be a **segment larger than a semicircle**, of which the base is <margin>10</margin> 12 cords <note>Original: "schoinia." A "cord" or "rope" was a standard Greek unit of land measurement, approximately 100 or 120 feet.</note> and the height is 9 cords; find its area. Proceed as follows: let the height always be extended until it meets the [opposite side of the] circle, and let it divide the cords of the base in the middle; they become 6. Multiply these by themselves; they become 36. Divide these by the <margin>15</margin> height, that is, by 9; they become 4. Therefore, the height of the smaller [complementary] segment will be 4 cords; thus the diameter of the whole circle is 13 cords <note>The diameter is the sum of the two heights: 9 + 4 = 13.</note>. If we then measure the smaller segment, whose base is 12 cords and height is 4 cords, and we also measure the circle whose diameter is 13 cords, and we <margin>20</margin> subtract the smaller segment from the circle, we will have measured the <margin>2</margin> remaining largest segment of the circle. For example: let the diameter of the whole circle be 13 cords. Multiply these by themselves; they become 169. Multiply these eleven times; they become 1,859. Take one-fourteenth of these; they become 132 $1/2$ $1/4$ $1/28$ <note>This is the Archimedean approximation for the area of a circle: $Area = \frac{11}{14} \times d^2$.</note>. <margin>25</margin> The area of the whole circle is this many cords. From these, let the area of the smaller segment be subtracted, which according to the previously set method is 34 $1/2$ $1/14$ cords; and the remainder—namely 98 $1/7$ $1/14$—shall be the area of the [larger segment]...

Subtract from this the arc of the smaller segment; the remainder will then be the arc of the larger segment.

<margin>13</margin> You will find the arc of the smaller segment in this way: Multiply the 20 of the base by 20, which is 400. Likewise, multiply the 3 1/3 of the height by 3 1/3, which is 11 1/9. Multiply [this] by four, which is 44 1/3 1/9 <note>44 4/9</note>. Then 400 plus 44 1/3 1/9 is 444 1/3 1/9. The square root of 444 1/3 1/9 is approximately 21 1/12. One-fourth of the height is 1/2 1/3 <note>1/4 of 3 1/3 is 5/6, which the Greeks wrote as 1/2 + 1/3.</note>. Then 21 1/12 plus 1/2 1/3 equals 21 1/2 1/3 1/12; this many cords will be the arc of the smaller segment.*) Subtract this from the circumference of the circle—that is, 104 1/2 1/7 1/14 1/21 minus 21 1/2 1/3 1/12—which equals 82 1/2 1/3 1/84; this many cords will be the arc of the larger segment.

<margin>A C 8</margin> If it is necessary, given some area—either a rectilinear shape <note>A shape made of straight lines, like a square or triangle.</note> or of any other kind—to create a circle equal to it, one must take 1/11 part of the area and multiply this fourteen times; then, taking the square root <note>original: πλευρὰν τετραγωνικὴν, literally "the side of the square."</note> of the result, declare the diameter of the circle to be that amount. For example: let the area of the given region be 154 units. Of these, 1/11 is 14. Multiply these fourteen times: the result is 196. Of these, the square root is 14. Therefore, the diameter of the circle will be 14 units. From the diameter, the circle is made clear from the methods described previously.

<column-break/>

<margin>9 15</margin> Given the sum of all three numbers—namely the diameter, the circumference, and the area of the circle—as a single combined number, to separate them and find each individual number. Proceed as follows: let the given number be 212 units <note>This is the sum of a circle where the diameter is 14, circumference is 44, and area is 154 (14 + 44 + 154 = 212).</note>. Always multiply this by 154: the result is 3 myriads <note>30,000</note> and 2,648. To these, add universally 841: the result is 3 myriads and 3,489. Of which the square root is 183. From these, subtract 29: the remainder is 154. Of which the 1/11 part is 14. This is the diameter of the circle. 

If you also wish to find the circumference, subtract the 29 from the 183: the remainder is 154. Multiply these twice: the result is 308. Of these, take the 1/7 part: the result is 44. This much is the circumference. To find the area, proceed as follows: the 14 of the diameter multiplied by the 44 of the circumference results in 616. Of these, take the fourth part: the result is 154. This much is the area of the circle. Added together, the three numbers equal 212 units.

### GEOMETRICA. 383

<margin>11</margin> If a circle is given within a square, and the diameter is 7 units, to find the area of the 4 pieces of the square that lie outside the circle. Proceed <margin>5</margin> as follows: multiply the 7 of the diameter by 7 = 49. Then, take the seventh part and the fourteenth part of 49 <note>original: "1/7 + 1/14"</note>, which equals 10 1/2. This will be the area of the 4 pieces of the square remaining outside the circle.

<margin>12</margin> In another way: multiply the 7 of the diameter by 7 = 49. Triple this (3 times 49) = 147. Take the fourteenth part of 147 = 10 1/2. This is the area of the 4 pieces.

<margin>10</margin> <margin>13</margin> You will find the area of each individual piece <note>meaning one of the four corners</note> as follows: half the diameter = 3 1/2. Multiply 3 1/2 by 3 1/2 = 12 1/4. Triple 12 1/4 = 36 3/4 <note>original: "36 1/2 1/4"</note>. Take the fourteenth part of 36 3/4 = 2 1/2 1/8 <note>equivalent to 2.625</note>. This is the area of each individual piece.

<margin>14</margin> An equilateral pentagon <note>a five-sided shape with equal sides</note> in which each side is 35 feet; <margin>15</margin> to find its area: I proceed as follows: 35 times 35 = 1225. Multiply 1225 by 12 = 14,700. Take the seventh part of 14,700 = 2100. The area will be that many feet.

<margin>15</margin> In another book by Heron <note>original: "Heron, Metrica p. 52, 9; Diophantus ed. Tannery II p. 18, 8"</note> it was found thus: let each side be 10 feet. 10 times 10 = 100. 5 times 100 <margin>20</margin> = 500. One third of 500 = 166 2/3. This is the size of the area.

<margin>16</margin> An equilateral hexagon <note>a six-sided shape with equal sides</note> in which each side is 30 feet; to find its area: Proceed as follows: 30 times 30 = 900. Always multiply 13 by 900 = 11,700. Take the fifth part of 11,700 = 2340. The area of the hexagon will be that many feet. <note>original footnote refers to Diophantus II p. 18, 20</note>

<margin>C</margin> ### Addition of a most illustrious theorem by Macarius. <note>Macarius was likely a later Byzantine mathematician or commentator whose work was appended to Heron's original text.</note>

<margin>28</margin> If I wish to construct an equilateral triangle <note>a triangle where all three sides are the same length</note> from a given area, I proceed as follows: multiply the proposed area by thirty, and taking a 13th part of the result, I consider this to be the multiplication of the side of the triangle by itself <term>the square of the side</term>. Then, by calculating the square root of this, I clearly have the number of the side of the equilateral triangle. <note>This formula, $side^2 = \frac{30}{13} \times Area$, is a practical approximation. The precise ratio is approximately 2.309, while 30/13 is approximately 2.307.</note>

<margin>29</margin> ### By the same author.

Further, let there be proposed to us an equilateral triangle having an altitude <term>the vertical height from base to tip</term> of 26 units. If I wish to find the length of each individual side from this, I proceed as follows: always multiply the altitude by two; then, taking a 1/3 part of the result, I add it to the units of the altitude, and thus I declare how many units the side of the triangle is. <note>Following the text’s instructions for an altitude of 26: $26 \times 2 = 52$; $1/3$ of $52$ is $17 \frac{1}{3}$; $26 + 17 \frac{1}{3} = 43 \frac{1}{3}$. Mathematically, the side should be approximately 30. This suggests the text may be corrupted or using a specific, non-standard surveying rule.</note>

<meta>This page continues the geometric definitions and calculations attributed to Heron, moving from properties of triangles and circles into a standardized list of linear measurements used in the ancient world, often attributed to Euclid.</meta>

# HERON

<margin>c</margin> In an acute-angled triangle <note>original: "ὀρθήν," though the context implies acute triangles where the square of the sides is greater than the square of the hypotenuse</note>, the two sides [forming the angle] are greater than the remaining side subtending the angle when they are multiplied by themselves <note>This is an ancient way of saying "squared."</note>.

And in every scalene obtuse-angled triangle, the two sides about the angle are less than the remaining side subtending the angle when they are multiplied by themselves.

And in every right-angled triangle, the two sides about the right angle are equal to the remaining side subtending the angle <note>The <term>hypotenuse</term>: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.</note> when they are multiplied by themselves.

<margin>10</margin> In every triangle, any two sides taken together in any combination are greater than the remaining side.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a triangle with vertices/sides labeled k, l, n. To the right of the diagram, the text reads: an impossible triangle</image-desc> <note>The text "ἀσύστατον τρίγωνον" refers to a figure where the lengths of the sides do not allow a triangle to be closed, violating the triangle inequality rule mentioned just above.</note>

And for every circle, the <term>perimeter</term> <note>The distance around the outside of the circle; the circumference.</note> is three and one-seventh times the <term>diameter</term> <note>The distance across the circle through its center.</note>.

<margin>15</margin> ## Euclidean Linear Measures.

# GEOMETRY.

[In an acute-angled triangle <note>The first line of the German text is missing the specific descriptor, but the context of the squares being "greater than" defines an acute-angled triangle.</note>, the squares of the] enclosing sides are greater than the square of the remaining, opposite side.

And in any right-angled triangle, the squares of the two sides enclosing the right angle are equal to the square of the remaining, opposite side.

**2** There are three kinds of "foot": the linear, the surface (square), and the solid (cubic). The linear foot is that which possesses length and width <note>In ancient Greek geometry, even a "linear" unit was sometimes described via its dimensions to establish its scale</note>; of this, only the length is measured. The surface foot is that which has a length of 1 foot and a width of 1 foot; by this, plane figures are measured. The solid foot has a length of 1 foot, a width of 1 foot, and a thickness of 1 foot; by this, solid shapes are measured. A solid foot holds 1 jar <note>original: "keramion," a standard liquid measure</note>, which is 3 bushels <note>original: "modioi"</note>; each bushel consists of 16 Italian pints <note>original: "xestai"</note>.

### OF HERON

[Multiply] half of the base by itself; subtract [this] from the collected [sum of the side squared] and of the remainder take the square root; this shall be the perpendicular <note>The "perpendicular" refers to the height of the triangle. Heron is describing the Pythagorean theorem applied to find the height: $h = \sqrt{side^2 - (base/2)^2}$.</note>.

**4** If we seek the area of any other triangle of whatever kind, always multiply the base by the perpendicular; <margin>5</margin> half of this shall be the area.

**5** To find the area of an **equilateral square**. [Multiply] the side by itself; and you will have the area. If [you seek] the diagonal of the same square, [multiply] twice the area; of which [take] the square root. <margin>10</margin>

**6** To find the area of an **oblong rectangle** <note>original: "heteromekes" — a four-sided figure with right angles but unequal adjacent sides.</note>. Multiply the side by the [other] side; that shall be the area. If [you seek] the diagonal of the same oblong rectangle, combine each side multiplied by itself; the square root of these shall be the diagonal. <margin>15</margin>

**7** To find the area of a **pentagon**. [Multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 5; one-third <note>original: "γ'"</note> of these shall be the area. <note>Heron uses the approximation Area $\approx 1.66 \times side^2$.</note>

**8** To find the area of a **hexagon**. [Multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 6; one-third and one-tenth <note>original: "γ' καὶ ι'"</note> of these shall be the area. <note>This equals $2.6 \times side^2$, a common ancient approximation for a regular hexagon.</note>

**9** To find the area of a **heptagon**. [Multiply] the side by <margin>20</margin> itself; multiply this by 43; one-twelfth of these shall be the area.

**10** To find the area of an **octagon**. [Multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 29; one-sixth of these shall be the area.

**11** To find the area of a **nonagon**. [Multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 51; one-eighth of these shall be the area. <margin>25</margin>

**12** To find the area of a **decagon**. [Multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 15; half <note>original: "∠'"</note> of these shall be the area. Alternatively, again: [multiply] the side by itself; multiply this by 38; one-fifth of these shall be the area. This [latter] one is more accurate.

**13** To find the area of an **hendecagon** <note>An 11-sided polygon.</note>. [Multiply] the side by <margin>30</margin> itself; multiply this by 66; one-seventh of these shall be the area.

# HERON'S GEOMETRY

<margin>14</margin> To find the area of a **dodecagon** <note>A twelve-sided regular polygon.</note>: multiply the side by itself; multiply this by 45; one-fourth <note>original: "δ'"</note> of this shall be the area. <note>This formula gives Area $\approx 11.25 \times side^{2}$. The modern value for a regular dodecagon is $\approx 11.196 \times side^{2}$.</note>

<margin>15</margin> To find the area of a **circle** from the diameter: multiply the diameter by itself; multiply this by 11; one-fourteenth <note>original: "ιδ'"</note> of this shall be the area. <note>This uses the Archimedean approximation of $\pi$ as 22/7. Since Area = $\pi r^{2}$ or $(\pi/4) \times d^{2}$, Heron uses $11/14$ as the approximation for $\pi/4$.</note>

<margin>16</margin> To find the **circumference** of a circle: triple the diameter and add one-seventh <note>original: "ζ'"</note> of the diameter; and you will have the circumference. And again in another way: having multiplied the diameter by 22, divide it; one-seventh <note>original: "ζ'"</note> of which [is the circumference].

<margin>17</margin> To find the area from the circumference: multiply the circumference by itself; multiply this by 7; eighty-eighth <note>original: "πη'"</note> [parts] of this shall be the area. <note>Mathematically, if $C = 2\pi r$, then Area $= C^{2} / (4\pi)$. Using $\pi \approx 22/7$, then $4\pi \approx 88/7$. Dividing by $88/7$ is the same as multiplying by $7/88$.</note>

<margin>18</margin> From the circumference and diameter—that is, if I combine the diameter and the circumference—to find the area: do as follows. To separate the diameter and the circumference from the [sum of] the diameter and circumference: I do as follows: [multiply] both values <note>original: "φωνὰς", literally 'voices' or 'sounds', here meaning the given numerical values.</note> by 60 <note>This 60 (ξ̅) is likely a scribal error in the manuscript for 7 (ζ̅), as the mathematical ratio for $D / (D+C)$ using $\pi = 22/7$ is $7/29$.</note> and divide; one-twenty-ninth <note>original: "κθ'"</note> of which [is the result]; you will have the diameter; and let the remainder be the circumference. Multiply half of the diameter by half of the circumference, and you will have the area.

### On semicircles.

<margin>19</margin> To find the area from the diameter: [multiply] the diameter by itself; these [times] 11; twenty-eighth <note>original: "κη'"</note> [parts] of which shall be the area. <note>This is half the area of the full circle ($11/14$), thus $11/28$.</note>

<margin>20</margin> To find the circumference <note>Here referring specifically to the curved arc of the semicircle.</note>: multiply the diameter by 22 and divide; fourteenth <note>original: "ιδ'"</note> [parts] of which shall be the circumference.

<margin>21</margin> To find the diameter from the circumference: [multiply] the circumference by 14; twenty-second <note>original: "κβ'"</note> [parts] of which shall be the diameter.

<meta>This page follows the calculations for regular polygons (pentagon, hexagon, etc.) found in Heron’s Geometrica. Here, Heron concludes the section on the twelve-sided polygon and begins a detailed series of rules for calculating the properties of circles and semicircles, utilizing the common ancient approximation of pi as 22/7.</meta>

# GEOMETRY

<margin>14</margin> To find the area of a **dodecagon** <note>A regular twelve-sided polygon.</note>: Side × side, then multiply this by 45; one-fourth <note>original: "$\frac{1}{4}$"</note> of this total shall be the area. <note>The ancient formula given here results in Area $\approx 11.25 \times side^{2}$, which is quite close to the modern value of $\approx 11.196 \times side^{2}$.</note>

<margin>15</margin> To find the area of a **circle** from the diameter: Multiply diameter × diameter, then multiply this by 11; one-fourteenth <note>original: "$\frac{1}{14}$"</note> of this shall be the area. <note>This formula represents the Archimedean approximation where the area is $11/14$ of the square of the diameter.</note>

<margin>16</margin> To find the **circumference** of a circle: 3 × diameter + $\frac{1}{7}$ diameter; in this way you will have the circumference. And again in another way: 22 × diameter, then [take] $\frac{1}{7}$ of that. <note>Both methods yield the same result, expressing the ratio of circumference to diameter ($\pi$) as 22/7.</note>

<margin>17</margin> To find the area from the **circumference**: Multiply circumference × circumference, then multiply this by 7; one-eighty-eighth <note>original: "$\frac{1}{88}$"</note> of this shall be the area. <note>Derived from the formula Area $= C^{2} / (4\pi)$. Using $\pi \approx 22/7$, then $4\pi \approx 88/7$; dividing by this is the same as multiplying by $7/88$.</note>

<margin>18</margin> To find the area from the **circumference and the diameter** together—that is, if I add the diameter and the circumference: Proceed as follows: the diameter and the circumference must be separated from the [sum]. I proceed thus: multiply the sum of both values × 7, and take $\frac{1}{29}$ of that; thus you will have the diameter; the remainder shall be the circumference. Then, $\frac{1}{2}$ diameter × $\frac{1}{2}$ circumference; thus you will have the area. <note>This uses the property that if $C = \frac{22}{7}d$, then $d + C = d + \frac{22}{7}d = \frac{29}{7}d$. Therefore, $d = (d+C) \times \frac{7}{29}$.</note>

->**On Semicircles**<-

<margin>19</margin> To find the area from the diameter: Diameter × diameter, then multiply this by 11; one-twenty-eighth <note>original: "$\frac{1}{28}$"</note> of this shall be the area. <note>Since the area of a full circle is $\frac{11}{14}d^{2}$, a semicircle is half of that: $\frac{11}{28}d^{2}$.</note>

<margin>20</margin> To find the **circumference** <note>Meaning the length of the curved arc of the semicircle.</note>: Diameter × 22, then one-fourteenth <note>original: "$\frac{1}{14}$"</note> of this shall be the circumference.

<margin>21</margin> To find the diameter from the circumference: Circumference × 14, then one-twenty-second <note>original: "$\frac{1}{22}$"</note> of this shall be the diameter.

<note>

Section 18 includes a note on "separating" the values when they are mixed (added) together. Section 21 is omitted in some versions but preserved in others.

HERON'S

22 To find the area from the perimeter <note>In this context, these formulas likely refer to a semicircle rather than a full circle, as the constants used are exactly double those used for a full circle earlier.</note>: Multiply the perimeter by itself; multiply this by 7; of which one-forty-fourth <note>original: "$\mu\delta'$"</note> shall be the area.

23 To find the perimeter from the area: Multiply the area by 44 and divide; [take] one-seventh <note>original: "$\zeta'$"</note> of this; and of the resulting <margin>5</margin> values take the square root; this shall be the perimeter.

24 To find the diameter from the area: Multiply the area by 28 and divide; [take] one-eleventh <note>original: "$\iota\alpha'$"</note> of this; and of the gathered <margin>10</margin> totals take the square root; this shall be the diameter.

## Heron’s Introductions.

<margin>23 ACS</margin>
1 Early geometry, as ancient tradition teaches us, was occupied with the measurements and divisions <margin>15</margin> of land, which is why it was called "geometry" <note>From the Greek *ge* (earth) and *metrein* (to measure).</note>. For the invention of measurement was discovered among the Egyptians because of the rising of the Nile. For many places that were visible before the rising were made invisible by the flood; many others became visible again after the water receded, and it was no longer <margin>20</margin> possible for each person to distinguish their own property. Because of this, the Egyptians invented this [method of] measurement of the land left behind by the Nile. They perform the measurement of each side of a plot of land using sometimes a so-called "rope" <term>schoinion</term> <note>A measuring cord of standard length.</note>, sometimes a "reed" <term>kalamos</term>, sometimes a "cubit" <term>pechys</term>, and <margin>25</margin> sometimes other measures. Since this practice was so necessary for mankind, the field was advanced further, so that the management of measurements and divisions even extended to solid bodies <note>Moving from 2D area (land) to 3D volume (solids).</note>.

---

Line 5: "resulting" ] found in manuscripts S and V; manuscript A uses a slightly different spelling.

## Heron's Introduction.

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>10</margin> The first geometry was concerned, as the ancient report teaches us, with the measurement and distribution of land, which is exactly why it was named "land-measuring" <note>original: "Geometrie," from the Greek words 'ge' (earth) and 'metrein' (to measure)</note>. The idea of measurement arose among the Egyptians because of the rising of the Nile; for many plots of land that
15 were visible before the rising were made invisible by the flood, and many became visible again after its sinking, and it was no longer possible for the individual to distinguish his own property; therefore the Egyptians invented the aforementioned measurement of the land left behind by the Nile. They use
20 measurement for every side of the plot, sometimes with the so-called <term>Schoinion</term> <note>A surveyor's rope used for long distances.</note>, sometimes with a <term>measuring rod</term>, sometimes with a <term>cubit</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note>, and sometimes also with other measures. And since the matter was of use to mankind, the art was further promoted, so that the procedure of measurements and distributions
25 was extended also to solid bodies.

<header>OF HERON</header>

<margin>2</margin> Therefore, for the discourse concerning measurements, it is necessary to understand the nature of the measures by which one wishes to measure, the form of every figure, and the method by which one must measure. We shall first explain the nature of the measures.

<margin>3</margin>
### Concerning Linear Measures.

Linear measurement is anything measured by length alone, such as the <term>strophioloi</term> <note>original: "στροφίολοι"; these are small moldings or pivots in decorative work</note> in marble tiling <note>original: "σκουτλώσεσιν," referring to *sectile* or inlaid marble floors</note> and <term>kumatia</term> <note>original: "κυμάτια," decorative wave-pattern moldings</note> in woodwork, and whatever else is measured by length alone.

<margin>4</margin> There are these types of measures: the <term>daktylos</term> (finger-breadth), <term>palaistēs</term> (palm), <term>dichas</term> (half-span), <term>spithamē</term> (span), <term>pous</term> (foot), <term>pygōn</term> (short cubit), <term>pēchys</term> (cubit), <term>bēma</term> (pace), <term>xylon</term> (staff), <term>orguia</term> (fathom), <term>kalamos</term> (rod), <term>akena</term> (pole), <term>amma</term> (rope), <term>plethron</term>, <term>iougeron</term> <note>The Latin *jugerum*, a unit of area roughly equal to 0.6 acres</note>, <term>stadion</term> (stadium), <term>diaulon</term> (double-stadium), <term>milion</term> (mile), <term>schoinos</term> <note>An Egyptian unit based on a knotted rope</note>, and the <term>parasangēs</term> (parasang) <note>A Persian unit of distance</note> [the smallest of these is the finger, and all smaller parts are called fractions].

<margin>5</margin> The palm, therefore, consists of 4 fingers; the half-span consists of 2 palms, which is 8 fingers.

<margin>6</margin> The span consists of 3 palms, which is 12 fingers; it is also called the [4] wood-sawing cubit.

<margin>7</margin> The foot—the one called "Royal" and "Philetaerian" <note>A Greek standard likely named after the ruler Philetaerus of Pergamum</note>—consists of 4 palms, or 16 fingers; however, the Italian foot consists of 13 1/3 fingers.

<margin>8</margin> The short cubit consists of 5 palms, or 20 fingers.

<margin>9</margin> The cubit consists of 6 palms, or 24 fingers [it is also called the wood-sawing cubit].

<margin>10</margin> The pace consists of 1 2/3 cubits, which is 10 palms or 40 fingers.

<margin>11</margin> The staff consists of 3 cubits, or 4 1/2 feet, which is 18 palms or 72 fingers.

<margin>12</margin> The fathom consists of 4 cubits, which is 6 Philetaerian feet or 7 1/5 Italian feet.

<header>GEOMETRICA.</header>

<margin>2</margin> For the study of measurements, it is necessary to understand the nature of the measures by which one intends to measure, the shape of every figure, and the method by which one should measure. First, we shall specify the nature of these measures.

<margin>3</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
## Concerning Linear Measures.

Anything that is measured by length alone is considered rectilinearly measurable, such as the <term>kraspeda</term> <note>original: "Kleiderbesätzen die Franzen" (fringes on clothing borders)</note>, the moldings in woodwork, and whatever else is measured only by its length.

<margin>4</margin>
<margin>10</margin> There are the following types of measures: the <term>daktylos</term> (inch/digit), the <term>palaistēs</term> (hand-breadth/palm), the <term>dichas</term> (forefinger-opening), the <term>spithamē</term> (span), the <term>pous</term> (foot), the <term>pygōn</term> (short cubit), the <term>pēchys</term> (cubit), the <term>bēma</term> (pace/step), the <term>xylon</term> (timber/staff), the <term>orguia</term> (fathom), the <term>kalamos</term> (rod), the <term>akena</term> (pole), the <term>amma</term> (rope), the <term>plethron</term>, the <term>iougeron</term> (jugerum), the <term>stadion</term> (stadium), the <term>diaulon</term> (double-stadium), the <term>milion</term> (mile), the <term>schoinos</term> (rope-measure), and the <term>parasangēs</term> (parasang) [the smallest of these is the <term>daktylos</term>, and all smaller units are simply called "parts"].

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>15</margin> The <term>palaistēs</term> (hand-breadth) consists of 4 <term>daktyloi</term> (inches); the <term>dichas</term> (forefinger-opening) consists of 2 hand-breadths, or 8 inches.

<margin>6</margin> The <term>spithamē</term> (span) consists of 3 hand-breadths, or 12 inches; it is also called the "wood-sawyer's cubit" <note>This term likely refers to a specialized short cubit used in carpentry.</note>.

<margin>7</margin> The so-called <term>Royal</term> or <term>Philetaeric foot</term> <note>named after Philetaerus, the founder of the Attalid dynasty of Pergamon</note> has
<margin>20</margin> 4 hand-breadths, or 16 inches; the <term>Italian foot</term>, however, consists of 13⅓ inches.

<margin>8</margin> The <term>pygōn</term> <note>a measure from the elbow to the first joint of the fingers</note> consists of 5 hand-breadths, or 20 inches.

<margin>9</margin> The <term>pēchys</term> (cubit) consists of 6 hand-breadths, or 24 inches [it is also called the wood-sawyer's cubit].

<margin>10</margin> The <term>bēma</term> (step) consists of 1⅔ cubits, 10 hand-breadths, or 40 inches.

<margin>11</margin>
<margin>25</margin> The <term>xylon</term> (timber/staff) consists of 3 cubits, 4½ feet, 18 hand-breadths, or 72 inches.

<margin>12</margin> The <term>orguia</term> (fathom) consists of 4 cubits, 6 Philetaeric feet, or 7⅕ Italian feet.

# HERO’S [MEASUREMENTS]

<margin>CS 24</margin> The uncia <note>original: "oungia"; equivalent to a Roman inch</note> consists of 1 1/3 digits.
<margin>25</margin> The palm consists of 4 digits, or 3 unciae.
<margin>26</margin> The span consists of 3 palms, or 12 digits.
<margin>27</margin> The foot consists of 4 palms, or 16 digits.
<margin>28</margin> The cubit consists of 6 palms, or 24 digits.
<margin>29</margin> The pace <note>original: "bēma"</note> consists of 10 palms, or 40 digits.
<margin>30</margin> The fathom <note>original: "orguia"</note> consists of 96 digits, or 6 feet.
<margin>31</margin> The <term>akena</term> <note>a measuring rod</note> consists of 160 digits, or 10 Philetairean feet; it is called *pertica* in Roman [Latin].
<margin>32</margin> The Greek <term>plethron</term> is 100 feet in length and 100 feet in width, forming a square.
<margin>33</margin> The Greek <term>iougeron</term> <note>the Greek equivalent of the Roman jugerum</note> is 240 feet in length and 120 feet in width, so that the square area becomes 28,800 square feet.
<margin>34</margin> The stadium consists of 6 <term>plethra</term>, or 60 <term>akenas</term>.
<margin>35</margin> The mile consists of 5,000 feet, 2,000 paces, or 500 <term>akenas</term>.
<margin>36</margin> The square uncia consists of 1 7/9 digits <note>original: "α β' ϑ'"; based on the calculation of (1 1/3) squared</note>.
<margin>37</margin> The square palm consists of 16 square digits; the solid <note>meaning "cubic"</note> palm consists of 27 cubic unciae, or 64 cubic digits.
<margin>38</margin> The square span consists of 81 square unciae, or 144 square digits; the solid span consists of 729 cubic unciae, or 1,728 cubic digits.
<margin>39</margin> The square foot consists of 144 square unciae, or 256 square digits; the solid foot consists of 1,728 cubic unciae, or 4,096 cubic digits.
<margin>40</margin> The solid cubit consists of 5,832 cubic unciae, 216 cubic palms, or 13,824 cubic digits.
<margin>41</margin> The square pace consists of 100 square palms, 900 square unciae, or 1,600 square digits.

# GEOMETRY.

<margin>24</margin> The ounce <note>original: "Unze"; equivalent to the Roman uncia</note> consists of 1 1/3 digits <note>original: "Zoll"; the Greek daktylos or finger-breadth</note>.
<margin>25</margin> The palm <note>original: "Handbreit"; the Greek palaistē</note> consists of 4 digits, or 3 ounces.
<margin>26</margin> The span <note>original: "Spanne"; the Greek spithamē</note> consists of 3 palms, or 12 digits.
<margin>27</margin> The foot consists of 4 palms, or 16 digits.
<margin>5</margin> <margin>28</margin> The cubit <note>original: "Elle"; the Greek pēchys</note> consists of 6 palms, or 24 digits.
<margin>29</margin> The pace <note>original: "Schritt"; the Greek bēma</note> consists of 10 palms, or 40 digits.
<margin>30</margin> The fathom <note>original: "Klafter"; the Greek orgyia</note> consists of 96 digits, or 6 feet.
<margin>31</margin> The <term>akena</term> <note>a measuring rod used by surveyors</note> consists of 160 digits, or 10 Philetaerian feet; it is called *pertica* in Latin.
<margin>10</margin> <margin>32</margin> The Greek <term>plethron</term> is 100 feet in length and 100 feet in width as a square.
<margin>33</margin> The Greek <term>jugerum</term> <note>a unit of land area</note> is 240 feet in length and 120 feet in width, so that its area becomes 28,800 square feet.
<margin>34</margin> The stadium consists of 6 <term>plethra</term>, or 60 <term>akenas</term>.
<margin>15</margin> <margin>35</margin> The mile consists of 5,000 feet, 2,000 paces, or 500 <term>akenas</term>.
<margin>36</margin> The square ounce consists of 1 2/3 1/9 <note>roughly 1.77</note> square digits.
<margin>37</margin> The square palm consists of 16 square digits; the cubic palm consists of 27 cubic ounces, or 64 cubic digits.
<margin>38</margin> The square span consists of 81 square ounces, or 144 square digits; the cubic
<margin>20</margin> span, however, consists of 729 cubic ounces, or 1,728 cubic digits.
<margin>39</margin> The square foot consists of 144 square ounces, or 256 square digits; the cubic foot, however, consists of 1,728 cubic ounces, or 4,096 cubic digits.
<margin>40</margin> The cubic cubit*) consists of 5,832 cubic ounces, 216 cubic palms, or 13,824 cubic digits.
<margin>25</margin> <margin>41</margin> The square pace consists of 100 square palms, 900 square ounces, or 1,600 square digits.

# HERON’S GEOMETRY

...600 feet, 400 cubits, 2,400 palms, 800 spans, 100 fathoms <note>original: *orgyiai*</note>, 60 rods <note>original: *akenai*</note>, 6 plethra, 4 plinthia.

53      A linear mile <note>original: *milion*</note> contains 72,000 digits <note>original: 62,000; likely a transcription error for 72,000</note>, 4,500 feet, 3,000 cubits, 18,000 palms, 6,375 spans, 750 fathoms, 450 rods, 45 plethra, 30 plinthia, and 7 1/2 stadia. They say the pace <note>original: *bema*</note> also contains 2 cubits, as should be understood in this context.

54      If you wish to include additional measures, the linear <term>schoinos</term> <note>an Egyptian unit of distance, literally "rope"</note>—which the Egyptians call by several names <note>the original Egyptian term is noted as corrupt in the source</note>—is equal to the <term>parasang</term> <note>a Persian unit of distance</note>. It contains 288,000 digits; this makes 12,000 cubits, 18,000 feet, 24,000 spans, 72,000 palms <note>original: 62,000</note>, 3,000 fathoms, 1,800 rods, 180 plethra, 120 plinthia, 30 stadia, and 4 miles.

->Concerning the naming of measures and weights.<-

55      Every talent has 60 minas, and the <term>mina</term> has 25 staters. The <term>stater</term> has 4 drachmas, which are units of weight <note>original: *holkai*</note>. Therefore, the talent contains 60 minas, 1,500 staters, and 6,000 drachmas. The <term>drachma</term> contains 6 obols, and the <term>obol</term> has 8 <term>chalkoi</term> <note>literally "copper pieces," the smallest unit of weight/currency</note>; thus, the drachma contains 48 chalkoi.

56      The Attic talent is equal in weight to the Ptolemaic and Antiochian talents and identical in all its numerical divisions. However, in terms of value <note>original: *dynamei*, "power" or purchasing power</note>, the Attic talent is four times the Ptolemaic according to the coinage, and one-and-one-third <note>original: *epitriton*</note> the Antiochian, while it is equal to the Tyrian talent. All other units should be understood proportionally according to the differences mentioned for the talent; for a mina will differ from a mina, a stater from a stater, and a drachma from a drachma by the same ratio as the overall difference between the talents.

57      I also know of another "wooden" talent used in Antioch...
