# HERON

57 ...which has 60 of its own unique <term>minas</term> <note>a unit of weight approximately equal to 1 pound or 430 grams</note>, nearly six times the quantity used in currency. The "wooden" weight <note>original: *xylikon*; likely a commercial standard for heavy goods like timber, as opposed to precious metals</note> used in Alexandria differs from the previously mentioned local weight by an excess of one-fifth.

58 The <term>talent</term> mentioned in Homer’s poetry was equal in value to the <margin>5</margin> <term>Daric</term> <note>a Persian gold coin named after King Darius I</note> that came later. Therefore, this gold talent weighs two Attic <term>drachmas</term> <note>the standard silver coin of Athens</note>, or 6 <term>grammata</term> <note>literally "letters"; a small unit of weight equivalent to a scruple</note>, which are clearly four <term>tetartai</term> <note>"quarters"</note>.

59 It does not escape my notice that there are many different types of drachmas. For instance, the <margin>10</margin> Aeginaean and the Rhodian mina are five times the weight of the Ptolemaic <note>the standard used in Hellenistic Egypt</note> mina, while the so-called "insular" <note>referring to the Greek islands of the Aegean</note> mina is six times larger.

60 One should use the Attic system for both weight and currency. For it is of equal value and weight <margin>15</margin> to the Italian <term>mina</term>. It consists of 25 <term>staters</term> <note>a "weight" or standard coin, usually worth two drachmas</note>, whereas the Italian <term>litra</term> <note>the Roman pound</note> consists of 24 staters. All other minas vary in weight.

61 The pound <note>litra</note> makes 12 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: *oungiai*</note> and the ounce makes 8 drachmas. The drachma consists of 3 *grammata*, and the *gramma* consists of <margin>20</margin> 2 <term>obols</term> <note>small silver coins; six obols made one drachma</note>. Furthermore, the *gramma* is divided into 3 <term>psemma</term> <note>literally "grains"</note>, while the <term>thermos</term> <note>a lupine seed used as a weight</note> is equal to 2 <term>carats</term> <note>original: *keratia*; literally "carob seeds"</note>. Thus, the pound consists of 96 drachmas, which are equal to 1,728 carats. The talent, then, is 62 1/2 pounds in currency; however, the "wooden" talent in Antioch is 375 pounds.

62 For the sake of completeness, the <term>denarius</term> <note>the standard Roman silver coin</note> is also subdivided <margin>25</margin> by the Romans into 1,252 parts. It consists of 12 parts, 4 <term>noummi</term> <note>a small Roman coin</note>, and 16 <term>assaria</term> <note>a copper coin</note>. The *noummos* has the weight of one ounce. The *assarion* is subdivided into halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths, ninths, tenths, elevenths, twelfths, sixteenths, eighteenths, <margin>30</margin> twenty-fourths, thirty-sixths, fortieths, fiftieths, and seventy-seconds. These fractional parts have their own specific names among Roman accountants.

<margin>C</margin>
### On Measures.

<margin>63</margin> The amphora <note>original: *amphoreus*; a large ceramic vessel used as a standard volume</note> is called a "measure" <note>original: *metrētēs*</note> by some; it consists of two half-amphorae, which some call jars <note>original: *kadoi*</note>, and the Romans call *urnae*. It contains 4 <term>brochoi</term> <note>a smaller liquid unit</note> and 8 <term>choes</term> <note>roughly 3 liters each</note>, which some call <term>congia</term> <note>original: *kongia*</note>, while we call them <term>kaboi</term>. The *chous* holds 6 <term>sextarii</term> <note>original: *xestai*; roughly a pint</note>, so that the amphora equals 48 <term>sextarii</term>. The Antiochian "measure" <note>metrētēs</note> is twice as large as the Italian one, plus one-sixth.

<margin>64</margin> The <term>sextarius</term> <note>original: *xestēs*</note> is divided into 2 <term>cups</term> <note>original: *kotylai*</note>, the cup into 2 <term>vinegar-cups</term> <note>original: *oxybapha*</note>, the vinegar-cup into 3 <term>cyathi</term> <note>literally "ladles"</note>, the <term>cyathus</term> <note>original: *kyathos*</note> into 4 <term>mystra</term> <note>original: *mystria*; small spoonfuls</note>, which are also called <term>listria</term>. The *mystros* or *listrion* is divided into two <term>spoonfuls</term> <note>original: *kochliaria*; literally "snail-shells"</note>. The <term>sextarius</term> is thus broken down into 96 spoonfuls. Measures for oil are similar, except that they take their starting point from the so-called <term>centenarium</term> <note>a hundred-weight unit</note>. The oil "measure" <note>metrētēs</note> has a capacity of 16 <term>dynata</term>, and it is called the <term>mo-ek-tais</term> <note>likely a phonetic corruption of *hekteis* or "sixths"</note>.

<margin>65</margin> The <term>modius</term> <note>a Roman dry measure, roughly 9 liters</note> contains two "half-sixths" <note>original: *hēmiékta*</note>; the "half-sixth" contains 4 <term>choenices</term> <note>original: *choinikes*; a daily grain ration</note>; the <term>choenix</term> contains 2 <term>sextarii</term>, so that the <term>modius</term> equals 16 <term>sextarii</term>. The small units for dry measures are the same as those for liquids. The Ptolemaic <term>medimnos</term> <note>the standard large dry unit in Egypt</note> is one-and-a-half times the Attic one and is composed of 2 old <term>artabae</term>. The <term>artaba</term> used to be 4 and 1/2 <term>modioi</term>, but now, due to Roman usage, the <term>artaba</term> is officially reckoned as 3 and 1/3.

<margin>66</margin> The Phoenician <term>koros</term> <note>a large Biblical and Phoenician unit of volume</note> is called 30 <term>sata</term>; the <term>saton</term> is 1/6 of a <term>modius</term> <note>this likely refers to a specific regional modius, as the proportions varied</note>. The <term>chous</term>, the six-sextarii measure, weighs 9 <term>pounds</term> <note>original: *litrai*</note> when holding wine, but 15 <term>pounds</term> when holding honey; indeed, every substance has a different weight for the same volume. An ounce <note>original: *ouggia*</note> of pepper contains 400 grains, and the <term>pound</term> <note>litra</note> altogether contains 5,000.

<margin>68</margin> Regarding the sowing and surveying of land, "rich soil" is the black earth that is praised by everyone, the kind that holds <margin>15</margin> rainwater. For soda-rich soil <note>original: *ennitrogeon*; land with high mineral/salt content</note>, it measures 100 iugera per one "head" <note>original: *kephalē*; a fiscal unit of taxation</note>. For a hay-meadow, it is 125 iugera per one "head." One *iugerum* has 133 1/3 cubits.

I proceed thus according to the Pythagorean method: since the first right-angled triangle discovered by Pythagoras is that with the sides 3, 4, 5, use these 3 as factors; let the first be 3 feet, the second 4 feet, the third 5 feet, but let the sum of all be 50 feet. <note>To scale the standard 3-4-5 triangle (total perimeter 12) to a perimeter of 50, one must multiply each side by $50 \div 12$, which is $4 \frac{1}{6}$.</note> Therefore, let the first side be $12 \frac{1}{2}$ feet, the second $16 \frac{2}{3}$ feet, and the third $20 \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{3}$ feet <note>The third side $20 \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{3}$ equals $20 \frac{5}{6}$.</note>; and the sum of all is 50 feet, which is the perimeter of the triangle.

### OF HERON

<margin>5</margin>...a square having 6, so that when multiplied it makes the area of a right-angled triangle. When multiplied by 36, it becomes 180 feet, and this will be the area of the right-angled triangle, of which the height is 9 feet, the base is 40 feet, and the hypotenuse is 41 feet. And I divide the 180 by 5, and it is 36, and the length <note>the square root</note> is 6. Take 1/6th of the sides, that is of the 9; it becomes $1 \frac{1}{2}$ feet. And of the 40, the 1/6th; the base becomes $6 \frac{2}{3}$ feet. And of the 41, the 1/6th; the hypotenuse becomes $6 \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{3}$ feet. <note>In Greek fractions, $1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6$. Heron is expressing $41/6$ as $6 \frac{5}{6}$.</note> Therefore the area is 5 feet. <note>original: "$\bar{\epsilon}$"</note>

<margin>10</margin> **6** A right-angled triangle, whose height is 12 feet, the base 16 feet, and the hypotenuse 20 feet; the area becomes 96 feet. To divide these among 16 men, giving each 6 feet in [the form of] right-angled triangles. I proceed <margin>15</margin> thus: divide the 96 by 6; it becomes 16 feet; of which the square root becomes 4 feet. Now I take 1/4th of the height; it becomes 3 feet; and 1/4th of the base; it becomes 4 feet; and 1/4th of the hypotenuse; it becomes 5 feet. And there will be 16 triangles having the <margin>20</margin> height of 3 feet, the base of 4 feet, the hypotenuse of 5 feet, and the area of 6 feet. <note>This demonstrates how to scale a geometric figure by the square root of the ratio of the areas ($96 \div 6 = 16$; $\sqrt{16} = 4$).</note>

**7** A right-angled triangle, whose height is 12 feet <insert>the area is 96</insert>; to find its base and the hypotenuse. I proceed thus: I add to the 12 of the height its <margin>25</margin> 1/3rd; it becomes 4 feet; together they become 16 feet. Let the base be that much, 16 feet. Again, I add to the base its 1/4th; it becomes 4 feet; together they become 20 feet. Let the hypotenuse be 20 feet. Let the area be 96 feet. <note>This is a shortcut for constructing a triangle with sides in the ratio of 3:4:5. If the height is 12 (3 units of 4), adding 1/3rd makes 16 (4 units of 4), and adding another 1/4th of that to the result makes 20 (5 units of 4).</note>

# GEOMETRY

<margin>5</margin> ...5 and a square number that contains 6, of such a kind that it can form the area of a right-angled triangle. <note>The author is looking for a scaling factor. Since $180 \div 5 = 36$ (a square number, $6^2$), the dimensions of a larger triangle can be divided by 6 to reach the desired area.</note> $5 \times 36 = 180$ feet, which is the area of a right-angled triangle whose height <term>vertical leg or kathete</term> = 9 feet, the base = 40 feet, and the hypotenuse = 41 feet. $180 \div 5 = 36$, and the square root of 36 is 6. Take $1/6$ of the sides: $1/6 \times 9 = 1 \frac{1}{2}$ feet <note>original: "$\bar{\alpha} \angle'$"</note> for the height; $1/6 \times$ <margin>10</margin> $40 = 6 \frac{2}{3}$ feet for the base; $1/6 \times 41 = 6 \frac{5}{6}$ <note>expressed as $6 + 1/2 + 1/3$</note> for the hypotenuse. The area is consequently 5 feet.

The hypotenuse is labeled $6 \frac{5}{6}$ <note>original: "ϛ̄ \angle' \gamma'"</note>. Inside the triangle is a symbol for area followed by 5 <note>original: "$\bar{\epsilon}$"</note>. Fig. 22.

**6** A right-angled triangle, whose height = 12 feet, <margin>6</margin> the base = 16 feet, and the hypotenuse = 20 feet; the area = 96 feet. To distribute this area among 16 <margin>15</margin> men, so that each receives 6 feet in the form of right-angled triangles, I proceed as follows: $96 \div 6 = 16$ feet, and the square root of 16 = 4 feet. I take $1/4$ of the height = 3 feet; $1/4$ of the base = 4 feet; $1/4$ of the <margin>20</margin> hypotenuse = 5 feet. Thus, 16 triangles are created, whose height = 3 feet, base = 4 feet, hypotenuse = 5 feet, and the area = 6 feet.

The hypotenuse is labeled 5 <note>original: "$\bar{\epsilon}$"</note>. Inside is the area symbol followed by 6 <note>original: "$\bar{\varsigma}$"</note>. Fig. 23.

**7** A right-angled triangle, whose height = 12 feet, <margin>7</margin> <margin>25</margin> and the area = 96 feet; to find its base and hypotenuse, I proceed as follows: $1/3 \times 12$ (the height) = 4; then $12 + 4 = 16$ feet, which is the base. <margin>30</margin> Then $1/4$ of the base = 4; $16 + 4 = 20$ feet, which is the hypotenuse. The area is 96 feet.

# HERON’S WORKS

<margin>8</margin>
If we are given the base of a right-angled triangle as 24 feet and we seek the height <term>kathete; the vertical leg</term> and the hypotenuse, I proceed as follows: I take 1/4 of the base; this makes 6 feet. Subtracting this leaves 18 feet; let the height be 18 feet. Again, add 1/4 of the base to the base; this makes 6 feet. Adding these together makes 30 feet; let the hypotenuse be 30 feet. The area is 216 feet <note>calculated as (18 × 24) ÷ 2 = 216</note>.

<margin>9</margin>
If you wish to find the base and the height starting from the hypotenuse, proceed as follows: if the hypotenuse is 30 feet, take 1/5 of the 30; this makes 6. The remainder is 24 feet; let the base be 24 feet. Again, from the 24 feet of the base, take 1/4; this makes 6 feet. The remainder is 18 feet; let the height be 18 feet. The area is 216 feet.

<margin>10</margin>
The area of a right-angled triangle together with its perimeter <margin>15</margin> is 280 feet. Separate the sides and find the area. I proceed as follows: always seek the factors that make up the number. The factors of 280 are: 2 times 140, 4 times 70, 5 times 56, 7 times 40, 8 times 35, 10 times 28, and 14 times 20. I considered that 8 and 35 <margin>20</margin> will fulfill the given requirement. Take 1/8 of the 280; this makes 35 feet. In every case, take a two from the 8; there remain 6 feet. Then 35 and 6 together make 41 feet. Multiply this by itself; it makes 1,681 feet. Now, 35 times 6 makes 210 feet; <margin>25</margin> always multiply this by the 8, which makes 1,680 feet. Subtract these from the 1,681; there remains 1, of which the square root is 1. Now take the 41 and subtract 1 unit; the remainder is 40; half of this <note>original: "∠´"</note> is 20. This is the height: 20 feet. <margin>30</margin> Then take the 41 again and add 1; it makes 42 feet; half of this is 21 feet. Let the base be 21 feet. <note>Heron is using an algorithmic method to find the sides of a triangle where Area + Perimeter = 280. The sides found are 20, 21, and 29. The area is 210. 210 + 20 + 21 + 29 = 280.</note>

<margin>20</margin> = 18 feet. Always take
5 minus 2 = 3, 18 + 3 = 21,
and 21 × 21 = 441. 18 ×
3 = 54 feet. Always take
8 × 54 = 432. Subtract 432 from 441 =
<margin>25</margin> 9, the square root of 9 = 3 feet.
21 minus 3 = 18, one-half × 18 =
9 feet; let the **height**
= 9 feet. Again, take 21 + 3 = 24 feet, one-half × 24 =
12; let the **base** = 12 feet. Again, 18 minus 3
<margin>30</margin> = 15; let the **hypotenuse** = 15 feet. The **area**
however = 54 feet. Add the three sides and the area;
it gives 90 feet.

### 428 OF HERON

<margin>Section 14</margin> To find the **inscribed** <term>enrolled or drawn inside another figure</term> square in a given triangle. I proceed as follows: if the triangle has a **height** <term>kathetos; the vertical side</term> of 21 feet, a **base** of 28 feet, and a **hypotenuse** <term>the diagonal side opposite the right angle</term> of 35 feet, and let a square be inscribed; find its sides. I proceed as follows: I multiply the base by the height, 21 times 28; it makes 588 feet. Then add the base and the height; together they make 49 feet. Now I divide the 588 by the 49; it makes 12 feet. Each side of the square will be 12 feet. <note>original: "φ̅π̅η̅" (588) and "μ̅θ̅" (49). The formula used here is (base × height) / (base + height) = side of inscribed square.</note>

<margin>Section 15</margin> <margin>10</margin> Let there be a square and let it have an **area** <term>embadon</term> of 100 feet; we shall find its sides. I proceed as follows: I take the **square root** <term>literally "side of the square"</term> of the 100, which is 10 feet. Let this be the side of the square.

<margin>Section 16</margin> Let there be an **oblong** <term>heteromekes; a rectangle with unequal sides</term> and let it have a length of 8 feet and an area of 40 feet; we find its side. I take the 40 and [divide by] the 8; it becomes 5 feet. Let the side be 5 feet. <note>The text notes a variation in the Greek verb tense: "we found" vs "we find" or "we shall find."</note>

<margin>Section 17</margin> Let there be a square and let it have each side at 4 feet, and let a circle be inscribed; find its **diameter**. The diameter of the circle will be found to be the same as the side of the square.

<margin>Section 18</margin> <image-desc>Figure 34: A geometric diagram showing a square with a circle circumscribed around it. The four sides of the square are each labeled with the numeral 4. Two intersecting diagonals are drawn within the square; one is labeled 5 1/2 1/14.</image-desc> Let there be a square and let it have each side at 4 feet, and let a circle be **circumscribed** <term>drawn around the outside so the corners touch the circle</term>; find its diameter. I proceed as follows: I multiply the 4 by itself; it makes 16. [I take] this twice: it makes 32. Of these I take the square root; it makes 5 1/2 1/14 feet. Let the diameter of the circle be this much. <note>Heron approximates the square root of 32 as 5 + 1/2 + 1/14. Using the Pythagorean theorem, the diameter of the circumscribed circle is the diagonal of the square: √(4² + 4²) = √32. 5 + 1/2 + 1/14 ≈ 5.57, which is a close ancient approximation of 5.656.</note>

To find the square **inscribed** <term>drawn inside so its corners touch the outer shape's edges</term> in a given triangle. I proceed as follows: let the **height** <term>kathete; the vertical side of a right triangle</term> be 21 feet, the **base** be 28 feet, the **hypotenuse** <term>the longest side opposite the right angle</term> be 35 feet, and let a square be inscribed; find its sides. I proceed as follows: base $\times$ height, i.e., 21 $\times$ 28 = 588 feet; base + height = 49 feet. Then 588 ÷ 49 = 12 feet; each side [of the square] will be 12 feet.*)

Let there be a square, and let it have an **area** <term>the total surface space</term> of 100 feet; we wish to find its sides. I proceed as follows: $\sqrt{100} = 10$ feet; let this be the side of the square.

<image-desc>Fig. 31. A square diagram with its top and right sides labeled with the Greek numeral for 10. Inside the square, the area symbol is followed by the numeral for 100.</image-desc>

<margin>16</margin>
Let there be a **rectangle** <term>literally an "oblong" or figure with unequal sides</term>, and let it have a length of 8 feet and an area of 40 feet; we find its side. I take $\frac{1}{8} \times 40 = 5$ feet; the side will be 5 feet.

<image-desc>Fig. 32. A rectangle diagram with horizontal sides labeled as 8 and vertical sides labeled as 5. The interior is marked with the symbol for area and the numeral 40.</image-desc>

<margin>20</margin>
Let there be a square, and let it have each side be 4 feet, and let a circle be inscribed within it; find its diameter. The diameter of the circle will be found to be as large as the side of the square is. <note>Since the circle fits perfectly inside the square, its width (diameter) matches the square's side.</note>

<margin>18</margin>
Let there be a square, and let it have each side be 4 feet, and let a circle be **circumscribed** <term>drawn around the outside so it touches the corners</term> about it; find its diameter. I proceed as follows: $4 \times 4 = 16$; $2 \times 16 = 32$; $\sqrt{32} = 5 \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{14}$ feet; let this be the diameter of the circle. <note>The diameter of a circle drawn around a square is equal to the square's diagonal. The calculation $\sqrt{32}$ results in approximately 5.656; the ancient approximation $5 \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{14}$ equals approximately 5.57.</note>

<margin>19</margin> Let there be an **oblong rectangle** <term>heteromekes; a four-sided figure where one pair of sides is longer than the other</term> and let it have a length of 4 feet and a side of 3 feet, and let a circle be inscribed within it; find its diameter. <margin>20</margin> A right-angled triangle, of which the **height** <term>kathete; the side perpendicular to the base</term> is 3 feet, the base is 4 feet, and the **hypotenuse** <term>the side opposite the right angle</term> is 5 feet; find the sides of the square inscribed within it. Then I take one-seventh of the 12; it becomes 1 1/2 1/7 1/14 feet. <note>original: "$\overline{\alpha} \angle' \overline{\zeta}' \iota\delta'$"; Heron calculates the side of the square using the formula (base × height) / (base + height). 12/7 equals 1 and 5/7, which is expressed here as the sum of unit fractions: 1 + 1/2 + 1/7 + 1/14.</note>

<margin>21</margin> In a right-angled triangle, the height is 15 feet, the base is 20 feet, and the hypotenuse is 25 feet. The outer sides take the same calculations plus their 1/3 and 1/9. <note>original: "$\gamma' \vartheta'$"; Heron is explaining how the larger triangle scales proportionally based on the added 2-foot margin.</note>

<margin>22</margin> Let there be a right-angled triangle ABC, and let <margin>20</margin> the height BD be drawn. Segment AD multiplied by segment CD makes the same area as the height BD multiplied by itself <note>This is the Geometric Mean Theorem: the altitude squared equals the product of the segments of the hypotenuse.</note>, and segment AD multiplied by segment CA makes the same area as the side AB multiplied by itself.

<margin>6</margin> ...6, 9 feet. And I multiply the 21 by the 12; it makes 252 feet. Now I divide by the 9; it makes 28 feet. Let this be the base, and let the **hypotenuse** <term>the longest side of a right-angled triangle</term> be 35 feet. <note>This text appears to be the conclusion of a problem from the preceding page involving proportional sides.</note>

<margin>24</margin> Consider an equilateral triangle having each side equal to 30 feet, and let a square be inscribed within it; find its sides as follows. I seek the **altitude** <term>original: "kathete"; the vertical height from the base to the top peak</term> of the triangle; it comes to 26 feet. <note>For a side of 30, the exact altitude is $15\sqrt{3} \approx 25.98$; Heron rounds to 26 for simplicity.</note> Add this to the 30 feet of the side; it makes 56 feet. Then I multiply the side by the altitude; it makes 780 feet. Now I divide [780] by the 56; it makes 13 1/2 1/6 1/14 1/21 feet. <note>Heron expresses fractions as a sum of unit fractions. $13 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/14 + 1/21$ equals $13 \text{ and } 11/14$. The precise formula $(base \times height) / (base + height)$ yields $13 \text{ and } 13/14$.</note> The side of the square will be this many feet.

<margin>25</margin> Likewise, for every triangle that has an inscribed square, the same method holds: multiply the base by the altitude, then add the base and the altitude together, and divide the **product** <term>original: "embadon"; while this usually means "area," here it refers to the product of base and height</term> [by that sum]; and you will have the sides of such a square.

<margin>26</margin> Let there be a right-angled triangle having an altitude of 6 feet, a base of 8 feet, and a hypotenuse of 10 feet, and let a circle be inscribed within it; find its diameter. I proceed as follows: I add the altitude and the base; they make 14 feet. From these I take away the hypotenuse; 4 feet remain. Let the diameter of the circle be 4 feet. <note>This follows the geometric rule that for a right triangle, the diameter of the inscribed circle equals $(a + b) - c$.</note>

<margin>27</margin> And again, find the diameter of the inscribed circle by another way. I proceed as follows: the area of the triangle is 24 feet; I take this four times; it makes 96 feet. Now add the three sides of the triangle together; they make 24 feet. Now I divide the 96 feet by the 24; it makes 4 feet. Let the diameter of the circle be 4 feet. <note>This alternative method uses the formula $Diameter = (4 \times Area) / Perimeter$.</note>

Consider an equilateral triangle where each side is 30 feet, with a square inscribed within it. To find its sides, proceed as follows: I seek the **altitude** <term>original: "kathete"; the vertical height from the base to the top peak</term> of the triangle; it is 26 feet. <note>For a triangle with side 30, the true altitude is approximately 25.98 feet; Heron rounds to 26 for ease of calculation.</note> Add the altitude of 26 to the side of 30 = 56 feet. Another way to find the diameter of the inscribed circle: I do as follows: the **area** <term>original: "Flächeninhalt"</term> of the triangle is 24 feet; multiply 4 × 24 = 96 feet. Then add the three sides of the triangle together, which gives 24 feet. Then 96 ÷ 24 = 4 feet; let the diameter of the circle be 4 feet. <note>This second method relies on the geometric principle that the diameter of an inscribed circle equals four times the area divided by the perimeter.</note>

<margin>28</margin>
If a triangle is **right-angled** <term>original: "orthogonion"; a triangle with one 90-degree angle</term>, and a circle has been **circumscribed** <term>drawn around the outside so it touches every corner</term> about it, what will be the length of its diameter? <margin>29</margin>
Consider an **isosceles triangle** <term>a triangle with two equal sides</term> having legs of 15 feet each and a base of 18 feet, and let a circle be **inscribed** <term>drawn inside so it touches every side</term>; find its diameter. I do it as follows: the **area** <term>original: "embadon"</term> of the triangle is 108 feet; multiply this by 4, which becomes 432 feet. Now add the three sides of the triangle together; they become 48 feet. Now I divide the 432 by the 48; it becomes 9 feet. Let the diameter of the circle be 9 feet. <note>Heron uses the formula: Diameter = (4 × Area) / Perimeter.</note>

<margin>30</margin>
Consider an isosceles triangle having legs of 15 feet each and a base of 18 feet, and let a circle be circumscribed; find its diameter. It is clear that the **altitude** <term>original: "kathetos"; the vertical height from base to peak</term> of the triangle is 12 feet. <note>Calculated via the Pythagorean theorem: $\sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = 12$.</note> Now I divide the 225 by the 12; it becomes 18 1/2 1/4 feet. <note>18.75 feet.</note> Let the diameter of the circle be of this amount.

# HERON'S GEOMETRY

<margin>Section 40</margin> ...of the remaining circle <note>This sentence continues from a previous page describing the area of a circle inscribed in a square.</note> **[of 38 1/2 feet]** into the given square.

<margin>40</margin> Alternatively, to find the area of the circle starting from the area of the square: I proceed as follows. Square the side of 7; it becomes 49. Subtract from the 49 its 7th part <note>original: "ζ'"; 1/7 of 49 is 7</note> and its 14th part <note>original: "ιδ'"; 1/14 of 49 is 3 1/2</note>. This makes 10 1/2. <margin>5</margin> The remainder is 38 1/2. Let the area of the circle be this many feet. 

But if the area of the circle is 38 1/2 feet, and you wish to find the area of the outer square, proceed as follows: take the 4th part <note>original: "δ'"; 1/4 of 38 1/2 is 9 5/8</note> and the 44th part <note>original: "μδ'"; 1/44 of 38 1/2 is 7/8</note> of 38 1/2. These together make 10 1/2 feet. <margin>10</margin> Add these to the 38 1/2. It becomes 49. Let the area of the outer square be 49 feet. 

If you wish to find the diameter of the circle from the 49, you take the 49, of which the square root is 7 feet. Let the diameter of the circle and the side of the square be 7 feet.

<margin>41</margin> Let there be a circle whose diameter is 28 feet and the <margin>15</margin> perimeter is 88 feet, and the area is 616 feet. From this, you wish to determine an **octahedron** <term>original: "ὀκτάεδρον"; likely a scribal error for an octagon or a specific division of the circle into eight parts</term>. I proceed as follows: half of the diameter; it becomes 14 feet. Multiply the 14 by 11; it becomes 154 feet. Take half of these; it becomes <margin>20</margin> 77 feet. Multiply this eight times; it becomes 616 feet; which was to be found.

<margin>42</margin> Method to find the perimeter if you have the area of a circle. Proceed as follows: if the area is 154 feet, multiply the area by 88; it becomes 13,552 feet. <margin>25</margin> Take the 7th part of these <note>The OCR reads "ξ'" (60), but the mathematical context and typical Heronian methods require "ζ'" (7)</note>; it becomes 1,936 feet. The square root of this is 44 feet. Let the perimeter be 44 feet.

# GEOMETRY

...this is the area of the circle that is inscribed in the square given to me. <note>The start of this page completes a calculation from the previous page, determining the area of a circle based on a square with side length 7.</note>

<margin>40</margin> Again, to find the area of the circle from the square in another way. I proceed as follows: $7 \times 7 = 49$. 
<margin>5</margin> Take $1/7 \times 49 + 1/14 \times 49 = 10 \frac{1}{2}$. Subtract this from 49: $49 - 10 \frac{1}{2} = 38 \frac{1}{2}$; <note>The original German OCR uses a division symbol, but the mathematical logic requires subtraction of these parts (1/7 and 1/14) from the square's area.</note> let this be the area of the circle. 

If, however, the area of the circle is $38 \frac{1}{2}$ feet, and you wish to find the area of the outer 
<margin>10</margin> square, proceed as follows: 
take $1/4 \times 38 \frac{1}{2} + 1/44 \times 38 \frac{1}{2} = 10 \frac{1}{2}$ feet. 
Then $38 \frac{1}{2} + 10 \frac{1}{2} = 49$; let the area of the outer square be $49$ feet. <note>This uses the ratio of 11:14 for the area of a circle to its circumscribed square, derived from $\pi \approx 22/7$.</note>

If you then wish to find the diameter of the circle from the 49 feet, 
<margin>15</margin> take the square root: $\sqrt{49} = 7$; let the diameter of the circle and the side of the square be $7$ feet.

<margin>20</margin> area is $616$ feet <note>See the method of circle calculation in the preceding description</note>; from this, you wish to take an eighth-sector. <term>eighth-sector: a portion of the circle equal to one-eighth of its total area, treated here as a triangle for calculation purposes.</term> 

I proceed as follows: $1/2 \times \text{diameter} = 14$ feet. 
<margin>25</margin> Multiply $14 \times 11 = 154$ feet. Take half of this: $1/2 \times 154 = 77$ feet. 
Then $8 \times 77 = 616$ feet; which was what we sought to find.

<image-desc>A circle with a horizontal diameter line. Above the circle is the Greek numeral π η (88), representing the circumference. Inside the upper semi-circle is written χ ι ς (616), the area. Below the diameter line is κ η (28), the diameter. Below the diagram is the caption "Fig. 55."</image-desc>

A method for when you wish to find the circumference of a circle from its area. Proceed as follows: if the 
<margin>30</margin> area is $154$ feet, take $154 \times 88 = 13552$ feet. Then $1/7 \times 13552 = 1936$ feet. The square root $\sqrt{1936} = 44$ feet; let the circumference be $44$ feet. <note>This formula is derived from the relationship: Circumference $= \sqrt{\text{Area} \times 4\pi}$. Using $\pi = 22/7$, this becomes $\sqrt{\text{Area} \times 88/7}$.</note>

# OF HERON

<margin>S 43</margin>
*If you wish to combine the diameter and the perimeter* <note>In ancient mathematics, "mixing" or "combining" refers to adding the numerical values of different types of measurements, such as a length and a circumference.</note> *and you wish to separate the diameter from the perimeter, you proceed as follows: if both together are 58 feet, always multiply the 58 by 7; it makes 406 feet. Now I divide [this] by 29; it makes 14 feet. Let the diameter be 14 feet and the perimeter 44 feet. Together they make 58 feet; let the circle be of such dimensions.* <note>Heron uses the ratio of 29:7 for the sum of the perimeter and diameter. This is derived from $\pi + 1$, where $\pi$ is $22/7$. $(22/7 + 7/7 = 29/7)$.</note> <margin>5</margin>

<margin>44</margin>
*If you wish to find the perimeter from the diameter, if the diameter is 14 feet, always multiply the diameter by 22; it makes 308 feet. Now I divide [this] by 7; it makes 44 feet. Let the perimeter be 44 feet.* <margin>10</margin>

<margin>45</margin>
*In another way again: if the diameter is 14 feet, always make the diameter triple; it makes 42. And a 7th part of the diameter [is] 2 feet. Add these to the 42; together it makes 44. Let the perimeter be 44 feet.* <note>This is a simplified way of calculating $3 \frac{1}{7}$ times the diameter.</note> <margin>15</margin>

<margin>46</margin>
*If I combine the diameter, the perimeter, and the area of the circle, and having combined them I find the sum of the amounts to be the number 212 feet, we shall separate each number from one another.* <note>This is a complex problem equivalent to a quadratic equation: $Area + Perimeter + Diameter = 212$.</note> <margin>20</margin> *I proceed as follows: I multiply the 212 by the number 154 as a general rule; it makes 32,648. To these I add 841 as a general rule; together it makes 33,489. Of these, always take the square root; it makes 183 feet. And from these subtract 29 as a general rule; the remainder is 154. An 11th part of which makes 14 feet. Let the diameter be of so many feet, and the...* <note>The text follows a specific geometric formula for solving the quadratic $11/14d^2 + 22/7d + d = 212$. The result, 14, is the correct diameter for a circle where the area (154), perimeter (44), and diameter (14) sum to 212.</note> <margin>25</margin>
